Democratic Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek defended his attendance record after being called out by his opponent, Republica...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Democratic Iowa State Rep. Josh Turek defended his attendance record after being called out by his opponent, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, R-Iowa, during a Tuesday night debate for the state's open Senate seat.

Hinson remarked on Turek's absences while responding to a question posed to both candidates about Iowa's rising cancer rates.

"You have to show up to vote for things like pediatric cancer research, and I've invested in legislation to make sure that we're redirecting those resources to get to where it needs to go to help get to the bottom of this cancer crisis," Hinson said.

As Fox News Digital first uncovered, Turek missed 261 votes in Iowa's state legislature from Jan. 12, 2026, through May 3, representing nearly 58% of the total votes during that time.

The debate's moderator asked Turek directly why he missed the votes.

DEM SENATE HOPEFUL RIPPED AS 'ABSENTEE LEGISLATOR' AFTER MISSING NEARLY 60% OF VOTES

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson, right, speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)

"I have gone out there, and I have met with Iowans all over the state, all 99 counties, hundreds of public forums," Turek responded.

FOX NEWS POLL: TUREK, HINSON IN CLOSE IOWA SENATE RACE

"Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's decided to run for U.S. Senate, has not done one in-person town forum. Also, in my first three years in the legislature, [I had] more than a 90% attendance record," Turek continued.

"I want to ask again, though, why did you miss those votes?" the moderator repeated.

MEDIA NARRATIVE PREDICTING BLUE WAVE IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE NOT MESHING WITH LOCAL REPUBLICANS: 'FIRED UP'

Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek speaks during a televised debate with Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)

"I'm out campaigning. I'm out meeting Iowans all over all 99 counties. I've done hundreds of in-person town halls. Meanwhile, Ashley Hinson, since she's running for the U.S. Senate, has not done a single in-person town hall," he said.

Hinson objected to the notion that she hasn't done any town halls during the campaign cycle.

FOX NEWS POLL: A CLOSE SENATE CONTEST IS BREWING IN IOWA

"I've done more town halls than the percentage of time he showed up to work this year. 42% of the time is all Rep. Turek showed up to work this year. That's two out of every five days of work," Hinson said.

"Iowans, if you're watching tonight, you should know if you don't show up to work two out of five days, you're not getting a promotion. You're getting fired. I am proud of my bipartisan record working with both parties to get things across the finish line. I rank in the top 20% of bipartisan lawmakers in Congress and I have a 99% attendance record even while running a statewide campaign," she concluded.

OBAMA ENDORSES DEMOCRATIC IOWA STATE REP RUNNING FOR US SENATE AGAINST TRUMP-BACKED HOUSE REPUBLICAN

Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Ashley Hinson speaks during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Josh Turek at WHO 13, Tuesday, Oct. 13, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (AP Photo/Charlie Neibergall)

Turek, before the moderator moved on, chimed in, adding, "She also missed 193 votes."

A spokesperson for the Hinson campaign clarified to Fox News Digital that the 193 votes Hinson missed accounted for her entire time in Congress, while the 261 votes Turek missed were in the 2026 legislative session alone.

IOWA GOP GOVERNOR NOMINEE RECOUNTS VIRAL CLASH THAT PUT OBAMA ON THE SPOT AT 2009 TOWN HALL

The Hinson campaign also disputed the idea that she hasn't held any town halls.

"Since being elected to Congress, Ashley Hinson has held 47 in-person town halls and more than 30 telephone town halls — speaking directly to Iowans about the issues that matter most to them," Billy Fuerst, the Hinson campaign communications director, told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP-BACKED IOWA US SENATE HOPEFUL SAYS IRAN WAR MUST 'BE BROUGHT TO A SUCCESSFUL AND IMMEDIATE END'

"Ashley has a 98.8% lifetime voting record while Josh Turek registered a 42% voting record in the State House this year. Ashley missed 16% (94 of 553) of committee amendment votes over the course of her congressional tenure, but has been present for all final passage votes (final passage votes include the amendment language) in her time on the Appropriations Committee — 70 total bills since 2021," Fuerst concluded.

Rep. Turek and his campaign did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital for comment.

Fox News Digital's Leo Briceno contributed to this report.

NHL players and Olympic gold medalists Brady and Matthew Tkachuk discuss the pride of representing the USA in sports. They reflect on their Olympic hockey wins and offer advice to the current US soccer team in the World Cup.

The Tkachuk brothers have already shown what they can do on the global stage, but now, Matthew and Brady have the ability to wow the league more often.

After helping Team USA win Olympic gold together earlier this year, Brady was traded to his brother's Florida Panthers, who won the Stanley Cup in the two seasons before the Carolina Hurricanes took home the hardware last season.

When the move was made, hockey fans knew it was a matter of when, not if, the brothers would create magic together.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Brady Tkachuk is congratulated by his brother Matthew Tkachuk after scoring a goal during the second period against the Columbus Blue Jackets at Nationwide Arena in Columbus, Ohio, on Oct. 13, 2026. (NHLI via Getty Images)

In just their seventh game of the season, Brady scored a hat trick on Tuesday night, with each of his goals being assisted by Matthew, who had two other assists on the night. Brady also had an assist, meaning the brothers combined for nine points in Florida's 7-3 win over the Columbus Blue Jackets.

All of Brady's goals came within 8:03 of ice time in the second period.

Brady Tkachuk became the ninth Panthers player with three goals in a period. He also had four points in the second as the brothers became the third and fourth Florida players with a four-point period.

Matthew Tkachuk and Brady Tkachuk of the Florida Panthers skate during the third period against the Carolina Hurricanes at Lenovo Center in Raleigh, N.C., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Jared C. Tilton/Getty Images)

PHILADELPHIA SPORTS HIT ROCK BOTTOM AS EAGLES, PHILLIES, FLYERS ALL ARE HAVING ABYSMAL OCTOBER

Brady became the ninth player in NHL history to have a hat trick in which each goal was assisted by his brother, and the first since Daniel Sedin got help from his brother, Henrik, in 2015.

The Tkachuks teamed up for the first time in the 4 Nations Face Off in 2025, where each brother got into a fight within the first three seconds of their game against Canada. It was the first time international hockey had been played in a best-on-best format since the 2014 Sochi Olympics.

United States' Brady Tkachuk (7) and Matthew Tkachuk (19) celebrate after the United States' win over Canada in the men's ice hockey gold medal game at the 2026 Winter Olympics in Milan, Italy, Sunday, Feb. 22, 2026. (AP Photo/Carolyn Kaster)

Canada won that tournament with an overtime gold medal game, but the United States got the ultimate revenge in February, taking home its first gold medal since 1980.

articles.title: Jamaica accepts first flight of third-country deportations from US amid looming Supreme Court battle
articles.excerpt:
Third-country nationals from the United States arrived in Jamaica Tuesday under a new agreement. (Associated Press)

Jamaica began receiving third-country deportations from the U.S. this week, with th...
articles.body_text:
Third-country nationals from the United States arrived in Jamaica Tuesday under a new agreement. (Associated Press)

Jamaica began receiving third-country deportations from the U.S. this week, with the first flight of migrants arriving on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump's administration has used the third-country policy to deport migrants who claim that their home countries are too dangerous to return to.

Tuesday's flight saw 22 migrants land at Kingston’s Norman Manley International Airport in Jamaica.

VENEZUELANS, CUBANS, COLOMBIANS ARRIVE IN AFRICAN NATION UNDER TRUMP DEPORTATION DEAL

A plane carrying deportees from the United States arrives at Roberts International Airport, Harbel, near Monrovia, Liberia, August 20, 2026. (REUTERS/Carielle Doe)

Jamaican authorities signed a Memorandum of Understanding with the U.S. in June to allow transfers to begin. The agreement caps the number of migrants arriving to 25 "per fortnight."

Jamaica's Ministry of National Security and Peace and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade released a joint statement clarifying the new program on Tuesday, according to NBC News.

LIBERIA AGREES TO ACCEPT 1,200 THIRD-COUNTRY DEPORTEES FROM US WITHIN A YEAR

"The government reiterates that this is a transit arrangement intended to facilitate the return of Third Country Nationals to their country of origin or other receiving countries, with the support of the IOM (International Organization for Migration)," the statement read.

President Donald Trump’s administration secured an interim Supreme Court victory allowing it to continue third-country deportations while the legal battle plays out. (Getty Images)

"The arrangement will not be funded by the Government of Jamaica," it continued. "No third-country national with criminal antecedents will be permitted to transit through Jamaica."

FEDERAL APPEALS COURT DEALS BLOW TO TRUMP DEPORTATION AGENDA

Third-country deportations have faced heavy attacks from critics of the Trump administration, and the Supreme Court is set to consider the legality of the policy in December.

The Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration in September to continue its deportations while the question is being litigated.

TRUMP PLANS TO DEPORT IRANIANS TO VIOLENCE-PLAGUED CENTRAL AFRICAN NATION IN NEW DEAL

Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson said they would have denied the administration's request for a stay.

The U.S. Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration to continue third-country deportations while the justices consider a legal challenge to the policy. (Getty Images)

The decision gives the administration the immediate relief it sought as it presses ahead with third-country removals, even as the Supreme Court has yet to decide whether the policy remains.

The dispute centers on the Trump administration's efforts to remove illegal aliens to third countries. Lower courts have not categorically prohibited those removals but have required procedures intended to give aliens an opportunity to raise claims that they could face persecution or torture in the destination country.

Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

articles.title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
articles.excerpt:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased t...
articles.body_text:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.

The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.

Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher gasoline prices which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

The elections are being fought over cost of living pressures across the US.

Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increase over time.

For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.

Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).

It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.

The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.

There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.

If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.

Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.

Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise

Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.

Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.

Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by gasoline prices.

Car fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.

In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau or Labor Statistics.

Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.

Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.

At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.

Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by the same amount - 3.6% - in 2027.

The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.

The cost of living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72m people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.

Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.

While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.

Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.

In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.

Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.

Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.

While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.

During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.

Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.

Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.

It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.

A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.

Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.

Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect prices to fall further. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine?

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

articles.title: What led Manchester United’s Martinez to meltdown in Madrid – all to know
articles.excerpt:
Manchester United’s season plunged to a new low on Tuesday.

A third-place finish last season after a late charge under manager Michael Carrick gave Manchester United fans reasons to dream of a bright...
articles.body_text:
Manchester United’s season plunged to a new low on Tuesday.

A third-place finish last season after a late charge under manager Michael Carrick gave Manchester United fans reasons to dream of a bright 2026-27 campaign.

But just two months in, hopes of a title charge or a top-four finish seem out of reach, with United registering their worst start to a football season in 40 years.

Their latest defeat – a 2-0 reverse at Atletico Madrid in the Champions League – is the third in five winless matches, and promoted centre-back Lisandro Martinez to blast the club’s board for a lack of support for the squad.

So where did it all go wrong for Man United? Al Jazeera explains:

When United lost to newly-promoted Hull City on the opening day of the top-flight season, the humiliating result gave supporters a glimpse of the disaster that would follow.

Of their nine matches across all competitions to date, United have won just two: August’s come-from-behind victory at home over Ipswich Town in the league, and the Champions League thrashing of Azerbaijani club Sabah last month.

A controversial Manchester derby defeat to Man City left a bitter taste, but the team had no excuses when they suffered a third-round League Cup exit to fellow league side Brighton & Hove Albion.

Then came identical 1-1 draws with Fulham and Tottenham Hotspur, two teams that are in the relegation zone.

The issues in United’s squad spread across departments, with the team failing to show any real urgency.

Sitting in 12th place, United’s points tally of six is their lowest total after six games since 1986.

United avoided a crisis at Craven Cottage in their last league game before the extended international break with a draw, needing a late equaliser to avoid a third consecutive defeat.

That dispiriting performance drew harsh words from pundits and ex-players, including Gary Neville, who particularly criticised the team’s second-half effort, calling it “absolutely pathetic”.

United boss Carrick, though, struck a defiant tone, trying his best to silence the noise surrounding one of the biggest clubs in world football.

“It’s not been ideal. It was always going to come at some point, and it’s come at the start of the season,” Carrick said.

The doom and gloom continued when United blew a late lead against 10-man Tottenham to draw 1-1 at Old Trafford on Saturday.

Carrick’s men were booed off at half-time and at the end of the match after a Tottenham side that began the day bottom of the table dominated for large spells.

“Obviously, it hurts, you know, it hurts a lot,” said Carrick, addressing the boos.

“It’s not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it. That’s how it is, you know. It’s coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it.”

The 45-year-old former United midfielder was expected to build on last season’s optimism during his spell as interim boss. But having hauled United from the wreckage of Ruben Amorim’s reign, Carrick is in danger of losing his way in his first season as permanent boss.

In the summer transfer window, United brought in three talented midfielders: Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos, and Youri Tielemans, as well as a backup goalkeeper, Karl Darlow. That cost them 155 million British pounds ($204m) and raised the question: should United have spent more?

The club’s decision not to buy an established left-back and a reliable striker left unresolved gaps in the squad, forcing the team to rely on makeshift options.

This was seemingly at the heart of Martinez’s Tuesday tirade in the Spanish capital.

“I expect more from our technical director [Jason Wilcox], I have to be honest, as players we have to do more. But it is also important when you make a strong squad to be ready for these kinds of nights,” the Argentina international defender said.

Away from the first team, transfer mania made news in the youth setup, but for the wrong reasons.

JJ Gabriel, widely considered one of football’s most exciting youth prospects, said he wants to leave the club and handed in a letter of de-registration. However, British media reported the club has no intention of granting that request and is hopeful a resolution can be found.

Recipient of the Premier League under-18 player of the year award last term, the promising winger has since drawn the interest of Europe’s top clubs such as Barcelona, Paris Saint-Germain and Bayern Munich.

Last month, United reported that their annual net loss increased by almost one third to 43 million pounds ($57m) despite record-breaking revenues.

The Old Trafford club reported 677.6 million pounds ($890.7m) in revenue in the year to June 30, up 1.7 percent.

However, the club announced a seventh straight annual loss after taxes as co-owner Jim Ratcliffe’s cuts to operating costs offset contractual payments to sacked manager Amorim and a big increase in loan repayments.

The club’s debt remains over one billion pounds ($1.3bn) despite record revenues that are unable to prevent losses at the UK football side.

British billionaire Ratcliffe has overseen wide-ranging, and often unpopular, cost-cutting measures, including widespread job cuts and increased ticket prices, after completing a deal to buy a minority stake in the club in February 2024.

Away from football, Ratcliffe has also sparked controversy with his latest comments about immigration, which prompted Manchester United’s Muslim Supporters’ Club (MUMSC) to call for his resignation.

In February, the 73-year-old Ratcliffe said the United Kingdom had been “colonised by immigrants” and later apologised if he offended anyone. He doubled down on those comments in a BBC interview, saying the country “is on the slide” because of it.

The MUMSC condemned Ratcliffe’s words earlier in the year and once again spoke out against his latest comments, describing them as “deeply disappointing”.

It wasn’t the first time the United faithful expressed their frustration – before losing to Man City, fans protested against the current ownership with a banner that read “the way you treat us is a disgrace”.

articles.title: Foul-mouthed anti-war protesters repeatedly derail Hegseth's remarks at Army event in DC
articles.excerpt: Demonstrators disrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s appearance at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference in Washington, where senior military leaders gathered to discuss the Pe...
articles.body_text:
Demonstrators disrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s appearance at the Association of the United States Army’s annual conference in Washington, where senior military leaders gathered to discuss the Pentagon’s plans for autonomous warfare.

Protesters repeatedly interrupted War Secretary Pete Hegseth’s headline appearance at the Army’s biggest annual conference on Wednesday, calling him a "war criminal" and a "coward" in protest of the Iran war.

At least five times in the first half hour of a panel, foul-mouthed anti-war protesters shouted at Hegseth, calling him a "f---ing Nazi" among other insults.

Hegseth responded with chuckles and sarcastic comments, at first — but his reactions became increasingly short and irritated as he slammed the "semi-coordinated" attack as one-by-one protesters emerged among the crowd in Washington, D.C.

A protestor is removed after interrupting a discussion with U.S. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth during the U.S. Army's 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center on October 14, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Secretary Hegseth participated in a discussion on the future of autonomous warfare. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)

PETE HEGSETH HEADS TO CAPITOL HILL TO DEFEND TRUMP'S IRAN WAR AS 60-DAY CONGRESSIONAL DEADLINE LOOMS

"You’re not a warrior you’re a coward!" one demonstrator shouted at Hegseth.

"She thinks highly of me," the Pentagon chief quipped after one outburst, which led to brief applause from the crowd.

The protesters were spread among the room and waited a few minutes between outbursts to interrupt the panel with their anti-war messages.

As Hegseth saw a pattern emerging among the outbreaks, he acknowledged: "Appears we have a bit of a tactic."

The demonstrators were forcibly removed by security for the event — with at least one woman needing to be carried out of the room by multiple officers while she continued to scream her protest.

A protestor is removed by security personnel as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)

The panel with Hegseth included acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink and assistant Secretary for Special Operations and Low-Intensity Conflict Derrick Evans.

As the disruptions continued, the speakers stopped pausing amid the din of shouting and tried to talk over the protesters.

It’s unclear how the protesters received credentials to attend the event known as AUSA, which brings together Army brass and the defense contractors that service them.

EMERGING TECH HAS NEW ARMY LEADERS WARNING TROOPS CAN'T ‘AI’ THEIR WAY TO VICTORY ON THE BATTLEFIELD

A protestor is removed by security personnel as Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., on October 14, 2026. The AUSA Meeting and Exposition is a defense trade show and networking event for the global defense community. (Jim WATSON/AFP via Getty Images)

The panel focused on Project Agincourt, the Pentagon’s initiative to accelerate the development and deployment of autonomous weapons and military systems.

Hegseth joined senior leadership from the service branches to discuss how the military plans to integrate drones, robotics and other autonomous technologies.

articles.title: Burnham says he wants to 'repair bridges' between Ukraine and US
articles.excerpt:
Burnham met Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of...
articles.body_text:
Burnham met Zelensky at the United Nations General Assembly in New York last month

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States, ahead of a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky at Downing Street.

It comes after President Donald Trump said he had struck a deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel.

Asked about Trump's move during Prime Minister's Questions, Burnham resisted criticising the US president, saying he wanted to "be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together".

However, he stressed that Zelensky would not be leaving the UK "empty-handed", as he said further military and financial support would be drawn up in the coming weeks.

Burnham is expected to use the visit to promise further sanctions against Russia, while also announcing the UK will accelerate its delivery of air defence missiles to Kyiv.

The UK will also urge allies to step up pressure on Russia, with Chancellor John Healey using International Monetary Fund meetings to call for a ban on Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).

During PMQs, Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey asked whether he agreed the diesel deal was "yet another shameful Trump betrayal of the Ukrainian people and European security".

In response, Burnham did not echo Sir Ed's condemnation of Trump, saying: "What I have to do in my role is try and repair bridges so that the support comes back and therefore I should at this moment in time be careful in terms of laying the ground to bring people back together."

The PM said he had spoken to Zelensky over the phone on Saturday "because I recognised it was another very dark and difficult moment for him as they contemplate a winter that will be severe for his people".

Analysis: Trump's global headaches worsen weeks before crucial elections

Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants

The phone call came after Trump announced that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to release millions of tonnes of Russian diesel into the US, as he suspended sanctions on diesel from Moscow.

Zelensky branded the move a gift to Putin, warning it would provide Moscow with money to continue its war against Ukraine.

Trump responded by saying it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president".

Meanwhile, Zelensky has said at least 600,000 people across Ukraine were left without electricity after deadly overnight Russian missile and drone strikes.

He said "critical" energy infrastructure had been hit – despite Trump's claim on Sunday that a ceasefire on strikes on energy infrastructure was in place between Russia and Ukraine.

Russia said its strikes had hit communications and energy facilities used by Ukraine's military.

Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries and other energy facilities if Moscow did the same.

But Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

The King held an audience with President Zelensky at Buckingham Palace as part of his visit to the UK

It is Zelensky's second visit to the UK since Burnham became prime minister.

He will be greeted by a military ceremonial guard when he visits Downing Street, in what is thought to be a first for a foreign leader.

While other world leaders have received military welcomes, Number 10 said it could not find a record of one taking place on Downing Street.

articles.title: Judge extends White House access for US media outlets amid Trump standoff
articles.excerpt:
A federal judge has extended access to several media organisations that United States President Donald Trump had sought to ban from the White House.

US District Judge Timothy Kelly said Trump likely ...
articles.body_text:
A federal judge has extended access to several media organisations that United States President Donald Trump had sought to ban from the White House.

US District Judge Timothy Kelly said Trump likely broke the law in banning journalists from CNN, MS Now and Politico from attending White House briefings.

The decision, published late Tuesday, expands on an emergency order issued by Kelly on September 24 that temporarily reinstated access to organisations. It said Trump likely discriminated against the news organisations based on their viewpoints, in violation of the First Amendment of the US Constitution.

He wrote that Trump’s “announcement of the ban and later remarks explaining the reason for it make this a straightforward conclusion: President Trump likely banned Plaintiffs from the White House because he believes that their reporting is generally inaccurate and biased against him”.

In announcing the ban, Trump had said the organisations “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States”.

The Department of Justice subsequently said the reporters’ White House passes were revoked on national security grounds.

“First, there is no evidence in the record that President Trump made the decision to revoke Plaintiffs’ hard passes on national security grounds from the get-go, nor at any time has he directly stated that national security was the reason for his decision,” he wrote.

The latest order stands until Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during the president’s first term, makes a final determination in the case, or until an appeals court steps in.

Trump has long been a critic of legacy US media and has previously sought to restrict access to certain organisations.

He has also lodged rhetorical attacks on individual reporters both in person and on social media, while launching an array of lawsuits against media companies.

Speaking during an October 8 hearing, Theodore Boutrous, a lawyer for the three banned organisations, said Trump was seeking to “coerce better coverage”.

The Freedom of the Press Foundation was among the groups cheering the latest court ruling.

“But this fight is far from over,” senior adviser for advocacy Caitlin Vogus said in a statement.

“We have every reason to expect the administration will appeal Kelly’s latest order and also continue to prevent CNN and Politico from participating in pool coverage of the president,” she said. “Trump must not be allowed to trample on fundamental First Amendment protections by handpicking his press corps or turning pool duties into a reward for favorable coverage.”

articles.title: Pope walking and recovering 'as expected' after surgery, doctors say
articles.excerpt:
Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis

Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.

The 71-year-ol...
articles.body_text:
Watch: What we know about Pope Leo's lung cancer diagnosis

Pope Leo XIV's recovery from surgery to remove a lower lobe of his lung is "progressing as expected", his doctors have said.

The 71-year-old pontiff has started to walk and has "resumed a normal diet" following the roughly 90-minute procedure, the medics said in an update shared by the Vatican.

The Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the surgery at Rome's Gemelli Hospital on Tuesday afternoon, which the Vatican said had been "successful" and proceeded without complications.

Blood tests and an X-ray early on Wednesday showed his recovery was "proceeding normally", the doctors said, and he has also undergone respiratory physiotherapy.

The whole lower lobe of the Pope's right lung was removed "to ensure the procedure was radical", the Vatican said following the surgery.

"After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room," it said earlier, before spending a "peaceful night" at the hospital.

The pontiff is expected to remain there for about a week as he recovers.

What we know about the Pope's lung cancer diagnosis

Pope's cancer diagnosis leaves Catholics questioning what comes next

Pope diagnosed with lung cancer but had successful surgery, Vatican says

He had announced that he would be admitted for the operation during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule on his lung "at an early stage" and advised him to have it removed.

Nodules are quite common and not necessarily cancerous, but after it was examined the medical team confirmed it was, "as suspected by pre-operative tests", the Vatican said. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma.

A Vatican source told news agency AFP that further tests were carried out to see whether the cancer had spread.

The Vatican has stressed that the Pope, who is generally thought to be fit, had no symptoms of infection or illness.

The news has shaken Catholics worldwide, many of whom will have recent memories of Pope Francis's hospital visits.

Pope Leo's predecessor, who died last year, also had part of his lung removed in his youth before suffering a series of respiratory infections later in life.

Pope Leo announced on Sunday that he would undergo surgery to remove a growth on his lung

Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer.

The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades.

Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss.

articles.title: Pope Leo recovering well after cancer surgery, Vatican says
articles.excerpt:
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.

A blood test and ch...
articles.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV is out of bed, walking, eating and has undergone respiratory physiotherapy, according to a doctor’s note published by the Vatican a day after his lung cancer surgery.

A blood test and chest X-ray revealed “normal post-operative” progress, doctors Luigi Carbone and Stefano Margaritora said, adding that values were “within the expected range for the type of procedure performed”.

“The Holy Father underwent respiratory physiotherapy and has begun walking in his room”, they said, adding that “he resumed his regular diet and had breakfast and lunch.”

“Recovery is proceeding as planned,” the doctors said.

The 71-year-old pontiff was diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican on Tuesday.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.

The Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.

A medical statement shared by The Holy See’s press office, following the surgery, noted the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.

After the procedure, Pope Leo returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.

The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

articles.title: Renewed fighting risks ‘humanitarian catastrophe’ in Yemen, aid groups warn
articles.excerpt: The humanitarian groups the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have sounded the alarm over the worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen amid ramped-up ...
articles.body_text:
The humanitarian groups the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) and the World Food Programme (WFP) have sounded the alarm over the worsening humanitarian situation in Yemen amid ramped-up fighting.

An estimated 800,000 people have been cut off from life-saving food assistance as front lines have rapidly shifted between Saudi-backed forces of the internationally recognised government and the Iran-aligned Houthis, according to the WFP.

“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP’s country director in Yemen.

The crisis is worst in Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city, where an estimated 600,000 people have no access to food assistance, including 200,000 women and children, the United Nations agency said in a statement.

Taiz has been the focus of recent clashes and is hemmed in by Houthi forces, imperiling aid deliveries.

The WFP said that the loss of access is especially alarming given that Taiz has some of the country’s highest levels of food insecurity.

Across Yemen, more than 18 million people do not have enough to eat, it added, while the latest monitoring shows a record 74 percent of households in accessible areas cannot meet their daily food needs.

Meanwhile, “overwhelmed” health facilities in Marib, Taiz and along the Red Sea coast were bearing the brunt of the fighting in those areas, according to a statement released by the ICRC, with some receiving more than 700 cases in a single week,

Firas Abu Samra, the ICRC’s health services coordinator, said only a handful of facilities operating in Yemen can provide comprehensive care for the injured.

Front-line hospitals are taking in large numbers of wounded while running short of surgical supplies, anaesthetics, oxygen and medicines, he said.

“Additional pressure on hospitals can mean fewer beds, fewer supplies and less capacity to treat people with conditions unrelated to the conflict”, said Eduardo Toro, an ICRC surgeon at Marib General Hospital.

Christine Cipolla, the ICRC’s head of delegation in Yemen, said the country’s battered health system is ill-prepared to cope with any more fighting.

“Our concern is that the system may have little capacity left to absorb a major surge in casualties,” she said.

articles.title: Boy, 17, accidentally shot dead with air rifle at Hampshire house party, inquest told
articles.excerpt:
Connor Bell died of his injuries after his friend Jack Beechy, 18, pulled the trigger, mistaking it for the safety catch

A 17-year-old boy died after he was accidentally shot in the head with an air ...
articles.body_text:
Connor Bell died of his injuries after his friend Jack Beechy, 18, pulled the trigger, mistaking it for the safety catch

A 17-year-old boy died after he was accidentally shot in the head with an air rifle by his friend at a house party, an inquest has been told.

Connor Bell had been drinking at a friend’s house in Basingstoke, Hampshire, on 8 November last year when Jack Beechy fired the fatal shot by mistaking the trigger for the safety catch, the inquest heard.

The boys were shooting the weapon out of the conservatory into the garden at targets such as bottles.

Beechy, 18, accidentally pulled the trigger when he was trying to put the safety catch on the air rifle while it was pointed towards Bell’s head.

Connor, from Tadley, Hampshire, was taken to Southampton general hospital but he died two days later from a severe brain injury.

The inquest at Winchester coroner’s court was told that the crank air rifle was stored in the cupboard under the stairs in the home of Connor’s friend Joshua Brown, now 18.

Paying tribute to his son at the inquest, Robert Bell said: “He was cheeky and mischievous but so kind and caring. He never took himself too seriously and had a wicked sense of humour.

“He also enjoyed a variety of sports, especially football. He was often the driving force in his friends, going out to play football or just doing stuff together.

“He was doing a sports course at college, and he had done a work placement at our local leisure centre in Tadley, and the manager there said as soon as he has got his certificate come back to us.”

Brown, who was 17 at the time of the incident, gave evidence at the inquest, saying his father had shown him how to safely use the gun on two occasions.

Talking about what his father told him, he said: “Not to point it at people.”

When asked if he had thought about putting the gun away after shooting in the garden, before his friends came over, he said: “I wanted my friends to use it. I just thought it would be fun.”

The inquest was told that Beechy was arrested by the police after the accidental shooting but no further action was taken.

Giving evidence on Wednesday, Beechy said he had been drinking cider and vodka at the party and he was “a little bit drunk”.

The Hampshire area coroner Jason Pegg ruled that Connor’s cause of death was a gunshot wound to the head and he died from cardiac arrest from a brain injury. He concluded that it was an accident.

Pegg said: “Connor was just 17 years of age at the time of his death. It is quite clear to me, having heard from [Connor’s family], that he was a son, grandson and a friend. He was a young man who had aspirations in the physical fitness field and had a life planned ahead of him. He was full of life and had a cheeky side and had much to live for.”

He added: “This demonstrates the real risk when you have a group of young people drinking alcohol. This is a deeply tragic case.”

The Philadelphia Phillies are committed to Don Mattingly.

The Phils fired Rob Thomson from his managerial post in the midst of the season and brought in Donnie Baseball on an interim basis.

With Mattingly in the clubhouse, the Phillies turned their season around but narrowly escaped a late-season collapse, and they lost in the National League Wild Card Series to the Atlanta Braves.

But the Phillies must have liked what they saw, Mattingly will have the interim tag taken off and be hired full time. He signed a two-year deal, the team announced Wednesday.

It, of course, should be noted that Mattingly's son, Preston, is the general manager of the team.

The Phillies were 9-19 when they fired Thomson, and Mattingly's Phillies went 73-45 in their next 118 games, but they lost five of their last 15.

Mattingly was the bench coach for the Toronto Blue Jays from 2023 through their pennant-winning season of 2025 but stepped down shortly after they lost the World Series.

Mattingly has been in professional baseball since 1979 and has yet to win a World Series — the 2025 Fall Classic was the first one he appeared in.

The Phillies' main core of Bryce Harper, Trea Turner and Kyle Schwarber isn't going anywhere, while Aaron Nola and Christopher Sanchez are under contract for several more years.
