articles.title: Zimbabwean author denies using AI to write award-winning story
articles.excerpt:
Simbarashe Kundizeza says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles in Zimbabwe

Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelli...
articles.body_text:
Simbarashe Kundizeza says he was inspired by a poem about fish tanks to write a story about his family struggles in Zimbabwe

Zimbabwean writer Simbarashe Kundizeza has denied using artificial intelligence (AI) to write his short story, which won this year's Caine Prize for African Writing.

His statement comes a week after he scooped the £10,000 ($13,000) award and a recent article in The Atlantic said AI-detection software Pangram had shown his work about a boy whose family falls on hard times was entirely AI generated.

"For the avoidance of doubt, I wrote The Blue Fighter," he posted on X, external.

The accusation has caused an uproar on social media and Caine Prize chair Ellah Wakatama told the BBC she was shocked that the US magazine had not waited for a full investigation before publishing.

"I do wish The Atlantic had spent more time investigating this so that alongside Pangram, they did have evidence of real human investigation of it before tainting the prize and tainting this winner," Wakatama told the BBC's Front Row programme.

The chair of the Caine Prize's board of trustees said she had been contacted on Friday about the allegation and Vauhini Vara's article - Yet Another Prizewinner Seems to Be AI, external - had been published on Sunday.

It follows rows over other literary prizes this year, in particular the Commonwealth Short Story Prize, which was won by Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir despite allegations that he had used AI, and the withdrawal of Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien from France's top literary award, the Goncourt, over allegations he used AI for his first novel, which he denies.

Vara, who quoted Wakatama in her article, said her wariness of Silicon Valley was "well founded and reasonable" but she said Pangram's internal research showed its assessments were rarely wrong.

The backlash to the article on social media has included comments from African writers with suggestions that such accusations are primarily being made against non-white writers.

Wale Lawal, the Nigerian founder of The Republic magazine, called out The Atlantic article for being "crazy, racist and wildly unethical", external.

Zimbabwean writer Joe Ruzvidzo, whose novel Welcome to Anywhere came out last year, said he stood by Kundizeza and that it was time "to fight this literary stop-and-frisk", external.

Nigerian publisher Modupe Daramola said it was necessary to discuss how "these AI allegations are targeting Black and African writers" and how they were often disproportionately scrutinised.

"There's something incredibly sinister about this," the Noisy Streetss Limited publisher posted on X, external.

"Pangram is itself AI-powered. Why should its assessment be treated as definitive?" she added.

Wakatama said as part of an internal investigation for the Caine Prize Kundizeza would be sending in documentation about his various drafts and there were ongoing conversations with all the judges and The Shallow Tales Review, the publication that first published The Blue Fighter in 2025, external.

In his statement, Kundizeza said had "a concrete, documented history" about the story's inspiration and he set out the chronology of its development.

Wakatama, who is also editor-at-large at Canongate Books, said Caine Prize submissions, which are all previously published, were not checked for AI, but writers vouched that their work was original.

She added that she was not against using AI per se to check entries, but she was "against is it being used as a final arbiter in this case".

Wakatama said it was also important to remember Pangram was "not yet tested".

"I am not happy for the work of writers, and in this case especially black writers, to form the testing ground for something that is at best still rough and ready."

Research has found that AI detectors can wrongly flag human writing as AI generated. Vara conceded that any AI-detection product, "including one as good of Pangram" was "not going to be 100% accurate".

In her article, as well as citing Pangram research she also quoted a recent paper by researchers at Free University of Brussels, external, which said it had found zero cases of Pangram, and two other AI-detection tools, getting it wrong when it came to  English-language writing by non-native English speakers.

The study notes that tools like Pangram should be considered "as an initial flag for further investigation".

Vara told BBC's Front Row programme that she had also used her own judgment "to suss out these things" and that every other previous Caine Prize winning story she had put through Pangram "came out as 100% human".

"I also found an earlier 2021 story by the same author. I ran that through Pangram. It also came out as 100% human. And what struck me was that was a really good, interesting story. And tonally, it's so different from this story, as if the same person hadn't written both."

In response Kundizeza wrote: "To suggest that a writer cannot write in different styles or genres, or improve his writing substantially after five or more years fundamentally misunderstands the craft of writing."

For Vara, one of the stylistic issues that stood out about The Blue Fighter was that it had used sentence constructions using "X but Y", which she says is common in AI-generated texts.

"Not with anger, but with the quiet resignation of someone who had known all along this moment would come," is an example she gave from the story that described the character of the mother.

"The proliferation of those struck me," Vara told Front Row, adding that the story also had a lot of metaphors, also prevalent in writing generated by AI.

The day after winning the Caine Prize, Kundizeza told the BBC he was inspired after hearing a poem read by South African Vangile Gantsho at an event in Ghana last year about her father's obsession with building fish tanks.

He said he had weaved that with fictionalised details from his own life around 2002 when Zimbabwe's economic troubles began.

"Much like the father in the story, my own dad... was an accountant, but he quit his job to grow tomatoes. So it kind of touches on both of our fathers," he told BBC Newsday.

On X, Kundizeza said he was heartened by "the numerous messages of solidarity from fellow writers and readers", ending his message by saying: "Most importantly, I will continue to write."

Africa basks in Booker boost for female writers

Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie: AI could make us increasingly stupid

Married couple win top African writing prize

Go to BBCAfrica.com, external for more news from the African continent.

Follow us on Twitter @BBCAfrica, external, on Facebook at BBC Africa, external or on Instagram at bbcafrica, external

articles.title: Abby Summers might be a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader, but her trip across the pond proves she's an Eagles fan
articles.excerpt:
Gronk and Julian Edelman break down the Eagles' devastating loss to the Jaguars after taking the lead with 8 seconds left in regulation.

We're through the first five weeks of the NFL season, and I'm ...
articles.body_text:
Gronk and Julian Edelman break down the Eagles' devastating loss to the Jaguars after taking the lead with 8 seconds left in regulation.

We're through the first five weeks of the NFL season, and I'm here to report that Cooper DeJean and Abby Summers continue to choose love over divisional rivalry. It's a beautiful thing to witness.

Forget any forced narratives being pushed by the league. The relationship between the Philadelphia Eagles defensive back and the Dallas Cowboys cheerleader should be getting a lot more attention.

Cooper DeJean attends the Kentucky Derby 152 at Churchill Downs in Louisville, Ky., on May 2, 2026. (Daniel Boczarski/Getty Images for Churchill Downs)

This is a romance that's defying all odds in the NFC East. These two are making it work despite being members of opposing franchises. Week 5 of the long season showed their commitment.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Abby was on the sideline and participated in the halftime show on Thursday night as the Cowboys lost at home to the backup quarterback-led Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

By Sunday, she had traded in her pom-poms and the iconic Cowboys cheerleader outfit for Eagles green as Philadelphia lost in unbelievable fashion to the Jacksonville Jaguars across the pond in London.

COWBOYS HIRE LONGTIME NFL COACH OUT OF RETIREMENT TO ADDRESS TEAM'S BRUTAL DEFENSIVE START

Now don't go around pointing fingers at Abby Summers as if she's responsible for the Eagles loss. That's not fair. They had that game in the bag until the crazy kickoff decision at the end.

As far as any of us know, mostly because she wasn't one of the WAGs who popped in the NFL's propaganda campaign, she wasn’t keeping Cooper DeJean out of the film room during training camp for social media videos.

Cooper DeJean of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on during an NFL game against the Jacksonville Jaguars at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London on Oct. 11, 2026. (DeFodi Images via Getty Images)

How each of them bounces back after tough losses will tell a lot about what the season has in store for them. In a couple of weeks, we'll know even more.

That's because the Cowboys and Eagles will play each other for the first time this season, and it will be on Monday Night Football in Philadelphia. That's going to be the first real test of this relationship.

OUTKICK IS NOW ON THE FOX APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

The Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders perform before the start of the game between the Dallas Cowboys and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at AT&T Stadium in Arlington, Texas, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images)

Flying out and playing WAG in London is one thing. Doing it at Lincoln Financial Field as a Dallas Cowboys cheerleader is something completely different.

If Cooper DeJean and Abby Summers can make it through that, they can make it through anything. Including a game on Thanksgiving in Dallas.

I'm not rooting for either team, but I will continue to root for the rival couple.

articles.title: Rams OL Alaric Jackson expecting two-game suspension after punching Bills defender Bradley Chubb
articles.excerpt: Dan reacts to one of the wildest, most chaotic weekends of college football in recent memory—and explains why Coach Curt Cignetti has officially ruined patience for every athletic director and booster...
articles.body_text:
Dan reacts to one of the wildest, most chaotic weekends of college football in recent memory—and explains why Coach Curt Cignetti has officially ruined patience for every athletic director and booster in the country.

The NFL is expected to suspend Los Angeles Rams left tackle Alaric Jackson for two games after punching Buffalo Bills edge rusher Bradley Chubb after Monday night’s shootout and potential Super Bowl preview.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Footage of Jackson's tirade is indisputable, and the consequences are entirely self-inflicted. Monday night’s childish spectacle saw Jackson marching into the midfield, losing his cool, and throwing a bare-knuckle punch at Chubb. Jackson is expected to appeal the suspension.

The official suspension statement read, in part: "After the game, as players were shaking hands and exchanging jerseys, Jackson struck Buffalo linebacker Bradley Chubb in the face after a brief confrontation, violating Rule 12, Section 3, Article 1, which applies to "any act which is contrary to the generally understood principles of sportsmanship."

Alaric Jackson No. 77 of the Los Angeles Rams warms up before the game against the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High in Denver, Colo., on Sept. 27, 2026. (Getty Images)

Chubb, to his credit, took the higher road and kept his composure, letting Buffalo teammates pull him back, and allowed Jackson to bury himself on national television. He understood what Jackson couldn't: the cameras are running, and the bill always comes due.

RAMS OFFENSIVE LINEMAN PUNCHES BILLS LINEBACKER AFTER THRILLING GAME: 'TEMPERS GOT FLARED'

After the game, Chubb gave his reaction. "It's just emotions," he said, "They always catch the second guy. So, I let him swing. And then my teammates held me back, and I just chilled."

Chubb is a smart man; Jackson, not so much.

With Alaric Jackson, poor judgment is more of a pattern than a fluke.

Just four months ago, in June 2026, Jackson was arrested on charges of felony domestic violence in Southern California.

While prosecutors bypassed formal criminal charges in favor of a pre-filing diversion hearing, the incident remains subject to ongoing NFL review.

Alaric Jackson No. 77 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during training camp at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles, Calif., on July 31, 2026. (Getty Images)

In 2024, the league slapped Jackson with a two-game suspension under the Personal Conduct Policy after he recorded intimate encounters on his phone without consent, an incident that later triggered a civil lawsuit.

NFL FACING A DOMESTIC VIOLENCE EPIDEMIC THIS OFFSEASON WITH ARREST OF RAMS LINEMAN THE LATEST CASE

At some point, the headaches are eclipsing the talent. Rams coach Sean McVay preaches accountability and culture, yet his starting tackle keeps showcasing eye-rolling volatility.

The Rams sit at 2-3 in a tight NFC race, desperately needing stability to protect Matthew Stafford’s blind side. Jackson will be out of action when his team needs him most.

Alaric Jackson #77 of the Los Angeles Rams looks on during the national anthem before an NFC Championship NFL football game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field in Seattle, Wash., on Jan. 25, 2026. (Getty Images)

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: Pentagon pushes hypersonic weapons production as startups slash costs
articles.excerpt:
Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier reports on the U.S. pursuit of hypersonic weapons and the capabilities and costs of advanced weaponry on ‘Special Report.’

As the U.S. works to refill its m...
articles.body_text:
Fox News chief political anchor Bret Baier reports on the U.S. pursuit of hypersonic weapons and the capabilities and costs of advanced weaponry on ‘Special Report.’

As the U.S. works to refill its missile stockpile, it is also looking to develop new weapons for its arsenal.

"We're going to need all three tiers of missiles. The cheap ones, the ones that are now the high-end like Patriot, and then maybe some hypersonics," said Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marines colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department.

The U.S. military is taking an increasing interest in hypersonic weapons, which are maneuverable and travel five times faster than the speed of sound.

"These hypersonic systems are now seen as the novel revolutionary system and the ballistic missile is seen as the archaic one," said UC Berkeley Senior Research Scholar Cameron Tracy.

US FALLS BEHIND IN HYPERSONIC RACE AS CHINA, RUSSIA GAIN EDGE

Defense startups are racing to make hypersonic missiles cheaper and easier to mass produce as the Pentagon looks to expand its arsenal. (Tom Brenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Sarah Nelson/ US Army Contracting Command)

But the weapons the military has traditionally invested in could come at a cost. Estimates from the Government Accountability Office show missiles for the Army’s long-range hypersonic weapon, the Dark Eagle, could cost more than $40 million each. As the Navy works to equip its Zumwalt Destroyers with hypersonics, the GAO puts estimates at $70 million per missile – which includes costs to develop and incorporate the necessary technologies. The GAO also notes the modernization project is two years behind schedule.

"In the long run, for example, the Army thinks that the long-ranged hypersonic weapon will become cheaper as production ramps up," said Xiaodon Liang, Arms Control Association Senior Policy Analyst for Nuclear Weapons Policy and Disarmament.

Tomahawk missiles cost around $2.6 million according to the U.S. Navy. Army budget documents show Patriot missiles cost nearly $4 million. Precision Strike Missiles or PrSMs cost $1.6 million per unit. The U.S. Navy could buy almost 27 tomahawks for the price of one hypersonic missile aboard the Zumwalt Destroyers. The Army could buy around 25 PrSMs for the price of one Dark Eagle hypersonic weapon.

"The U.S. has invested in recent years in several of the programs that are starting to become into fruition," said Liang. "These are exquisite weapons. And I think that the military is acquiring them for exquisite purposes."

Hypersonic weapons travel up to 20 times faster than traditional missiles and an adversary’s reaction time is thought to be six times shorter. Hypersonic speeds are also vital for both evading enemy defense systems and executing strikes. The Atlantic Council estimates 75% fewer hypersonic weapons would be needed for a mission.

US ARMY OFFERING DEFENSE FIRMS 'CONCIERGE ACCESS' TO TEST WEAPONS AT MILITARY RANGES

Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, at an undisclosed location, February 28, 2026. (U.S. Navy/Handout via Reuters)

Startups are hoping to bring down some of the costs to produce hypersonic weapons with more affordable missiles and increased testing capabilities.

"The weapon itself is under $500,000, which if you know about munitions, that's incredibly cheap," Castelion co-founder and CEO Bryon Hargis said.

The Army and Navy are investing in Castelion's Blackbeard hypersonic weapon, which the company says it is designed for mass production.

"It is a story about hypersonics and what they can provide in terms of a weapon, but it's really a story of American manufacturing," Hargis said. "The company is focused on providing America options to have that middle deterrence layer and we're doing that through production."

This year Castelion began building what it says will be the largest dedicated hypersonic weapon production facility in the U.S. Project Ranger is expected to produce thousands of Blackbeard weapons annually. Those will eventually be used to fill Castelion’s various contracts, such as integrating the weapons into the U.S. Navy's F/A-18 Super Hornet Jets, incorporating the system into the U.S. Army’s HIMARS and deploying Blackbeard on unmanned surface vessels.

"The advantage of a hypersonic system is that it goes very far, it gets there quickly, and it's highly survivable because of that maneuverability. And that's important for achieving deterrence because it's hard to shoot down," Hargis said.

Hypersonic weapons remain mostly in Earth’s atmosphere. The missiles are maneuverable during flight and can strike a target quickly, in 15-30 minutes from around 1,725 miles away.

US REBUILDING WEAPONS STOCKPILE COULD DELAY ORDERS FROM ALLIES

"If you don't know what the target would be initially, unlike a ballistic missile where you can calculate where it'll land, you might misinterpret, for example, an incoming strike as a decapitation attempt. And that would be very concerning," Liang said.

Developers say the U.S. speaks with other countries about missile launches and what the intended targets are. But there are other concerns that hypersonic maneuverability could lead to inaccuracy.

Guided-missile destroyer USS Thomas Hudner fires a Tomahawk land attack missile in support of Operation Epic Fury, on March 1, 2026. (U.S. Navy via Getty Images)

"Technologies do tend to improve over time as testing and especially as experience with use builds up, but there are pretty important physical constraints on the performance of these systems," said Tracy.

Defense contractor Rocket Lab is working with the War Department to improve hypersonic missile capabilities through an increasing number of test launches.

INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

"With our HASTE program, what we have enabled is low cost, high frequency hypersonic and missile defense testing. And when you can say that you can get that cheaper and faster, now you're looking at more of a shots on goal approach to demonstrating capability of the technology insertion cycle," Vice President of Global Launch Services at Rocket Lab Brian Rogers said.

Rocket Lab’s HASTE is a suborbital testbed launch vehicle that provides flight test opportunities for the government to advance hypersonic and suborbital system technology development. The vehicle is derived from Rocket Lab’s Electron rocket, which has launched nearly 100 missions.

"Rather than saying we need to be stuck in an analysis environment and then it's a very rigorous test campaign that costs a lot of money and involves a lot people, now you can say we're planning 12 tests this year. We don't have to bet the farm on any one of them. Which allows us to take more risk and really move the needle in terms of technology development," Rogers said.

The U.S. military has never used a hypersonic weapon but has explored deploying its Dark Eagle to the Middle East.

"I would be very surprised if we used them and would be even more surprised if we used it extensively because of the small number of missiles that exist and the concerns already about the munitions stockpile," Liang said.

Bret Baier currently serves as FOX News Channel's (FNC) anchor and executive editor of Special Report with Bret Baier (weeknights at 6-7PM/ET), chief political anchor of the network and co-anchor of the network’s election coverage. Baier is also host of FOX News Audio's "The Bret Baier Podcast" which includes Common Ground and The All-Star Panel. He joined FNC in 1998 as the first reporter in the Atlanta bureau and is now based in Washington, D.C. where he was recently described as "the most influential news anchor in America right now" at the 2025 Semafor Trust in News summit.

articles.title: Fostering in crisis: can flexible care models fix England’s child placement shortfall?
articles.excerpt:
New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care places

Viennetta Basterfield, 67, spent two decades fostering more than 100 children in her west...
articles.body_text:
New recruitment campaign to target adults in their 30s and 40s in bid to create 10,000 new foster care places

Viennetta Basterfield, 67, spent two decades fostering more than 100 children in her west London home before she and her husband handed in the reins during Covid.

Her own mother had died when she was nine and she was brought up by another woman who took her in. There was no doubt in her mind that she wanted to dedicate her life to passing that gift on to others.

“I can’t say I wasn’t frightened. Every single placement I was frightened because you think, are we going to be OK? Are they going to accept us?” she said. “But it was the most rewarding thing I’ve ever done. We still have a full house for Sunday dinners, for christmas, for birthdays.

“The greatest gift you can give a child is to show them that they matter.”

But she worries about the future of fostering – she said the bureaucracy around the process was putting people off, and younger generations had more reservations about doing it, especially juggling it with caring for their own children.

On Wednesday, the government is launching the country’s first national foster carer recruitment campaign, due to declining numbers at a time when there is a growing number of children in care.

The number of fostering households has dropped 10% since 2021, and the foster care population is ageing, with over one in three foster carers now aged 60 or over.

The appeal will target adults in their 30s and 40s, urging them “to open their hearts and homes to some of the most vulnerable children in society”, with the aim of creating 10,000 new foster care places by the end of this parliament.

It will run alongside trials of new foster care models, such as short-term “respite fostering” or fostering at weekends, which the government hopes will make it accessible to a wider range of people.

The children’s minister, Josh MacAlister, said he wanted the public to respond to the campaign in the same way many did to the Homes for Ukraine scheme, when hundreds opened their homes to refugees.

“There was this massive national moment where we understood that something was happening and people asked themselves, could we help? We need that kind of moment, to prompt people to have conversations in their homes,” he said.

“Lots of families won’t be able to do it, but we’re trying to open up fostering to a wider group of people, by making it intergenerational or part-time, for instance.”

He urged families not to wait for the “perfect moment”. “You’ve already got a lot of what it takes. Just step forward and start the process and see where you go,” he said.

“Unless we rapidly, dramatically expand the foster care system, we will end up with children waking up every single day in residential care who could be in a family home, and children who are sent to live miles away from where they’ve grown up.”

Speaking at an event ahead of the campagin at Downing Street on Tuesday, Marie-France van Heel, the prime minister’s wife, revealed for the first time that she had wanted to foster children.

She was put off the idea because of her husband’s job and feeling she had to “transform myself into a different type of person to be able to give foster care”. “This campaign is really trying to dispel some of those myths and misconceptions,” she said.

Fostering is the primary form of care for looked-after children in England. Out of 81,770 looked-after children, there are about 56,400 children in foster care at any one time.

New research by the Coram Institute for Children found over half a million adults want to foster and an estimated 3.4 million are interested.

Dame Carol Homden, CEO of Coram, said there was a “substantial pool of people who are open to becoming foster carers” and the charity welcomed the government’s ambitious plans to recruit more.

Their research has identified certain groups with a higher fostering propensity who could be targeted, including women, larger households and those from minoritised ethnic backgrounds, particularly black households.

But there also needs to be a focus on retaining current foster carers as well as recruiting new ones, Homden said.

Research has shown a number of factors are pushing foster carers to leave the sector, including feeling undervalued or ignored by social workers, and financial strain – the Fostering Network found only 33% of carers report their allowances fully cover the cost of raising a child.

“We need to see a focus on targeting key areas and groups, clear information and practical support to boost both recruitment and retention of foster carers,” said Homden.

Polling by the Department for Education found that two-thirds (66%) of people believe they could be a good foster carer if practical barriers were removed.

articles.title: Australian politics live: Chalmers says ATO surcharge was joint intervention with PM; Nationals MP defends ‘shamed and stoned’ remark
articles.excerpt:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Chalmers says intervention on credit card tax payments was a joint decision with the PM

I have an open door too, says Jim Chalmers, after ...
articles.body_text:
Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Chalmers says intervention on credit card tax payments was a joint decision with the PM

I have an open door too, says Jim Chalmers, after the PM yesterday seemed to take credit for delaying a ban by the ATO on credit card payments.

Anthony Albanese says he received a text from Australian chamber of commerce and industry boss Andrew McKellar on Thursday morning and by Friday morning the problem was address.

Chalmers, not wanting to be seen to be left out of this, says he was in the conversation with ACCI too – and that it was a joint decision with the prime minister to intervene.

double quotation markI have an open door. I’ve met with ACCI in recent weeks, in fact, and we were engaging on these issues as well …

Last week on the Wednesday, I had discussions with the prime minister. We agreed that it would be appropriate to find a better way through for small business. We engaged with the business community on the Thursday, as we do frequently, on these sorts of issues.

Then [the assistant treasurer] Daniel Mulino and I took a proposal to ministers on the Friday morning after I discussed with the tax commissioner very early on Friday morning. And by late Friday morning, we had stepped in.

‘Greedy’: Taylor condemns trust tax changes

The opposition has made it clear it will not be supporting the government’s changes to impost a minimum 30% tax on discretionary trusts.

Angus Taylor, speaking to journalists at the entrance of parliament, says the government is trying to implement the changes because it loves to spend money.

double quotation markSmall businesses are going to see over $13bn of restructuring costs here, as we’ve seen reporting in the last couple of days, $13bn they’re going to have to wear. The government didn’t think about any of this. They didn’t think about the stamp duty implications of their tax changes, they didn’t think about the restructuring costs. In the end, they’re greedy for the money. They need the money because they love to spend it.

On RN Breakfast, Nationals MP Kevin Hogan said that while small businesses will be able to change their settings to avoid some of the additional tax (and they’ll have until mid 2028 to do it), their compliance costs will be high.

double quotation markI think the compliance costs are estimated to be more than what the government’s going to collect in revenue from this as well. So again, makes us a less productive country.

We all make heat of the moment comments, says Nationals MP Kevin Hogan, defending his colleague Angie Bell, who yesterday said the prime minister and minister for small business, Anne Aly, should be “shamed and stoned” over the ATO credit card ban.

Aly revealed on social media later that day that she had recently received 19 death threats, and called the comments “racist” and “misogynistic”.

Speaking to RN Breakfast this morning, Hogan disagrees that they were racist and misogynistic.

double quotation markWe all make comments and I’ve been guilty too in the heat of the moment to use terms or phrases that shouldn’t be used and Angie quite rightly got up and withdrew it straight away and apologised … No, I don’t think they were racist or misogynistic.

A small fact check here: It took about eight minutes for Bell to withdraw, after she was asked to do so by leader of the House, Tony Burke.

‘None of us is beyond criticism’: Chalmers on governing through murky waters

Jim Chalmers does find himself in pretty rough economic seas to sail through – with high inflation, rising interest rates, and people angry with the increasing cost of living.

At the halfway point of the term, and with One Nation’s rise in the polls, the government has around 18 months to turn things around and convince voters they’re still solid economic managers.

In a speech last night, Chalmers said the government should genuinely acknowledge the pressures people are under, and that the economy would get better.

This morning, he’s asked if the government is struggling to sell its economic message to voters. He says:

double quotation markThere are always a range of views. When you do a senior job in a government which is governing in difficult times, there will always be a range of views. And I’ve tried to always take the approach that none of us is beyond criticism.

Some people would like us to do more, some people would like us to do less. That’s just the reality of a senior job in a government in difficult times. And so I accept that. I try and take all of the feedback that I get, good, bad, or indifferent, on board.

‘More than 95% of people don’t get trust income’, Chalmers defends tax changes

Jim Chalmers says the government is right to hit trusts which are being used as tax loopholes, and that the majority of regular people don’t use them and don’t receive any benefit from them.

The Coalition is dead opposed to the changes and says small businesses will be hit hard.

Chalmers says around 10% of small businesses will be impacted, and the changes have been urged for decades.

double quotation markThere are legitimate reasons for trusts, but they also allow a small proportion of people to manage their tax in ways that’s not available to most working Australians. And that’s why there’s been 50 years of reviews now recommending that they be reformed.

The use of these trusts, discretionary trusts, has doubled in the last 20 years, but still more than 95% of people don’t get trust income, and still less than 10% of small businesses would be affected by the changes that we’re proposing today doesn’t come until the middle of 2028.

The Greens have told the ABC this morning that the government should ensure that trust loopholes can’t be used by parents to pay for private school fees.

Chalmers says that issue hasn’t yet been raised with him, and that the legislation has “reasonable arrangements for charities, for not-for-profits” – which private schools could be included in.

Chalmers says intervention on credit card tax payments was a joint decision with the PM

I have an open door too, says Jim Chalmers, after the PM yesterday seemed to take credit for delaying a ban by the ATO on credit card payments.

Anthony Albanese says he received a text from Australian chamber of commerce and industry boss Andrew McKellar on Thursday morning and by Friday morning the problem was address.

Chalmers, not wanting to be seen to be left out of this, says he was in the conversation with ACCI too – and that it was a joint decision with the prime minister to intervene.

double quotation markI have an open door. I’ve met with ACCI in recent weeks, in fact, and we were engaging on these issues as well …

Last week on the Wednesday, I had discussions with the prime minister. We agreed that it would be appropriate to find a better way through for small business. We engaged with the business community on the Thursday, as we do frequently, on these sorts of issues.

Then [the assistant treasurer] Daniel Mulino and I took a proposal to ministers on the Friday morning after I discussed with the tax commissioner very early on Friday morning. And by late Friday morning, we had stepped in.

Australia missing out on $45bn of revenue from resources: Greens

As Labor prepares to introduce its bill for a gas reserve, the Greens are pointing out that there are tens of billions being left on the table because the government won’t properly tax the resource.

The Greens say a recent report by the Prosper Australia Research Institute shows Australia is missing out on about $45bn of revenue a year – if it taxed the petroleum and mining sectors more.

The report says Australia collects about 14% of petroleum value in public revenue, while Norway collects around 40%.

The Greens’ deputy leader, Steph Hodgins-May, says this is a political choice and the government could tax fossil fuels more if it wanted to:

double quotation markWe’re giving away billions in resource wealth while families struggle to pay the rent, put food on the table and afford basic healthcare.

Labor can find billions to prop up the fossil fuel industry, but when it comes to making corporations like Santos, Woodside and Adani pay a fair return, suddenly it’s all too hard.

PM has a ‘fetish for humiliating his treasurer’, says Wilson

The shadow treasurer, Tim Wilson, says the prime minister’s intervention to delay the ATO banning credit card payments shows a “pattern” of Anthony Albanese overruling his treasurer.

As we brought you below, the PM yesterday implied that he intervened after the ATO had announced the ban. He said within 24 hours of being texted by the business lobby, there was more money on the table to delay the ban.

Wilson tells News24 it’s more evidence of Albanese going over Jim Chalmers’ head.

double quotation markThe prime minister has a kink for punishing small businesses and a fetish for humiliating his treasurer. So I say this is a consistent pattern of behaviour where the prime minister constantly goes in, overrides his treasurer, humiliates him in public. I suspect it’s going to sour the relationship somewhat.

Yesterday the prime minister said the ATO’s credit card ban was delayed just 24 hours after Andrew McKellar, head of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (ACCI) texted him asking him to interview.

Speaking at an ACCI event yesterday, McKellar praised Anthony Albanese for having his door open to feedback after the changes were announced.

double quotation markMy door is always open. Andrew [McKellar] did text me last Thursday morning and by Friday morning we had an announcement.

Jim Chalmers made the announcement on the Friday morning that the government would provide additional funding to delay the credit card ban until at the end of June.

Forecasts suggest ‘cautious confidence’ in the economy, says Chalmers

In the wake of the IMF report warning of a “clear and present danger” to the world economy, Chalmers said that Treasury and Reserve Bank forecasts suggest some “cautious confidence” is appropriate on things getting better, and as a result, helping the standing of Labor against One Nation.

He said Treasury, the RBA and economists expect inflation to be better, unemployment to be lower and the effects of tax reform to be positive.

double quotation markThey don’t expect things to get a lot better in the next 12 weeks but they do expect things to get a bit better over the next 12 months.

Good morning, Krishani Dhanji with you here, thanks to Martin Farrer for getting us started.

We’re at the halfway point of this sitting week – but there’s still plenty to come. For the government, all eyes will be on the resources minister, Madeleine King, introducing the gas reservation plan today. Labor will also probably be hoping to stretch their Josh Frydenberg distraction card out another day and taunt the Liberals with it during question time.

And there’ll likely be more reaction today to the proposed livestreaming of an execution by firing squad in the US, with the government and opposition strengthening their language, saying Australians should not be seeing that footage. The government’s putting the onus on the streaming platforms because the eSafety commissioner does not at the minute have the power to force them to block the stream.

I’ve got my coffee, I hope you’ve got yours – let’s get cracking.

Josh Frydenberg reiterates that he hasn’t ‘closed the door’ to politics

The Josh Frydenberg book-promotion/comeback-to-politics tour continues.

The former treasurer and ousted member for Kooyong appeared on 7:30 last night, again raising the possibility of his return to frontline politics.

His memoir, A Grateful Son, is the Trojan Horse that legitimises questions like: “Do you think you’d make a good prime minister?”

“Look, I haven’t closed the door to reentering politics,” Frydenberg reiterated. “That would involve running for a seat, winning it, joining the party room and then proceeding after that. So there are a lot of steps.”

He told host Sarah Ferguson that “if I was to run, it would be at the next election”, but insisted “it’s not a decision that I have taken”.

Full marks for persistence: Ferguson tried again. “Do you have what it takes to lead the country?”

Frydenberg: “Look, I think it’s important to know what you believe in, and I certainly do, to have policy ideas that can take the country in the right direction, and to be consistent with the philosophy and the values of our great party, and that’s what I articulate in the book.”

Gas companies would be forced to set aside 20% of exports for Australian use under new legislation for a national gas reservation scheme to be introduced, with Labor committing to more transparency and tighter rules to prevent the system from being gamed.

The resources minister, Madeleine King, will introduce the amended bills that will give the Australian Energy Regulator the power to force companies to meet a target of 110% of demand each year.

It will also limit ministerial discretion and replace the Turnbull-era domestic gas security mechanism.

In a speech to be delivered at the National Press Club King will say a successful energy transition for the country will rely on a “guaranteed supply of affordable gas” for households, renewable energies and the processing of critical minerals and rare earths.

King will also say Australia must continue exporting traditional commodities, including gas and coal.

double quotation markNo two countries will follow exactly the same pathway to reducing emissions. What remains important is the commitment to the goal and a peaceful and inclusive journey toward it, so that we can minimise the damage caused by climate change, while making sure our communities have the energy they need.

Dreyfus says platforms should prevent execution livestream from being shown

Mark Dreyfus has fired off a warning to social media platforms about the livestream of US military execution planned for December.

The former attorney, who is now the special envoy for international human rights, said Australia held longstanding opposition to the death penalty and had raised it with the United States.

double quotation markAustralia opposes the death penalty in all circumstances, for all people ... the proposed livestreaming of an execution is deeply distressing. Platforms have a responsibility to prevent this disturbing content from being shown to Australians.

Yesterday, Anthony Albanese said he found the proposed streaming of a firing squad execution “completely abhorrent”, adding “we should do whatever we can to stop that occurring”.

The prime minister told ABC social media platforms risked harming their reputation for allowing streams of the execution but the government was limited in the ability to shut them down.

Albanese said the government was receiving advice on its options. He said:

double quotation markIf there is something, anything we can do, we will do. I assure you of that.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, has urged progressives not to disregard voters that are attracted to One Nation’s message in the Bernie Fraser oration at the Shine Dome in Canberra last night.

Chalmers said Pauline Hanson would be a disaster in government, calling One Nation “inexperienced, incompetent and incapable of managing the economy or our international reputation”.

But the treasurer said a significant number of Australians see value in the One Nation-aligned message of returning to the “good old days”.

double quotation markOur role as progressive people is not to scold those who see appeal in that message. It’s not to mock them, dare I say cancel them, or talk down to them.

He said the government should instead genuinely acknowledge the pressures people are under and deliver measures to make people’s lives better.

double quotation markThe far right strategy is to divide people and it’s working; their goal is to talk down our economy so that their endless negativity becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Their core message is often clear and sometimes very appealing: let’s just go back to a more nostalgic version of the world we remember.

We have all the facts to push back on this, but facts don’t beat feelings. Feelings are as real as facts.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Krishani Dhanji with the main action.

articles.title: Greta Thunberg joins massive French student protests as cars burn, police fire tear gas
articles.excerpt: The Swedish activist rallied alongside students outside a high school near Paris as demonstrations over classroom conditions spread across France, with clashes erupting in several cities. (Credit: AP)...
articles.body_text:
The Swedish activist rallied alongside students outside a high school near Paris as demonstrations over classroom conditions spread across France, with clashes erupting in several cities. (Credit: AP)

Climate activist Greta Thunberg joined student protesters in France on Tuesday after weeks of violent confrontations with police, thousands of arrests and widespread school closures over demands for education reform.

The 23-year-old Swedish activist appeared outside a high school in Saint-Denis, north of Paris, where students were demanding more teachers, better facilities and shorter school days, Reuters reported.

More than 6,800 people have been detained since the protests began in September, according to French authorities. Demonstrators have set fires, erected barricades and confronted riot police in cities across France, although many protests have remained peaceful.

FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION

Climate activist Greta Thunberg speaks with students outside a high school in Saint-Denis, near Paris, France, on Oct. 13, 2026, as nationwide protests over education reform continue. (JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP via Getty Images)

Thunberg, who rose to prominence organizing school strikes over climate change, criticized the French government's response to the demonstrations.

"We are inspired by the young people who are demanding their basic rights," Thunberg told reporters, according to Reuters. She also described the police response as "extremely violent."

About 161,500 people marched across France on Tuesday, including 41,500 in Paris, according to Interior Ministry figures. The Education Ministry said 214 schools were closed.

FRENCH SCHOOL RIOTS DEEPEN AS EXPERTS POINT TO FAR-LEFT ALLIANCE FUELING ‘BROADER CONFRONTATION’

French high school students gather outside the Lycee Voltaire high school as part of nationwide protests to demand the hiring of substitute teachers, increased resources and better learning conditions, in Paris, as more than 400 schools remain closed following days of student protests that have escalated into violence in some places, France, October 2, 2026. (Sarah Meyssonnier/Reuters)

President Donald Trump weighed in on the turmoil last week, blaming mass migration rather than complaints about education.

"What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social on Oct. 6.

The demonstrations have become a political flashpoint ahead of France's presidential election next May, with far-left presidential hopeful Jean-Luc Mélenchon accusing the government of excessive force against young protesters.

FRANCE IS DEVOURING ITSELF AS SCHOOL RIOTS REVEAL A CRISIS FAR BIGGER THAN BROKEN CLASSROOMS

Greta Thunberg meets with students in Saint-Denis, France, on Oct. 13, 2026, as demonstrations over school conditions and education funding enter their fourth week. (JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP via Getty Images)

Mélenchon joined demonstrators in Paris on Tuesday, while right-wing National Rally leader Marine Le Pen has condemned violence by protesters and called for those responsible for damaging schools to pay for repairs.

The police response has drawn criticism following an incident last week in which a 15-year-old boy lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police dispersal grenade that detonated during a demonstration in Lens.

French authorities subsequently suspended the use of the type of stun grenade involved in the incident.French President Emmanuel Macron has called for restraint and dialogue as the demonstrations continue.

Students have complained about deteriorating buildings, teacher shortages and school days that can stretch from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu has asked ministers to address their demands.Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond contributed to this report.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: Burnham to host Zelenskyy at No 10 in show of ‘rock-solid’ support
articles.excerpt:
Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump

Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK...
articles.body_text:
Prime minister reiterates UK backing after the Ukrainian president’s latest round of difficulties with Donald Trump

Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelenskyy at Downing Street on Wednesday as the UK seeks to further underline its support for the Ukrainian president, in contrast to his difficulties with Donald Trump.

The UK prime minister said his message to Zelenskyy and his country would be: “We are with you for as long as it takes.”

To coincide with the visit, the UK has said it will move more rapidly in providing Ukraine with British-made lightweight multi-role missiles (LMMs) to help protect it from attacks by a new generation of Russian jet-powered drones.

In parallel, Burnham and his ministers will push for a full international maritime services ban on exports of Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG).

The pair have already met twice since Burnham took office in July, when Zelenskyy visited a naval base in Portsmouth in the same month and when Burnham travelled to Kyiv in August.

Zelenskyy’s latest visit comes as Ukraine faces increased Russian missile and drone attacks, and after Donald Trump made a deal to buy Russian diesel, called for Ukraine to have a new leader, and announced a supposed ceasefire connected to energy infrastructure that the Ukrainian president said “was news to him”.

Trump is an often wayward ally for Ukraine, and Zelenskyy has expressed anger at the diesel deal, saying subsequent Russian attacks on civilian targets in Ukraine amounted to a “thanks” from Vladimir Putin.

UK governments have previously welcomed Zelenskyy after difficult experiences with Trump. He met Keir Starmer at Downing Street the day after Trump and his vice-president, JD Vance, publicly berated the Ukrainian president in the Oval Office 18 months ago.

During that trip Zelenskyy was also hosted by King Charles, who, in a pointedly personal touch, saw the Ukrainian president at Sandringham in Norfolk, which is a royal family home and rarely used for such visits.

Announcing the latest Downing Street meeting, No 10 said part of an ongoing £1.6bn package to deliver more than 5,000 LMMs to Ukraine would be sped up to help combat attacks by jet-powered drones.

These are quicker and higher-flying than the propeller-driven Shahed drones previously used, making them much harder to shoot down, allowing Russia to strike more targets in Ukraine, including in Kyiv.

The chancellor, John Healey, will separately use meetings at the ongoing International Monetary Fund summit in Bangkok to push other countries to ban Russian LNG.

In a statement before his meeting with Zelenskyy, Burnham said: “Our rock-solid support to Ukraine is vital for keeping us safe here in the UK and ensuring those on the frontlines have the equipment they need to push back Russia.

“My message to the Ukrainian people could not be clearer: we are with you for as long as it takes, and we will go further and faster in our support to back your courageous fight for peace in Europe.

“It is not just the right thing to do, but it’s the necessary thing to do. Russia’s aggression cannot be allowed to succeed on our continent.”

articles.title: California coastal homes battered and bruised after weekend of intense waves and flooding
articles.excerpt:
Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of e...
articles.body_text:
Boardwalk destroyed in Long Beach and homes damaged, while Baja California in Mexico and Las Vegas also affected

Southern California coastal communities are picking up the pieces after a weekend of extreme weather brought flooding that overtook city streets and intense waves battered beachside homes.

The remnants of Tropical Storm Rachel hit Mexico’s Baja California over the weekend as well as southern California and Las Vegas. While meteorologists noted that Rachel weakened into a post-tropical cyclone as it approached California, it still left a trail of destruction.

Footage showed massive waves crashing into Long Beach homes, destroying a boardwalk and forcing residents to flee. The damage to homes was significant, leaving some at risk of collapse.

At least nine have been deemed unsafe to enter, the Long Beach Post reported, meaning displaced residents cannot return to retrieve personal items. The storm has cost the city more than $1m from its emergency reserves, according to the outlet.

Farther south, the city of Newport Beach declared a local emergency and briefly closed piers to “protect public safety”, citing “higher-than-normal surf” that inundated streets.

By Monday, cleanup work was under way and Newport Beach had reopened the piers, but officials advised residents to exercise caution near the water.

In Las Vegas, a raging torrent of water rushed over a street near the strip, and the city tied an all-time daily rainfall record for October with 1.08in (2.74cm) of rain into Sunday morning, according to the US National Weather Service.

The impacts are just a taste of what’s to come across southern California as a historic El Niño unfolds in the Pacific, threatening to unleash severe storms across the region this winter.

Already, the last five hurricanes in the Pacific all reached major status and saw with winds of at least 111mph (178.6 km/h), and one set a record for time spent at category 5.

“This year, just everything that forms is just lasting a long time and getting really powerful,” Phil Klotzbach, a Colorado State University researcher who forecasts and studies storm activity, told the Associated Press, adding that the last month has been “berserk”.

The El Niño climate phenomenon, characterized by warmer than average equatorial sea surface temperatures, has the potential to supercharge extreme weather around the world. While it’s expected to strengthen through the end of this year and into next, the excess warmth already measured is climbing off the charts. Forecasters have warned its effects could become exceptionally destructive.

In California – especially in the southern part of the state – El Niños typically carry higher risks of severe storms, and with them elevated threats from landslides, debris flows and flash floods. These dangers become more pronounced around recent burn scars, adding hazards to several areas, including in the neighborhoods still recovering from the 2025 Los Angeles firestorm and swaths of Big Sur above Highway 1.

“This year’s tilt in the odds toward wet and stormy conditions in California will be profoundly unsubtle,” climate scientist Daniel Swain said in a recent analysis, adding that its unlike anything he’s observed before.

Throughout the winter months, El Niño could also add an additional foot of sea level rise in California on top of the 8in to 12in caused by the climate crisis over the last century, according to Michael Anderson, a state climatologist.

Already, El Niño has elevated sea levels up and down the California coast, from the Mexico border up to the San Francisco Bay Area. Warm waters expanding from an extreme marine heatwave combined with a coastally trapped Kelvin wave – a large underwater band of warm water – have already inundated parts of the North American shoreline. More Kelvin waves are likely and California is already bracing for unusually high king tides to hit during holiday weekends this year, arriving near Thanksgiving and Christmas.

While the impacts from heavy rains and high surf are each destructive in their own right, when they align and overlap they can cause even more calamity.

“Between November 2026 and January 2027, I would anticipate multiple significant coastal flood events that are worse in severity and also much more widespread than what we are currently seeing,” Swain said. “Even a moderate storm could bring water levels higher still, and a strong storm would likely produce widespread damaging, and probably historic, coastal flooding.”

Meanwhile, as cities across California begin preparations for intense winter weather, there are still months left before the risks from fire begin to subside. The National Weather Service issued fire weather watches for parts of southern California, including in Los Angeles, as seasonal strong, dry winds align with high temperatures. Forecasters warned that there would be “high risk for extreme fire behavior with any new fire starts Thursday through Friday”.

With the threat of fire, heat and sea level rise colliding, as the state readies for more incoming effects from El Niño, Kevin McGowan, the director of LA’s office of emergency management, urged residents to be ready. “People should continue to prepare not just for one hazard,” he said during a recent briefing, – but all hazards.”

The Associated Press contributed reporting

articles.title: Florida officials say six people dead from Hurricane Isaias
articles.excerpt:
Governor Ron DeSantis says death toll ‘sad’ but praises work of local officials for helping to minimize storm’s impact

Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias.
...
articles.body_text:
Governor Ron DeSantis says death toll ‘sad’ but praises work of local officials for helping to minimize storm’s impact

Six deaths have been confirmed in Florida in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias.

In a press conference on Tuesday, Florida governor Ron DeSantis praised the work of local officials for minimizing the impact of the storm, which made landfall late on Friday, ⁠bringing strong winds, rain, flash floods and tornado ​threats across parts of the ​US south-east, leaving hundreds of thousands ​of residents without power.

DeSantis confirmed that there are six deaths linked to Hurricane Isaias, including two previously confirmed deaths.

One person was killed after a fallen tree on a home resulted in a direct fatality. Another individual was found deceased in their garage with a running generator in Escambia county.

DeSantis confirmed that the remaining deaths linked to the storm include a car accident at an intersection, and storm-related disruptions to two people’s medical treatment.

Despite there being half a dozen of deaths, the governor praised Floridians and local officials for taking proper precautions, linking it to there being a lower death toll, compared to previous storms.

“We’re sad to hear that. At the same time, we’ve had some where there have been a lot more. So I think that people did take precautions and I think the local officials did a good job of spreading the word,” DeSantis said Tuesday.

There are about 5,000 people in Florida state that remain without power north-west of where the storm landed, according to DeSantis.

Free supplies are being provided at different locations of distribution to Floridians that have been impacted by the hurricane.

Isaias is the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season. As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is also the first hurricane to make landfall in the continental US in two years, since Milton struck western Florida in October 2024.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) said there is increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surges along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi.

articles.title: Pope Leo diagnosed with cancer after surgery to remove part of lung
articles.excerpt:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lun...
articles.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with cancer after an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, according to a medical bulletin published by the Vatican.

Tests confirmed a diagnosis of lung adenocarcinoma, the Vatican added, noting the diagnosis had been suspected by preoperative tests. It did not provide details on the recovery outlook or course of treatment.

In a statement released Tuesday, the Vatican said the procedure lasted 90 minutes and that the surgery “was successful, and there were no complications”.

The 71-year-old has returned to his room at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, where he is expected to recover for a week, with all his audiences through October 20 cancelled.

The Vatican said doctors are not currently discussing chemotherapy or other therapies pending the results of other tests.

The Holy See’s press office noted the medical statement spoke of the “radical” removal of the lobe as an indication that doctors removed all suspect tissue in the hope of eliminating any lingering traces of the cancer.

Before the procedure, Leo waved to dozens of well-wishers gathered at the hospital’s main entrance.

In an unusually transparent update on papal health, Leo first revealed that doctors found a small nodule during his Sunday noon prayer in St Peter’s Square.

“The doctors believe it’s best to take action, so, following their advice, I’ve decided to have surgery to remove it,” he said during remarks delivered in Italian.

The pope has no reported history of serious illness and is considered physically active, routinely swimming and playing tennis.

The surgery comes ahead of an official Latin America tour scheduled for November 6-17, with stops planned across Uruguay, Argentina and Peru.

It is unclear whether his recovery will affect the ambitious itinerary, which includes a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and significant altitude changes in Peru.

The pope told reporters on Sunday that he intends to make the journey.

articles.title: Atletico Madrid beat Manchester United 2-0 as winless run continues
articles.excerpt:
Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick.

Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Di...
articles.body_text:
Atletico Madrid eased to a 2-0 win over Manchester United in the Champions League on Tuesday to pile pressure on Red Devils coach Michael Carrick.

Pablo Barrios pounced inside the first minute for Diego Simeone’s side and after Leny Yoro’s 74th minute red card set United back further, Ademola Lookman added another for the hosts in Madrid.

Man United have made their worst domestic start in 40 years and this league phase defeat in the Spanish capital was another blow, with the team now winless in five games across all competitions.

Carrick handed Carlos Baleba his first start for the club since arriving from Brighton this summer, as well as pushing captain Bruno Fernandes out to the right side.

Atletico were without their skipper Koke, after the death of his mother, while coach Simeone selected Julian Alvarez from the off for the first time this season at the Metropolitano stadium, after he tried to force a departure this summer.

“Defend what we love,” Atletico fans ordered their supporters with a banner display before kick-off. The Rojiblancos were ahead after just 50 seconds.

Alex Baena found a way in behind United’s defence and cut the ball across for Barrios, with Ayden Heaven unable to keep the midfielder’s shot from crossing the line.

Bryan Mbuemo might have equalised for the visitors, nudging the ball through Cristian Romero’s legs but firing just wide.

Alejandro Grimaldo came inches away from extending Atletico’s lead with a free-kick which hit the angle between post and crossbar.

The hosts thought they had a second when Johnny Cardoso finished neatly from the edge of the box before half-time but the goal was disallowed after a VAR review showed the ball had struck Marcos Llorente’s hand during the build-up.

Alvarez, yet to score this season for Atletico, hit the post early in the second half.

United rallied and Fernandes’s lob drifted narrowly wide before the Portuguese playmaker hit the crossbar from the left of the box after a corner routine.

However, the three-time European champions suffered a setback when defender Yoro was harshly dismissed after a VAR review for bringing down Canada striker Jonathan David as the last man.

It opened the door for Atletico to grab their second, with David foiled by goalkeeper Senne Lammens but London-born Nigeria international Lookman on hand to tuck home the rebound after 79 minutes.

Carrick withdrew playmaker Fernandes, looking ahead to the weekend visit to face rivals Leeds in the English top flight, where improvement is badly needed.

Atletico goalkeeper Jan Oblak saved from United substitute Matheus Cunha in the final stages but there was no way back for United.

Simeone’s side were able to claim their first points after an opening defeat at Liverpool.

articles.title: JIM GRAY: Mike Ditka did it his way. Football will never see another like him
articles.excerpt:
Legendary Chicago Bears coach Mike Ditka passed away at 86. Fox News contributor and sportscaster Jim Gray speaks on Ditka's passing.

America knew him as a football legend. He became the NFL’s symbol...
articles.body_text:
Legendary Chicago Bears coach Mike Ditka passed away at 86. Fox News contributor and sportscaster Jim Gray speaks on Ditka's passing.

America knew him as a football legend. He became the NFL’s symbol of toughness and the emblem of Chicago. Mike Ditka was more than a Hall of Fame player and head coach who led the Bears to their unforgettable Super Bowl XX championship. He was a man who reached well beyond the football field. Coach Ditka was my partner on the radio for a nearly a decade.

On our show and podcast this week, "Let’s Go!," broadcast on SiriusXM NFL Radio, I paid tribute to and honored the life of Coach Ditka, along with my fellow co-hosts past and present — Tom Brady, Bill Belichick, Matthew Stafford, Drew Brees and Peter King. They joined me to speak about what Ditka meant to them and to the game of football. Here was our tribute.

It's been a very difficult few days since we've learned of the passing of Mike Ditka on Oct. 9, at age 86. Guys like Ditka are very rare. He was a once in a lifetime man. He seemed indestructible. I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die.

NFL COACHES SHARE INCREDIBLE MIKE DITKA STORIES AS FOOTBALL WORLD MOURNS THE BEARS LEGEND

America's Coach, that's what I called him, and that's who he was. He was my partner on the radio for many, many years. I truly loved him. He was so much fun. He lived his life to the absolute fullest.

Jim Gray is a 12-time Emmy Award winning Hall of Fame sportscaster and Fox News sports analyst and contributor. He is pictured here with legendary NFL coach Mike Ditka. (Courtesy Jim Gray)

Tough yet tender. Generous, yet demanding. Funny as hell and a temper that was explosive. He could make you laugh, make you nervous, make you cry, and also feel like the most important person in the room, sometimes all in the same conversation.

LIONS HEAD COACH PAYS TRIBUTE TO MIKE DITKA AFTER LEARNING OF HIS DEATH FROM A PRESS CONFERENCE QUESTION

He was never polished, never predictable, never interested in being politically correct or being liked by everybody.

Head Coach Mike Ditka of the Chicago Bears looks on from the sidelines against the Washington Redskins during an NFL football game November 26, 1989 at RFK Stadium in Washington, D.C.. Ditka was the head coach of the Bears from 1982-92. (Focus on Sport/Getty Images)

But perhaps there was no one in sports more beloved by his teammates, by his players, by his colleagues, by his opponents, and even by his critics.

MIKE DITKA TRIBUTES POUR IN FROM AROUND THE NFL INCLUDING FANS DRESSING LIKE HIM IN GREEN BAY

He was Iron Mike. Da Coach. A man of character, who was, a character.

The tombstone of Jackie Robinson reads, "A life is not important, except in the impact it has on other lives." Ditka's impact was enormous on Chicago, the NFL, sports, pop culture, and across the country.

I thought he would beat everything and everyone, and that he just might live forever because a guy like Mike Ditka isn't supposed to die.

He was bigger than life. Yet, he was always there and available for me personally. He traveled a great distance to introduce me and give the induction the day I was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. His words were heartfelt, helpful, and instructive.

Mike Ditka rides in the Pro Football Hall of Fame Enshrinement Festival Grand Parade in downtown Canton, Ohio, on Saturday, August 3, 2013. (Rodger Mallison/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) ( )

"I tell you what an honor this is when you really think about it. I don't know anybody else on this Walk of Fame, but I know you," Ditka said to me and the assembled audience. "What a great honor to be recognized by your peers for your achievements. And I know that you are a professional in everything you do, because when you do it, you do it right. Now I know that there's an art to everything in life. And if there is art to an interview, then you are Michelangelo, believe me, because you are good at that. Now, why is he good? Because he asks tough, hard, fair questions that you've got to answer. And the reason you've got to answer them is because the interview wouldn't work without your answer. And that's what makes him so good. I'm really proud to be your friend. We've been together for a long time," Ditka continued.

"Let me tell you something that I know for a fact about life. If you have no critics, you have no successes. God bless you."

CHICAGO, IL - CIRCA 1980's: Head Coach Mike Ditka of the Chicago Bears on the field before a mid circa 1980's NFL football game at Soldier Field in Chicago, Illinois. Ditka was the head coach of the Bears from 1982-92. (Photo by Focus on Sport/Getty Images) ( )

That sentiment, is so enlightening and edifying to anyone in public life. He knew it, and he chose successes. Critics be damned.

Ditka truly had it all. The mustache, cigar, volatility, the winning, the loyalty. He was one of a kind.

And for the people who knew him beyond the public persona, there was another side. The one of extraordinary kindness. They saw the moments when the bluster disappeared. Mike Ditka helped, truly helped, so many people. Whether they were fellow players in need, youngsters in crisis, seniors in peril, families that were struggling, or strangers in distress. Ditka was the most generous person I've ever known. I saw his commitment to contribute, respond, and was constantly giving of his time and resources. And he wanted and expected absolutely nothing in return for his countless, truly endless acts of goodwill.

That's the part you can't put in a highlight reel, and maybe that's the part that matters most.

Mike Ditka was coaching the New Orleans Saints when he met with Dan Campbell ahead of the 1999 NFL Draft. (RHONA WISE/AFP via Getty Images)

His life was lived to the lyrics of the song, "My Way."

"For what is a man? What has he got? If not himself, then he has not. To say the things he truly feels, and not the words of one who kneels. The record shows I took the blows and did it my way."

When somebody like that is gone, you don't just miss what he did. You miss his presence.

Bears Coach Mike Ditka and Hall of Fame sportscaster Jim Gray in an undated photo. (Jim Gray)

There will never be another Mike Ditka because as Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote,

"When nature removes a great man, people explore the horizon for a successor; but none comes, and none will. His class is extinguished with him."

Mike Ditka, my dear friend, America's coach, an institution and national treasure, was in a class all his own.

Every time we ended a conversation, Mike would never say goodbye. His words would always be, "God bless, Jimmy."

So, I won't say goodbye to Coach Ditka. I will follow his lead. God bless, Coach.

May God rest your soul and bless your family.

Here is what the all-time greats had to say during the show about Coach Ditka. This week’s episode of "Let’s Go!" can be heard here.

"There are so many things I loved about Coach Ditka from watching from afar and getting to know him over the course of my NFL career. He was as tough as the city that he coached in and he was the first tight end ever in the Hall of Fame. I heard Gronk on the pregame show say he owed a lot to Coach Ditka. Without Coach Ditka, there are no players like Rob Gronkowski who revolutionized the tight end position. And without Rob Gronkowski, I'm down a bunch of Super Bowls. So I gotta thank Coach Ditka for a lot of reasons. He won a Super Bowl as a player, he won a Super Bowl as a head coach. And as a quarterback, I always know what a great tight end means to an offense. He is my safety valve. That's your third down answer. And every one I ever threw to owes something to Mike."

"On TV, he also revolutionized the game with his media career. He never softened on a word. There was never a filter. There was no fluff. It was just all football. Rest easy, Coach Ditka."

"As a player, Mike was extremely tough, competitive, all business, a guy you certainly didn't wanna mess with and he set the tone for the teams that he played on. It was similar as a coach. He had that same toughness that transferred to his team and, and players. And you knew anytime you went up against him, like you were going to be in an absolute brawl and fight all the way to the finish because that's the way he and his teams competed. Loved Mike. Loved Mike and what he meant to the game. And we'll miss him."

"I had the pleasure of being on some of the NFL shows with him. You know, his presence was really something else. All these guys, they play football, they coach football, then they move to talking about football and they become just a guy that talks about football. But Ditka was always coach, right? I mean, and I remember, getting to do those shows with him. He had the cigar unlit under the table. He was just true to himself and that was such a cool thing to be a part of."

"He was not only an incredible player, but an incredible coach. There's a type of leadership where you just see things happen before they happen. You just have a vision for what the way that things should be, and then your contributions to getting it to that point. It's a rare trait. I think Mike was no question, was certainly one of those guys and man, he's gonna be missed."

"Nothing ever about Mike Ditka was invented, was put on anything. He always was himself. Ditka, as a player, as a coach, as a broadcaster, was authentic and he was perfect and he was dedicated to be great at whatever he did at that moment."

Jim Gray is a 12-time Emmy Award-winning Hall of Fame sportscaster and Fox News sports analyst and contributor.

articles.body_text:
"A referee gets tough because he's got a whistle. Screw these guys. Like at least the guys in the, at least the guys in Major League Baseball, just big fat guys that wallow around. Now, I think every ref should be suspended for the conduct of others. I hate them, I hate refs, I hate umpires, I hate officials, I hate all of them."

The National Football League is seemingly getting with the times.

The league rescinded its fine against Jameson Williams for his apparent smoking celebration after the Detroit Lions wide receiver argued that "marijuana is legal."

Recreational marijuana is legal in Michigan, where Williams plays his home games, along with 23 other states and Washington, D.C.

"Although I rescinded this fine, please make every effort to celebrate with your teammates in the best professional manner possible," appeals officer Derrick Brooks wrote, according to the NFL Network.

Williams' teammates have yet to hear back on their appeals.

Detroit Lions wide receiver Jameson Williams (1) reacts after scoring a touchdown during the first half of an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday, Nov. 16, 2025, in Philadelphia. (AP Photo/Matt Rourke)
