articles.title: ‘Peace through strength’: Trump Gaza plan gains global backing one year on
articles.excerpt: Ret. Four-Star Gen. Jack Keane breaks down the next phase of President Donald Trump's Gaza peace deal on 'Fox & Friends.' Keane explains how the historic agreement mandates the complete disarmament of...
articles.body_text:
Ret. Four-Star Gen. Jack Keane breaks down the next phase of President Donald Trump's Gaza peace deal on 'Fox & Friends.' Keane explains how the historic agreement mandates the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups, leading to the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the transition of power to a new Palestinian government.

A year has passed since President Donald Trump made history by brokering a ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, setting in motion an ambitious peace plan aimed at bringing lasting stability to the region.

In the days and months since the ceasefire and Trump’s 20-point peace plan took hold, progress has drawn support from across the globe — including from unexpected quarters.

Senior advisor to the Board of Peace Josh Gruenbaum told Fox News Digital that the success of the last 12 months was largely attributable to President Donald Trump’s leadership and commitment to seeking peace.

TRUMP-BACKED BOARD OF PEACE, ISRAEL 'WILL TAKE ACTION' IF HAMAS REMAINS OUT OF COMPLIANCE: NETANYAHU ADVISOR

U.S. President Donald Trump poses with the signed agreement at a world leaders' summit on ending the Gaza war, amid a U.S.-brokered prisoner-hostage swap and ceasefire deal between Israel and Hamas, in Sharm el-Sheikh, Egypt, October 13, 2025. REUTERS/Suzanne Plunkett/Pool (Suzanne Plunkett/Reuters)

"The unlock was somebody who came in, who really knew the file because they had the chance to study it and understand it," Gruenbaum said. Trump and his team, including U.S. Special Envoy to the Middle East Steve Witkoff, U.S. Special Envoy for Peace Jared Kushner and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, "created working relationships with regional actors with trust, overlaid with peace through strength," while also forcing Hamas to finally understand that "this was either going to end the very hard way for them, or there was an off-ramp and a way to do this in a more dignified way, which is what the 20-point-plan was."

He said this has been achieved by "building consensus through the world, including through Europe, that this is the only game in town. This is the only pragmatic approach to make this thing stop." A particular point of strength for the Board of Peace, Gruenbaum added, has been "cultivating really strong relationships with the United Nations."

In Nov. 2025, the United Nations endorsed the Board of Peace through Resolution 2803.

Prior to his meeting with President Trump at the White House, Prime Minister Netanyahu signed up, in the presence of Secretary of State Rubio, as a member of the Board of Peace. (@IsraeliPM)

European Union Commissioner for the Mediterranean and for Demography, Dubravka Šuica, announced at a high-level briefing at the Board of Peace in September that the European Union had "gathered about $1 billion for early recovery in Gaza," and would sign recovery projects with the UNDP and UNICEF. "We are doing this in alignment with the priorities of the Board of Peace and the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG)," Suica stated.

US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION

The International Stabilization Force, which will train a future police force in Gaza and oversee demilitarization, has received commitments from Kazakhstan, Morocco, Albania and Kosovo, with other countries said to be in the pipeline for admission.

Notably absent from Gaza’s future, per the Board of Peace plan, is the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA). The Board of Peace has been unequivocal that UNRWA will have no involvement in Gaza. One U.S. agency, the USAID Office of the Inspector General, is currently investigating over 1,500 UNRWA employees for involvement in terror groups.

Hamas terrorists stand guard on the day of the handover of hostages held in Gaza since the deadly October 7 2023 attack, as part of a ceasefire and a hostages-prisoners swap deal between Hamas and Israel, in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, Feb. 22, 2025. (Hatem Khaled/Reuters)

On X, the Board of Peace recently stated that it "will only work with trusted partners who deliver for the people of Gaza and contribute to a deradicalized Strip," and emphasized that "UNRWA fails on those litmus tests."

The Board of Peace’s effort has support from unlikely corners. Former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton wrote in a June editorial in the Financial Times that while the plan was "not the one many of us would have drafted," she believes "it remains the only framework backed by sufficient leverage, political engagement and potential resources to move parties towards implementation."

The Board of Peace has received about $18 billion in pledges for reconstruction, the BBC recently reported. A Board of Peace official told Fox News Digital that next steps in the reconstruction program include a six-month program with 66 recovery initiatives, including rubble clearance, unexploded ordnance clearance, construction of temporary housing and destroying tunnel infrastructure. The initiatives are expected to cost $2.45 billion, and tenders for some projects have been submitted.

KUSHNER GIVES HAMAS STARK ULTIMATUM: DISARM OR ISRAEL GETS US BACKING TO ‘FINISH THE JOB’

In the year ahead, the Board of Peace must clear a number of hurdles, including a full demilitarization and de-radicalization of Hamasin Gaza. Gruenbaum says that the Board of Peace is "realistic and sober" but is also "in a historic place with Hamas," having secured verbal agreements and offering a path to amnesty for those who qualify.

Gruenbaum also says that the 20-point plan is Hamas’ best path forward and that regional dynamics leave them with few remaining options. Mediators are increasingly supporting the Board of Peace, Tehran is focused on its current war, and Israel is continuing to apply pressure, though Gruenbaum says the Board of Peace continues to stress that they must comply with the ceasefire.

Hamas terrorists carrying clubs and firearms secure, and divert humanitarian aid trucks in the northern Gaza area of Jabaliya on June. 25 (TPS-IL)

Gruenbaum said that deradicalization will never be a top-down process led by the U.S., but will be managed through the NCAG. He said that the NCAG’s members "have kids that have been brought up" under the current UNRWA-run system, so "they understand the situation." The approach will involve the new technocratic government, whose members have extensive experience in civil service, taking the lead on "vetting teachers" and "vetting people who are involved in civil governance."

Gruenbaum celebrated the potential of bringing together the NCAG and Israeli authorities through the transformation of Gaza. "This is a monumental opportunity for the Palestinian people of Gaza where their governing body is going to be uniquely focused on delivering services for its constituents and if we could create this amazing relationship where we build trust between Israel and the NCAG, we deliver on both sides of the equation – security for Israel and freedom and a better life, self-determination and prosperity-building inside of Gaza. That’s a two-way trust building system."

Gruenbaum added that the successes in Gaza could lead to successes elsewhere. "Maybe these best practices get learned by the Palestinian Authority. Maybe Israel starts adding more trust with different people in the system. I think this is a huge moment in the history of the Middle East."

Beth Bailey writes on the United Nations, worldwide antisemitism, and regions in conflict for Fox News.

articles.title: British and Irish governments ‘should negotiate paramilitary disbandment in Northern Ireland’
articles.excerpt:
Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups

The British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to negoti...
articles.body_text:
Report finds ‘window of opportunity’ for formal process involving loyalist and republican groups

The British and Irish governments should engage with paramilitary groups in Northern Ireland to negotiate their disbandment, according to a report.

A “window of opportunity” exists to establish a formal transition mechanism for loyalist and republican groups, provided certain conditions are met, it said.

The Independent Report on Paramilitary Group Transition to Disbandment, commissioned by both governments and published on Tuesday, said groups should not receive financial rewards for engaging in the process.

Fleur Ravensbergen, a Dutch conflict resolution expert who authored the report, said in Belfast: “I have concluded that there is sufficient merit in and support for a formal process of paramilitary group transition.”

Ravensbergen said she found “significant willingness to engage” among paramilitaries during a year-long scoping exercise.

She added: “There was limited support for the term ‘disbandment’ as the endpoint of a transition process. However, objections to disbandment appeared to be less about what transition should achieve and more about the wording.”

Paramilitary groups were expected to fade after the 1998 Good Friday agreement, but some endured and evolved into lucrative enterprises involved in drug dealing, extortion and coercive control.

Agreeing a transition process was more important than the terminology used to describe disbandment, said Ravensbergen, a lecturer in conflict resolution and governance at the University of Amsterdam.

She said: “I believe that the risks of the persistence of paramilitary structures, continued drift and unmanaged fragmentation outweigh the risks associated with attempting a structured and time-bound transition process. Inaction is not a neutral option. My consultations suggest that a window of opportunity exists to pursue further progress, but that this may weaken over time.”

Chris Bryant, the Northern Ireland secretary, thanked Ravensbergen and said the government was committed to ending paramilitarism.

Bryant said: “While these groups may pose as protectors of their communities, they are largely engaged in criminality including drug dealing, extortion and intimidation, blighting the very communities they perversely claim to protect. Their continued influence is a stain on our collective conscience.”

He said the government would consider the report and liaise with authorities in Dublin before responding to the proposed transition mechanism.

He added: “It is evident from the report that the implementation of any process will face challenges and will need the support from across the political community in Northern Ireland.”

Naomi Long, Northern Ireland’s justice minister and a member of the Alliance party, criticised Ravensbergen’s appointment as an interlocutor last year, saying engagement with paramilitaries and criminal gangs risked giving them a veneer of legitimacy.

Long said at the time: “The idea that paramilitary groups can transition into law-abiding entities has long since moved beyond the point of credibility. They cannot continue to be treated as if they are genuinely committed to reform – that moment passed long ago.”

The report did not identify individuals or specific organisations because discussions were held on a confidential basis.

It said: “The nature, extent and impact of paramilitary influence vary considerably between paramilitary groups, communities and geographical areas. However, it is clear that residual paramilitary structures continue to cause harm in some communities.”

Ravensbergen said a transition mechanism would need credible monitoring and verification of progress and robust law enforcement.

She declined to comment on the recent standoff between the Orange Order and nationalist residents at Garvaghy Road in Portadown, saying it was outside the report’s remit. There is speculation that renewed tension over the Drumcree parade may boost paramilitary recruitment.

articles.title: Texas man run over by ICE has never met the person agents were allegedly chasing
articles.excerpt:
Miguel Parra-Hernandez suffers from serious hip and leg injuries in Houston and remains in ICE custody, according to his representatives

US man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him an...
articles.body_text:
Miguel Parra-Hernandez suffers from serious hip and leg injuries in Houston and remains in ICE custody, according to his representatives

US man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him and daughter

A Texas man whose leg was broken in multiple places after being struck by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) vehicle during a weekend traffic stop has never met the person the federal agents were allegedly pursuing, according to his representatives.

Miguel Parra-Hernandez, 48, suffered serious injuries including a shattered ankle and hip when he was run over in Houston, Texas, on Saturday by an SUV driven by an officer chasing two men who ran from a pickup truck.

ICE, according to multiple media reports, said it was in pursuit of another man, Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, during an early-morning operation and attempted a vehicle stop before the occupants ran away. It said Parra-Hernandez was not its target – but he ran in front of the ICE vehicle and was struck.

Video of the incident aired by ABC News affiliate KTRK, however, shows a dark-colored, unmarked SUV following Parra-Hernandez and veering towards him as he ran across empty spaces in the shopping center parking lot in Harris county, whose seat is Houston.

Parra-Hernandez’s attorney, Kim Bruno, and Cesar Espinosa, executive director of the immigrant advocacy group FIEL Houston, told reporters at a news conference on Monday that Parra-Hernandez remained in ICE custody and faced more surgery as well as many weeks of recovery.

Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez was hit “in a violent and brutal fashion”. Bruno said he told her that he fled because he did not know who was in the dark-colored vehicle. Neither he nor the other person in the car, whom he had picked up for work, knew Mendoza-Cervantes, she said.

The ICE vehicle, she added, was not using a siren or displaying flashing lights.

Earlier in October, ICE adopted new rules for traffic stops, including ensuring that vehicles are equipped with lights and sirens to let the public know they are law enforcement vehicles, although it did not mandate their use.

The guidelines, in a memo written by Marcos Charles, executive associate director of ICE, and obtained by the Associated Press, state that ICE officers are no longer permitted to chase vehicles that refuse to stop. The memo came after a series of violent and fatal confrontations involving federal immigration officers over the summer.

Espinosa said he and Bruno were able to meet briefly with Parra-Hernandez at the hospital on Monday morning. But their visit ended after about 15 minutes when ICE agents entered the room and began recording their conversation, and they were made to leave.

“To add insult to injury, Mr Miguel is in the custody of the ICE agents who ran him down,” Espinosa said, as reported by NBC News.

“This is so disheartening and so angering that Miguel has to face the people that brutally attacked them every single day, 24 hours a day.”

The Guardian has contacted ICE for comment.

Espinosa said Parra-Hernandez sustained hip and leg injuries, including a shattered ankle. Doctors have said he cannot put weight on his leg for at least six weeks, and Parra must wait for swelling to recede before reconstructive surgery can take place, Espinosa said.

Parra was struck at about 7.30am on Saturday. Witnesses said he remained on the ground for at least seven minutes after he was struck.

Bruno said Parra-Hernandez told her that the other person in the car was not Mendoza-Cervantes, who ICE has identified as an illegal immigrant with multiple previous arrests and a judicially issued final order of removal from the US.

She said Parra-Hernandez has lived in the US for 34 years, having arrived at age 14, and has no criminal record.

Harris county district attorney Sean Teare said Monday his office was investigating the Parra-Hernandez case.

The Harris county sheriff’s office said in a statement that it was called by ICE after the crash, which occurred as the agency has been met with nationwide criticism throughout Donald Trump’s second presidency for its aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.

Footage from Saturday’s case appeared to show an ICE agent entering the pickup truck Parra was in and driving it into the parking lot, before driving off in an unmarked vehicle. Maj Anthony McConnell told the Texas news outlet KTRK that ICE personnel moved the truck before his officers arrived.

articles.title: Memphis coach Penny Hardaway says he paid $2.6 million of his own money to Tigers' revenue share

"I've said before, there are three great days in a coach's life … Birth of a child, wedding day, and a road win. And of course, the order depends on how big a win. That's a big win for Charlie Huff and the fellows at Memphis coming in their first game going against the Mountain West favorites."

It is no secret that this upcoming college basketball season is a make-or-break year for Penny Hardaway and the Memphis Tigers, and the head coach is doing everything he can to make it a successful campaign, including putting nearly his entire annual salary back into the team's roster budget.

Hardaway, entering year nine as the Tigers' head coach, revealed to the Memphis Commercial Appeal during American Conference media day that he is contributing $2.6 million of his own money into Memphis' revenue share. His salary this season is $2.9 million, and the contribution brings the team's revenue share to $9 million, according to the outlet.

"They were saying if you want more money you have to put your money in. So I did," Hardaway told the Commercial Appeal, while also clarifying that the university did not ask him to make the contribution.

Head coach Penny Hardaway of the Memphis Tigers reacts during the game against the Arkansas State Red Wolves at FedExForum on December 08, 2024 in Memphis, Tennessee. (Photo by Justin Ford/Getty Images) (Justin Ford/Getty Images)

Hardaway's contribution back into his program comes as the Tigers are welcoming nine newcomers via the transfer portal in 2026, with the group being headlined by forward Rihards Vavers from Washington State and point guard Brandin Cummings out of Pitt. Memphis is also hopeful Nemanja Popovic, who played professionally in Poland a season ago, takes the floor for the program this season.

With Memphis being a city that eats and breathes the game of basketball and consistently produces top-tier talent, the Tigers should be a dominant force in what is now a well-below-average American Conference.

The Tigers seemed to be building something special in 2021 by winning the NIT and then advancing to the Round of 32 during the 2022 NCAA Tournament, but simply have not managed to take a step forward over the course of the last few seasons.

Hardaway is under contract until April 2028, and while the paper indicates that his job is secure beyond this season, he's well aware of what is at stake.

"I didn’t want to fail two years in a row, because I already know what that means for me," Hardaway shared with the Commercial Appeal.

With Hardaway being a Memphis native and a Tiger legend himself, it has felt like he's been given the benefit of the doubt when other coaches in his situation would not have been, but another season without an NCAA Tournament berth could be the end of his run in the 901.

articles.title: Majority in US say Trump prioritises personal wealth over all else: Poll
articles.excerpt: Most US adults believe President Donald Trump has placed his personal financial interests and those of his inner circle ahead of the country’s since returning to the White House in 2025, according to ...
articles.body_text:
Most US adults believe President Donald Trump has placed his personal financial interests and those of his inner circle ahead of the country’s since returning to the White House in 2025, according to a new nationwide poll.

The poll, conducted by the Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research and released on Tuesday, suggests that public perception of the Republican president leans heavily critical: Over half of surveyed adults view Trump’s second term as self-serving by investing in his own business and commercial pursuits “a lot”. Roughly one quarter believe he focuses on national interests, but only 11 percent feel Trump represents regular Americans. Fifty-five percent of Republicans surveyed said that Trump has prioritised his personal business interests “a lot” or “some”.

Half of the respondents report that Trump has placed zero priority on people “like them”.

As Trump’s family business pulls in record funds from new ventures helped by his policies, the poll results suggest that most US adults think growing his own finances has been the north star of Trump’s presidency, at least to some extent.

Trump’s June financial disclosure revealed massive post-election influxes of foreign and corporate capital into his business empire, stemming primarily from over $1bn in cryptocurrency ventures after he loosened regulation on the industry, as well as from international real estate.

During his first year as president, the Trump Organisation – Trump’s multinational family-owned enterprise dedicated to property development and global brand licensing – made eight real estate deals with authoritarian or one-party foreign states. Some speculate these countries were highly motivated to maintain favourable relations with the US to keep Trump happy on fronts like trade tariffs, military protection and private business dealings.

The administration, meanwhile, has repeatedly dismissed concerns over Trump’s business conflicts of interest, maintaining that he acts solely in the interest of Americans.

In late September, a separate Reuters/Ipsos poll found that Trump’s approval rating has fallen to 32 percent – the lowest of his ⁠political career – as his fellow Republicans soured on his handling of the cost of living crisis amid the deeply unpopular Iran war.

The dip in performance and approval ratings follows a high point in January 2025, when the newly inaugurated president boasted a 47 percent approval rating right after taking office.

According to the AP-NORC poll, which surveyed more than 2,000 US adults in late September, general sentiment around the administration’s ethical conduct is highly polarised, with far more citizens feeling that the president has neither prioritised the country as a whole nor everyday Americans.

Just over 40 percent of respondents believe Trump has “done something illegal” vis-a-vis allegations of personal enrichment while in office, with another 18 percent viewing his financial dealings as “unethical but not illegal”.

Opinions surrounding the lawfulness of the president’s financial practices split sharply along party lines, with Democrats overwhelmingly viewing the actions as illegal, compared with about three in 10 independents and about one in 10 Republicans, who largely see his behaviour as justified.

articles.title: UK spy chief says Iran is stepping up targeting of military bases
articles.excerpt:
UK PM says RAF base incidents 'likely coordinated' by Iran

The head of the United Kingdom’s domestic spy agency has said Iran is ramping up attempts to strike sensitive military targets after a serie...
articles.body_text:
UK PM says RAF base incidents 'likely coordinated' by Iran

The head of the United Kingdom’s domestic spy agency has said Iran is ramping up attempts to strike sensitive military targets after a series of incidents at airbases in Britain, even as Tehran has denied any involvement.

In his annual speech, M15 Director-General Ken McCallum on Tuesday said there had been a major shift in Tehran’s calculus this year and that “Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites”.

McCallum’s warning came after UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) was “almost certainly” behind a suspected plot against Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford, an airbase used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran. The incident prompted the United States to withdraw its military jets from the facility over security concerns earlier this month.

British police declared a major incident after three “suspicious” vans drove close to the RAF Fairford airbase in Gloucestershire on September 27. Five British men in their 20s were arrested “on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act”, but all were released on bail.

Police said they found a supply of petrol in three vans linked to the suspects, but no explosives. The men were later released without charge on police bail “under stringent conditions”.

Two others were arrested later, including a British-Iranian national, but were later released. None of the men have been charged.

Two Latvian men were arrested for trespassing at RAF Molesworth, which is used by the US military and NATO for intelligence operations, on Friday. The men were also released on bail.

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that the government was sanctioning two Iranians for their “role in facilitating or engaging in hostile activity on behalf of the Iranian regime”.

One is Ruhollah Bazghandi, the head of IRGC counterespionage operations, and the other is Shahram Ali Reza Tamarzadeh Jakki, whom British officials described as a facilitator for Iran’s Zindashti criminal network.

McCallum said he could not speak about the recent incident at RAF Fairford because it was an ongoing investigation, but added, “The RAF Fairford incident … is ⁠not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world.”

The spy chief said UK authorities had carried out 50 arrests over the past year to disrupt Iran-linked operations.

However, he said he doubted Iran’s ability to launch complex attacks, perhaps using explosive drones, due to the limited sophistication of operatives Tehran used in the UK.

“Given what we’ve actually seen in practice in the UK ⁠in recent years, that has not been anywhere near [that] level of capability,” McCallum said.

“That said, clearly it is the case that in countries closer to its own homeland, the IRGC has quite ⁠deep experience of using more conventional and hybrid technology in a more aggressive and ⁠sophisticated way,” the MI5 boss added.

Tehran has rejected accusations ‌of involvement in the Fairford incident or any other accusations of harmful activity in Britain.

articles.title: Hundreds of early-release prisoners in England and Wales not being tagged, say MPs
articles.excerpt:
Clive Efford says Serco has failed to source enough tags, as police and probation struggle with influx of newly released offenders

Hundreds of prisoners released early across England and Wales, inclu...
articles.body_text:
Clive Efford says Serco has failed to source enough tags, as police and probation struggle with influx of newly released offenders

Hundreds of prisoners released early across England and Wales, including stalkers and violent offenders, are not being tagged by Serco, MPs have said, despite promises of the “toughest supervision in British history”.

As the government begins to release a second tranche of 650 offenders to relieve the prison overcrowding crisis, police and probation officers have said they are struggling to cope with a new influx of offenders who are supposed to be monitored in the community.

Speaking during an urgent question in the Commons on Tuesday, the Labour MP Clive Efford asked why the outsourcing company Serco had failed to ensure there were enough tags for prisoners as they leave each prison.

“They are not actually fulfilling their contracts. It can’t be beyond the tech firm’s ability to tag people on release. So what are these companies going to do about it?” he said.

The shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, said most prisoners were not being tagged before release, despite assurances from the government that the tagging system would be the “toughest in history”.

“The justice secretary told the country that proper safeguards would be put in place with a presumption that all released prisoners would be tagged. He called it the toughest tagging regime in history, but that was nonsense,” he said.

Jake Richards, the justice minister, replied: “We are working closely with Serco and have seen an improvement in the implementation since March this year. Although there is a presumption of every person being tagged, ultimately it is an operational decision.”

About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.

Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.

Typically, those being released should expect to be electronically tagged and subject to other monitoring conditions for the second third of their sentence.

But the probation service union, Napo, said the releases were putting enormous strain on its members, who monitor offenders in the community.

The union held a pre-ballot meeting on Tuesday on taking strike action over pay and workloads. Pay negotiations ended earlier in October with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.

The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early from 2022.

A senior Prison and Probation Service source said a failure to place tags on released offenders as they left prison meant it could then be up to a month before they were tagged. “If we do not tag them as they leave prison, there is a good chance that we won’t tag them at all before they reoffend,” they said.

Mark Rowley, the Metropolitan police commissioner, said many of those who breached the terms of their tags – by consuming alcohol or drugs, or by breaching a curfew, for example – were not facing sanctions if arrested. “We’re seeing 95%-plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition. So there is zero sanction,” he said.

The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.

Alex Norris, the justice secretary, has said released offenders will be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”. New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure their victims.

However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan was “not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

articles.title: White House says it has asked Kimberly Guilfoyle to resign as US ambassador to Greece – live
articles.excerpt:
Guilfoyle has been under immense scrutiny after the Wall Street Journal reported on a series of questionable acts prior to securing her role in Athens

Katie Zacharia said today the administration has...
articles.body_text:
Guilfoyle has been under immense scrutiny after the Wall Street Journal reported on a series of questionable acts prior to securing her role in Athens

Katie Zacharia said today the administration has asked Kimberley Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, to resign.

“She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well,” the new press secretary said at her first media briefing, without providing any further details.

A reminder that Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, was under immense scrutiny after the Wall Street Journal reported on a series of questionable acts prior to securing her role in Athens. This included an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to wield influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a $100,000 credit card bill.

Trump also teased, again, the possibility of helping Saudi Arabia in its ongoing conflict against Iran-backed Houthi rebels, after an attack over the weekend at Riyadh’s main international airport killed 13 people.

“The Houthis have acted very badly,” Trump said, noting that he wouldn’t reveal if he had made a decision.

He also said that he “might” encourage President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan of Turkey to help the operation in Yemen. “He’s a great friend of mine,” Trump said.

It wasn’t immediately clear what Katie Zacharia answered when reporters asked her today when and where she passed the bar exam to practice law.

The State Bar of California doesn’t yield any results for Zacharia, or her maiden name – Black.

The new press secretary will now travel with the president over the coming days for several campaign rallies in Alaska, Arizona and Montana.

Speaking to reporters outside the White House, with the new press secretary waiting in the background, Donald Trump said the US is still sharing intelligence with Ukraine, after the president and Volodymyr Zelenskyy feuded this weekend, following the announcement that the US would lift diesel sanctions on Russia.

“We are helping them, and we are sharing intel. We want the war to end. So we’re working with them and with Russia on getting the war to end,” Trump said, after Katie Zacharia was unable to answer the question in the briefing room earlier.

“Honestly, they both want it to end, and they don’t know how to get to that point. There’s a lot of hatred there between the two of them,” the president added.

And as the midterms come sharply into view, my colleague Rachel Leingang has compiled a list of the 10 under-the-radar races in this election that are worth watching.

From Senate competitions to House races that have now caught our attention in this final sprint, here are the ones we’re keeping an eye on:

While speaking to reporters, JD Vance also addressed the reports that top Republican donor groups are pulling support from certain races throughout the country, particularly key House races they once saw as competitive.

One of those is for New Jersey’s seventh congressional district, where Republican incumbent Tom Kean Jr is facing Democrat Rebecca Bennett, a former US navy helicopter pilot. A reminder that Kean was absent from Congress for several months this year, which led to immense speculation, before he revealed that he was being treated for depression.

“Look, New Jersey is a very blue state. It was always going to be a really, really big thing for us to win in New Jersey,” Vance said, when discussing the GOP’s chances at holding on to the lower chamber. “I think there are a number of races, for example, in Minnesota, in traditionally blue areas, where we think we have a real chance. So I think the nature of a midterm election is sometimes these races have more of an individual rather than a national character. I feel good about where we are.”

Vance also said today that he “did not have advance notice” that Ilhan Omar’s Washington home was being raided by federal agents.

“We try to let the law follow the facts rather than creating facts just to prosecute people we don’t like. And because of that, I think the president and I largely try to stay out of Department of Justice investigations and other prosecutions,” the vice-president claimed. “Now, I do know that there are some serious allegations against Ilhan Omar. We’re going to look into those. And again, if there’s a real case there, we’re going to follow the facts. If there’s not a real case there, then we won’t.”

While Trump prepares to head to Wasilla, Alaska today, vice-president JD Vance will be in Tyler, Texas to campaign for Ken Paxton, the beleaguered Republican attorney general in a competitive Senate race against Democratic state legislator James Talarico.

Speaking to reporters Vance said acknowledged that Paxton, who is trailing Talarico in recent polling, is in a “tight race”.

“I think he’s ultimately going to win,” the vice-president said. “I know from personal history, when a lot of money comes against you, that can have an effect even in the red state.”

Republican aligned groups, however, have spent more than $170m to boost Paxton’s chances, outpacing the amount Democratic groups have spent supporting Talarico’s bid.

The Supreme Court agreed Tuesday to hear a case that could decide whether the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) must release information that is requested under the Freedom of Information Act (Foia).

The Trump administration had asked the high court to intervene in the dispute between Doge and a government watchdog group called Citizens of Responsibility and Ethics. The group had requested internal communications between Doge leaders, Doge employees and government officials.

Doge, a government initiative led by Elon Musk, played a key role in mass firings of government employees, restructuring federal agencies and widespread cancelation of government contracts.

Administration officials have argued Doge is not required to comply with Foia requests because it is not an official agency; rather, it is a presidential advisory group.

Overall, Zacharia kept her briefing short, and only took five questions from three reporters.

On foreign policy, Zacharia was unable to answer whether the US had stopped sharing intel with Ukraine, after Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy feuded over the US president’s decision to lift sanction on Russian diesel imports.

Katie Zacharia said today the administration has asked Kimberley Guilfoyle, the US ambassador to Greece, to resign.

“She has been a wonderful asset to the team, and we wish her well,” the new press secretary said at her first media briefing, without providing any further details.

A reminder that Guilfoyle, who was once engaged to Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, was under immense scrutiny after the Wall Street Journal reported on a series of questionable acts prior to securing her role in Athens. This included an alleged threat to a host country official, accepting improper gifts and services and offering to wield influence inside the administration in return for the payment of a $100,000 credit card bill.

Zacharia also said she would travel with the president for his upcoming allies in Alaska, Arizona and Montana, in the final three-week sprint until the midterm elections.

She has also run through many of the White House talking points touting the administration’s self-proclaimed achievements.

“Real wages are up 1.2% since President Trump took office, with average annual earnings outpacing inflation by $800,” Zacharia said. However, according to the latest figures from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), inflation, which sits at 3.4%, is still outpacing wage growth, currently at 3.1%.

Katie Zacharia has just stepped up to the podium as she kicks off her tenure as White House press secretary.

“I want to thank President Trump for his trust that he has placed in me. I have wanted to work for him for a very long time,” Zacharia told a briefing room packed with reporters. “I’m looking forward to working with each of you as well, especially as we are in the middle of the midterm blitz, with energy and excitement never seen before.”

Today we can expect a ruling from federal judge on the administration’s attempts to ban CNN, Politico and MS Now from the White House.

A reminder that Judge Timothy Kelly temporarily blocked Donald Trump from blocking the newsrooms, and extended this pause until Tuesday 13 October. In court last week, a lawyer for the three outlets insisted that the ban violated the first amendment, and that the administration’s reasoning was squarely based on the fact that Trump does not like their coverage. He also undermined the justice department’s claims that the newsrooms compromised national security through their reporting.

Kelly has also expressed criticism at the White House’s decision to revoke access without providing ample notice to CNN, Politico and MS Now.

The outlets are requesting that Kelly extend his temporary restraining order while the litigation plays out. We’ll bring you the latest as we hear more.

articles.title: IMF raises UK growth forecast as economist says Healey should ‘stay the course’
articles.excerpt:
Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to ‘edge down’ next year

IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

John Healey should “stay t...
articles.body_text:
Fund upgrades UK’s GDP growth forecast for 2026 to 1.3%, but says it is likely to ‘edge down’ next year

IMF warns global economy ‘could soon test the limits of resilience’

John Healey should “stay the course” and continue repairing the UK’s public finances, the International Monetary Fund’s top economist has said, after the fund lifted its growth forecast for Britain.

Little more than a fortnight before Healey’s first budget, Silvana Tenreyro, the IMF’s economic counsellor, said the UK “stands out” among G7 countries in having a plan to narrow its deficit.

“The UK has already started a consolidation process,” she said. “The message for the UK is simply, stay the course.”

Tenreyro, a former member of the Bank of England’s monetary policy committee, was speaking at the launch of the IMF’s twice-yearly World Economic Outlook (WEO) at the Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok.

Healey is under pressure to announce a generous energy support package in the budget, before the sharp rise in energy bills expected in January.

But in its WEO, the IMF advises member governments against across-the-board subsidies, saying any support should be “temporary, targeted and non-distortionary”.

In a fillip for the chancellor, who is poised to arrive in Bangkok later this week, the IMF has upgraded its growth forecast for the UK this year, but expects a modest slowdown in 2027 as higher energy prices take their toll.

Responding, Healey said: “conflict in the Middle East and Europe is hitting people in the UK and around the world. But Britain’s economy is showing strong international resilience in the face of these challenges.”

The IMF predicted GDP growth of 1.3% for the UK this year – up 0.3 percentage points from its most recent update in July.

UK GDP growth has been stronger than expected in early 2026, at 0.6% in the first quarter and 0.5% in the second quarter. The Office for National Statistics has pointed to the strong expansion of AI-related businesses as one factor behind the upside surprise.

However, the IMF warned that prolonged high oil prices and rising interest rates meant growth was likely to “edge down” in 2027, “as higher energy prices and long-term interest rates weigh on consumption and investment”.

It cut its UK growth forecast for next year modestly to 1.2%, from 1.3%.

Markets have been revising up their expectations of future inflation and interest rates across big economies, since the Middle East conflict re-escalated in the summer.

The Bank of England’s nine-member monetary policy committee is now widely expected to raise the policy rate at its November meeting – echoing similar moves by the Federal Reserve, European Central Bank and Bank of Japan.

Mortgage rates in the UK have already been rising in response to higher funding costs for banks in financial markets.

BoE policymaker Megan Greene argued on Tuesday morning that the IMF’s growth upgrade was proof that UK interest rates should be higher.

Speaking to the Atlantic Council at the International Monetary Fund meetings in Bangkok, Greene argued that interest rates were currently not very restrictive.

“There’s more recently been some labour market data that has also suggested that maybe slack in the labour market has peaked, so the labour market is loose,” Greene said.

The IMF singled out the UK as among the countries – also including Japan – where core inflation, which excludes volatile commodities such as energy, is not expected to return to the 2% target until late next year.

It expects average inflation in the UK to be 3.3% this year, and to remain at 2.8% in 2027 – a challenge for Healey and the prime minister, Andy Burnham, who are promising to offer voters a “breathing space” from rising costs.

Healey will spend little more than 24 hours in the Thai capital before flying home to put the finishing touches to his 28 October budget.

He is expected to focus on plans to devolve more tax revenues to mayoralties, alongside measures to help households cope with higher energy bills before the winter.

A string of other challenging decisions, including when the UK should be aiming to spend 3% of GDP on defence, is expected to be delayed until a big spending review at some point next year.

The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned this week that the budget would be a “work of fiction” unless Healey explained how he would deal with what it said were £35bn of future spending pressures.

articles.title: Two ships hit by drones of unknown origin off Bulgarian coast – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Rescue operations underway after one vessel damaged and another sunk in the Black Sea

Over in Warsaw, Poland’s parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty is beginning his opening speech telling the aud...
articles.body_text:
Rescue operations underway after one vessel damaged and another sunk in the Black Sea

Over in Warsaw, Poland’s parliament speaker Włodzimierz Czarzasty is beginning his opening speech telling the audience that Europe is “at the turning point” of “civilisational” significance.

Addressing the Warsaw Security Forum, he says “for those who have any doubts that the president of the Russian Federation is a murderer and aggressor, and Ukraine is a victim.”

He says “it has to be said: there is no free Poland and free Europe, without a free Ukraine.”

Just as he says it, Poland issues a (now fairly routine) emergency alert to residents of a south-eastern region neighbouring Ukraine, putting them on high alert because of Russian strikes across the border.

The foreign ministers of Britain, Germany, Poland and Norway should be up on the main stage shortly.

The latest update from Bulgaria says that 11 crew members from the sunken ship are still missing.

The number of people rescued from the ship has now gone up to five, with authorities hoping they will be able to offer more insight into what happened overnight.

Drones of unknown origin struck two ships in the Black Sea off Bulgaria this morning, sinking one and prompting emergency rescue operations, the country’s prime minister Rumen Radev said.

Only one person was rescued from the sunken vessel, and 15 people were picked up from the other one.

The attack comes exactly a week after a similar incident in which one ship sank with its crew on board, and the other one was evacuated, with 18 people rescued.

PM Radev said the attacks were “absolutely unacceptable,” and said he would seek assistance from Nato and the European Union.

He said that while there is no “clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility” yet, “the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation.”

The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said “the Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine.”

“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea. We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable.”

The incident comes amid growing fears about Russia’s war against Ukraine and as several European foreign ministers meet at the Warsaw Security Forum in Poland, including Britain’s Ed Miliband, Germany’s Johann Wadephul, and Ukraine’s Andrii Sybiha.

I will monitor their comments and bring you the top lines.

Separately, the French high school protests are expected to intensify today after key groups called for “a day of mobilisation” across the country.

Over in Spain, the Spanish royals are expected to visit the autonomous city of Ceuta in northern Africa, which continues to see its every day’s life disrupted by the migration crisis.

In Sweden, the Social Democrats leader Magdalena Andersson is due to report back on the progress of her talks on government formation today. But early reports suggest she does not quite have everything lined up yet, and the process is likely to take more time.

Finally, in the Vatican, Pope Leo is expected to be hospitalised today to remove a lung nodule discovered in his body to test it if the lesion is malignant. He is likely to stay there for about a week.

So, lots for us to cover. I will bring you all the key lines here.

It’s Monday, 13 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Emergency calls from botched Christa Pike execution released to US media
articles.excerpt: A series of newly-released calls made after the failed execution of US death row inmate Christa Pike reveal emergency services were delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison off...
articles.body_text:
A series of newly-released calls made after the failed execution of US death row inmate Christa Pike reveal emergency services were delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials.

The recordings, first obtained by the Associated Press, show that minutes passed as officials and responders attempted to confirm whether the request for emergency help in the execution chamber at Riverbend Prison was legitimate.

The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released several calls between the agency and other departments - including police and highway patrol.

"We are trying to find out if that is an actual thing that is happening and we need to send an ambulance and, or if you need police assistance or if this is someone that is just basically prank calling or, like, swatting us," one dispatcher can be heard saying during a call.

Another recording shows Kelly Gleason, Christa Pike's defence attorney, calling for help.

"She is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care," she says.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death after murdering Colleen Slemmer with her then-boyfriend in 1995. She survived two injections of the drug pentobarbital on 30 September and was taken to hospital in a critical condition.

More on this story: Could Christa Pike face execution again and by what method?

articles.title: Palestine weekly: Gaza marks year of ‘ceasefire’ with more Israeli killing
articles.excerpt:
The Gaza “ceasefire” marked its first anniversary on October 10, but more than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations said it exists “in name only”.

Islamic Relief noted that Israeli forces ...
articles.body_text:
The Gaza “ceasefire” marked its first anniversary on October 10, but more than 100 humanitarian and human rights organisations said it exists “in name only”.

Islamic Relief noted that Israeli forces have killed or wounded a Palestinian in Gaza on average every 90 minutes since the ceasefire took effect.

Gaza’s Health Ministry put the toll since the truce at 1,493 killed and 5,299 wounded as of October 12, up from 1,460 a week earlier; the cumulative death toll since October 2023 stood at 74,382.

In statements describing attacks, Israel’s military claimed several of those killed this week were Palestinian fighters.

The Israeli military said two men killed near the Jordanian Field Hospital were Islamic Jihad operatives; Wafa identified one as a recently released former prisoner.

It separately said a civil defence worker killed while responding to the wounded near Kamal Adwan Hospital in northern Gaza had been a Hamas sniper; Hamas rejected the claim, and it has not been independently verified.

Israeli forces have also continued pushing the so-called Yellow Line demarcating Israeli control further into residential Gaza City neighbourhoods this week, triggering fresh displacement.

One year into the ceasefire, the Board of Peace – Gaza’s transitional oversight body – has failed to meet most of its central commitments: no international stabilisation force has deployed, aid trucks are entering at roughly a third of the agreed rate, and Israel now controls nearly two thirds of the Strip — well above the roughly 50 percent it was supposed to retain before further withdrawal and a future handover of control to Palestinians.

The Palestinian olive harvest – traditionally a time of family and celebration – gathered pace as Israeli settlers and soldiers intensified efforts to disrupt it. Harvesters were killed, attacked and blocked, while isolated families faced dayslong settler sieges.

The attacks followed a familiar shape village to village, according to Wafa and field reports from local residents and activists:

Israeli forces frequently blocked the harvest, too. Soldiers used drone-mounted loudspeakers to drive farmers out of Wadi Abwein and turned pickers away in several locations elsewhere.

Israeli settlers’ own chat groups reveal how they frame such attacks in reverse — through a messianic lens, casting Palestinian harvesters reaching their own land in Deir Abu Mash’al as attempting to “seize” the land, and the olive harvest itself as cover for Palestinians gathering “intelligence” rather than picking olives that families have harvested there for generations. Settlers have been documented repeatedly stealing olives from Palestinians’ lands since harvesting unofficially started late last month.

Once again, Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas postponed Palestinian legislative elections – this time to September, citing Israeli restrictions on election materials and observers entering Gaza and East Jerusalem, and ongoing settler violence. Mustafa Barghouti, of the Palestinian National Initiative, said the decision reflects that “everything is concentrated in the hands of the executive authority”, with no parliament or independent judiciary to check it.

In Israel, with high-stakes parliamentary elections scheduled for October 27, Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said his alliance – made up predominantly of Palestinian citizens of Israel – was prepared to support a coalition against current Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from outside government.

The support would be given in exchange for policy commitments, including a pathway to Palestinian statehood, The Times of Israel reported – a potential route to a majority that polls suggest neither bloc can reach without Arab party support.

Israeli authorities also began demolishing homes this week in al-Dahiya, an unrecognised Bedouin village in the Naqab, after a district court rejected a request to freeze the orders; roughly 60 homes face demolition.

In diplomatic news, the UK’s consulate in occupied East Jerusalem formally became a reduced “mission” after Israel’s deadline for its closure passed; it has long handled the UK’s relations with Palestinians.

articles.title: Drone attack sinks ship off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, PM says
articles.excerpt:
Two ships have been hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was sailing under a Maltese fl...
articles.body_text:
Two ships have been hit in drone attacks off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, with one of them sinking, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.

The Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3, which was sailing under a Maltese flag, was hit by three drones and damaged about 18 nautical miles (33km) off Bulgaria at about 1:30am on Tuesday (22:30 GMT on Monday), Radev said.

Radev said its 15-man crew, seven of them Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijanis, was rescued. Five crew members received medical assistance, and no one was seriously injured.

He added that one crew member from the ship that sank was also rescued.

Radev called the incident “absolutely unacceptable”.

“Another attack in the immediate vicinity of Bulgarian territorial waters,” he said in a televised address, adding, “I am due to speak with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte.”

Radev said there was no clear evidence of who carried out the attack, but “the outcome benefits” Russia and that the Russian ambassador would be summoned over the incident.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack on the ships.

“The Black Sea has become another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine,” she said.

“This is unacceptable. I strongly condemn the drone attacks on merchant ships near Bulgaria’s coast. Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea,” she wrote on X.

“We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response. Those responsible should be held accountable,” von der Leyen added.

As a member of the NATO military alliance, Bulgaria holds a strategic position on the Black Sea, where Russia and Ukraine have vital ports.

The incident comes as concerns grow over hybrid attacks involving Russia.

Last week, drones hit two ships off Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, causing one to sink. All 10 crew members from the ship that sank remain unaccounted for.

articles.title: India 'cockroach' leaders detained after entering barricaded protest site
articles.excerpt:
CJP members were detained after they managed to "sneak" into Jantar Mantar on Tuesday morning

Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavil...
articles.body_text:
CJP members were detained after they managed to "sneak" into Jantar Mantar on Tuesday morning

Leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) were detained early on Tuesday after they entered a heavily-guarded protest site and chanted slogans demanding the country's election chief resign over a controversial revision of electoral rolls.

Party founder Abhijeet Dipke shared a video showing Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das being taken away by police from Jantar Mantar, a historic Delhi observatory popular for protests.

Footage showed the two - along with others - climbing over police barricades before chanting slogans while holding the Indian flag.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi's opponents allege the voter list revision benefits his party, a charge it and the Election Commission reject.

There have been days of protests demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.

Police have stepped up security across Delhi as demonstrators challenge restrictions on where protests can be held.

Early on Tuesday, Dipke, Das and Ranka all shared videos showing Das and Ranka entering Jantar Mantar.

"You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X.

Das also posted a message declaring that the site had been "reclaimed" and that they were being detained.

It was not immediately clear where police had taken the leaders.

Ranka later appeared on an Instagram live broadcast from a police bus alongside other detainees where they appeared cheerful and said they would not back down.

There is heavy security deployment in Delhi since last weekend

The detentions came a day after the federal home ministry announced that Jantar Mantar, long associated with public protests in Delhi, would no longer be a designated protest venue. Authorities instead identified three alternative locations where demonstrations can be held with permission.

Before the decision, the CJP had met Delhi Police officials to seek permission for a peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar and had warned that it would announce further demonstrations if it received no response.

"30 mins after we went to Delhi Police asking for a date when we can go to Jantar Mantar, Jantar Mantar was de-notified as a protest site," Ranka had earlier posted on X.

Most of the party's leadership has been in Delhi in recent days. Dipke, however, had travelled to his hometown in Maharashtra after the death of his grandmother. He was among several CJP leaders detained ahead of a planned demonstration on Saturday and was released the next day.

The CJP had called for a protest at Jantar Mantar on Saturday, but authorities imposed extensive security restrictions across the capital to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site.

Several metro stations were closed, train services were disrupted and thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed.

Over the weekend, the police detained and released thousands of people, including several journalists. Some videos and photos from the protest show police dragging people, including women, by force and pushing them into buses.

Tens and thousands of people gathered in Delhi on Monday

Separately, opposition parties held a march in Delhi on Monday from Connaught Place - a major shopping district in the heart of the capital - to the Supreme Court.

The Congress, India's main opposition party, also petitioned the Supreme Court on Monday, challenging the Election Commission's voter revision exercise, which has resulted in tens of millions of names being removed from electoral rolls.

Critics say the exercise risks excluding eligible voters and making it harder for them to prove their eligibility.

Anger over the revision exercise intensified after The Indian Express reported that Kumar had disregarded concerns raised by the two other election commissioners over changes to voter registration. The Election Commission has said its decisions were unanimous.

The current protests follow student-led demonstrations earlier this year over exam irregularities and demands for education reforms.

The CJP led weeks of action that culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.

The group began as online satire after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people seeking change.

After the summer protests, the CJP evolved into a pressure group, tapping into wider anger over unemployment, exam irregularities and government accountability.

articles.title: Second wave of early prison releases under way in England and Wales
articles.excerpt:
About 2,000 criminals are being freed this month to ease overcrowding, while probation union moves towards strike

The second wave of early prison releases has begun, with hundreds of offenders walkin...
articles.body_text:
About 2,000 criminals are being freed this month to ease overcrowding, while probation union moves towards strike

The second wave of early prison releases has begun, with hundreds of offenders walking out across England and Wales under the government’s controversial plan to ease overcrowding.

About 2,000 criminals, including domestic abusers and violent offenders, are being freed this month, with another 3,000 to follow in stages over the next year. The total was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by Andy Burnham.

Prisoners convicted of manslaughter are excluded, meaning the killers of PC Andrew Harper, who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.

The second tranche of early releases comes as members of the probation union, Napo, hold a pre-ballot meeting on taking strike action over pay and workloads.

Pay negotiations with probation officers ended with a “best and final” conditional pay offer worth 5%, which the union’s negotiating committee rejected. Members will be asked to vote for industrial action on pay, along with a question on workloads, in a formal ballot on industrial action to launch on 19 October.

The union says probation officers have been required to take on large amounts of extra work since tens of thousands of prisoners began being released early from 2022.

The number of people in prison has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population in England and Wales was at 87,499 on Monday, according to Ministry of Justice data, up from 85,761 on 29 June, a rise of 2%.

The MoJ said released offenders would be monitored under the “toughest supervision in British history”. New restriction zones designed to control the movements of the highest-risk sexual and violent offenders should confine released prisoners to areas a few miles wide, in an effort to reassure the victims of their crimes.

The MoJ said it had expanded electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be tagged and monitored when they leave prison. Technology rolling out this year is said to give probation services near-live access to tagging data, helping staff spot breaches.

However, this month the victims’ commissioner, Claire Waxman, said the government’s confidence in the plan “is not yet matched by the reality on the ground”.

articles.title: The return of the prodigal son? Why speculation is rising over Josh Frydenberg’s future
articles.excerpt:
The spectre of a leadership alternative is hardly helpful for Angus Taylor. But would Frydenberg do a better job?

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

A reasonable query for L...
articles.body_text:
The spectre of a leadership alternative is hardly helpful for Angus Taylor. But would Frydenberg do a better job?

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

A reasonable query for Liberals at this point is: if Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question?

There was a whiff of weariness in some corners of parliament this week, as the former treasurer and deputy Liberal leader happily stoked another round of “Josh for Canberra” speculation. With more rumoured comebacks than Oasis, Frydenberg’s latest foray into the national political arena saw him bouncing around TV, radio and podcast interviews to promote his new book, and pointedly refuse to rule out trying to rejoin the parliament.

His book – part family history, part treatise on antisemitism and social cohesion, part political manifesto – is titled A Grateful Son. But is he instead the prodigal son? The one who set out on his own but is destined to be welcomed back to the Liberal party family with joy and celebrations?

Frydenberg is young enough, bright enough and certainly energetic enough to still make a difference in public life. His addition to what is often a tired Coalition party room would certainly spice things up, and give a new weapon in its arsenal. The ideas in his book – a remix of the GST to fund income tax cuts, concerns about the future of his party, changes to the system of federalism, yet more calls for civic service for school leavers – are politically inconvenient for the federal Coalition as well as the Victorian Liberals headed for an election win, but are worth considering.

The talk around parliament is that Frydenberg is privately telling people he is unlikely to seek a return. But the fact he has pointedly refused to rule it out in a conga line of media interviews, saying only that he would make his mind up later, seems opportunistic. The spectre of a potential leadership alternative is hardly a help for Angus Taylor.

Labor sources have helpfully shared key quotes from Frydenberg’s book and media tour, pointing out his calls for changes to GST and the labour market, and criticisms of the Liberal trajectory – again, none helpful to the leader.

The problems facing the modern Liberal party, under Taylor’s leadership, are myriad. Its hostile right flank is barracking for Pauline Hanson and One Nation, its centre is still eyeing the teal independents, and Taylor – now eight months into the job – has a lower primary vote than Sussan Ley when she was dumped. The Guardian Essential poll found the Coalition primary vote at a record low 22% in September, compared to 25% in January, a fortnight before Taylor rolled Ley.

These are all reasons for alarm for the centre right. It’s just not clear if Frydenberg is the answer to any of these problems. One question echoing around parliament this week was: would he do a better job than Taylor on anything substantive? In other words, is he yesterday’s man?

A return to the party room would give the Coalition a well-known face and a policy brain in a team which could benefit from both. Maybe Frydenberg would be content to return as a loyal soldier under Taylor, serving in an appropriately senior cabinet role. But maybe not. Few think he’d give up a well-paid job in banking to sit on the frontbench instead of the leader’s chair.

The loudest cheer Hanson got at last weekend’s Cpac conference was when she sledged Taylor, saying Australians didn’t want a “smarmy management consultant” replacing Anthony Albanese as prime minister. Would any of those voters more prefer the chair of investment bank Goldman Sachs, the role Frydenberg currently holds? Taylor in recent times has tried throwing a bone to that fringe of the rightwing movement, producing more off-the-cuff videos with unpolished deliveries (and swearing) a la Hanson – would Frydenberg, at home in boardrooms and business lunches, be able to win back the voters furious at “politics as usual” and career politicians?

Maybe, then, Frydenberg could chart a course back to the middle for the Coalition: not chasing its right flank further to the fringe, but setting a mainstream course back toward the centre, where elections in Australia are won.

That would be a decent idea, if you forget how Frydenberg was ejected from parliament in the first place: bundled out in 2022 by Monique Ryan in the big community independents wave which swept half a dozen moderate-ish urban Liberals from their seats.

Ryan was supported by Climate 200. That group’s origin story may be relevant here: Simon Holmes à Court, a former donor to Frydenberg’s Kooyong 200 fundraising vehicle, was reportedly ejected from a supporter event and set up his own group in response. Climate 200 would hardly respond to Frydenberg’s comeback, or potential leadership, with party poppers and a “welcome back” card.

The teal wave that swept Frydenberg and several other moderate Liberals from office in 2022 hasn’t exactly swelled into a tsunami since then, and some could argue the conditions of four years ago are not there today – just ask Tim Wilson, who lost Goldstein to teal Zoe Daniel in 2022 but wrested it back in 2025.

No Liberals we spoke to this week were jazzed about the prospect of Frydenberg’s return, or the distraction it provides.

But if there were any people happy about his potential return, they were on the government benches.

Albanese joked to Labor’s caucus meeting on Tuesday that Frydenberg was now the “shadow opposition leader”, claiming “Josh Frydenberg’s priority has always been Josh Frydenberg”.

“I’m surprised Josh Frydenberg isn’t trying to bump me off this program,” the PM joked on the ABC later in the day.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, claimed his old sparring partner was “stalking” Taylor for the leadership. One senior Labor source cheekily joked that we should call it “the Fryre festival”, a reference to the ill-fated and chaotic Fyre festival in 2017, which had its own short-lived and catastrophic comeback in 2024.

Frydenberg’s media tour is likely to continue over coming days. The speculation over his potential comeback will linger even longer – Labor will make sure of it.

articles.title: Man and woman charged after baby boy found dead in Adelaide motel
articles.excerpt:
South Australia police say infant was aged between six and seven months old and had been ‘deceased for a period of time’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man and a woman...
articles.body_text:
South Australia police say infant was aged between six and seven months old and had been ‘deceased for a period of time’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A man and a woman have been charged after a baby boy was found dead in a motel.

Benjamin Nicholas Houghton, 40, and Yue Ning Lieu, 42, are in custody after police discovered the child during a welfare check at a Glen Osmond motel in Adelaide’s south on Saturday.

“The infant had been deceased for a period of time,” South Australia police said in a statement on Tuesday.

A post-mortem confirmed the boy was aged between six and seven months old, police said.

The man and woman had been living at the Tollgate Motel since they arrived in SA at the start of the year, police said.

Houghton and Lieu have been charged with criminal neglect and destroy human remains to pervert the course of justice.

Their matters appeared in Adelaide magistrates court on Monday.

They did not apply for bail and were remanded in custody until 3 May 2027.

SA police’s eastern district detectives conducted the initial investigation.

“However, due to the nature and complexity of the incident and the resources required, Major Crime Investigation Branch have taken over the investigation,” a police statement said.

“Police are seeking assistance from anyone who has stayed at the Tollgate Motel, and specifically anyone who has information about the occupants of room four to contact Crime Stoppers.”

articles.title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
articles.excerpt:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A four-month inve...
articles.body_text:
Cocaine seizures in Europe are up more than fivefold in 10 years as a host of cartels take root. A four-month Guardian investigation reveals the true scale of a continent-wide shift

A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.

The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.

These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.

Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.

“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”

Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. An unpublished report by the São Paulo public prosecutor’s office, partly based on data from the Brazilian intelligence agency (Abin) – which the Guardian reviewed – shows, for example, that the PCC, now Brazil’s biggest criminal group, operates in 16 European countries, including the UK, Ireland, Iceland, Serbia, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey.

The suspicion that Latin American cartels and factions are seeking to become established in Europe is not new. Since at least the 1980s, Colombian criminal organisations such as the Cali and Medellín cartels had footholds in regions of Spain such as Galicia. In 2013, a Europol report in 2103 warned of their rise. But what authorities are witnessing now is on an another level.

A Europol report this year states that “Latin American MTCNs [most threatening criminal networks] have also settled in the EU, from where they direct operations that affect the EU. This is particularly the case for mobile criminal networks involved in organised property crime.”

Interpol, led by the Brazilian federal police officer Valdecy Urquiza, has been approached, but has not commented.

The problem has become more visible over the past decade. Drug production in Latin America in that time has increased roughly fourfold to reach a record of about 4,100 tonnes in 2024. This comes after growth of up to 35% at the beginning of the decade. More cocaine is now produced in Colombia than during the era of the notorious drug lord Pablo Escobar. Nearly all the world’s cocaine and many related substances originate from Latin America, particularly Colombia.

Víctor Manuel Sánchez Valdés, an academic at the Autonomous University of Coahuila in Mexico who is an expert on organised crime, says: “The main ones are the Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco cartel [CJNG] in Mexico; the Comando Vermelho and the PCC of Brazil; the Gulf Clan and different factions of the Colombian Farc; the Lobos and the Choneros of Ecuador; and Tren de Aragua of Venezuela.”

He believes that the Latin American presence in Europe is even more widespread than is generally recognised. “Sinaloa cartel and the CJNG have a presence in more than 20 European countries. Obviously, that does not mean they dominate or have large cells,” he says. “Rather, they are business emissaries.”

The UN Office on Drugs and Crime’s 2026 World Drug Report on illicit crimes states that global cocaine production in 2024 was between 3,800 and 4,700 tonnes – more than four times higher than it was in 2014. South America remains the main production hub, with coca cultivation covering a record 385,000 hectares over the past decade – three times the 2014 figure.
