articles.title: Stolen Renoir paintings found behind wall in France following arrests
articles.excerpt: Two paintings by the impressionist master Renoir which were stolen from a French museum last month have been found damaged behind a false wall in a private home after police made several arrests ahead...
articles.body_text:
Two paintings by the impressionist master Renoir which were stolen from a French museum last month have been found damaged behind a false wall in a private home after police made several arrests ahead of what prosecutors say was an imminent second heist.

Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said six suspects were arrested on Wednesday after authorities discovered they were planning to target the Fondation Maeght in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, home to one of Europe’s largest collections of modern art.

Bessone said the arrests were prompted by the “very strong suspicion that another heist was imminent”.

“We were very clearly looking at the repetition of a criminal scheme”, said Eric Antonetti, the head of the Alpes-Maritimes judicial police.

On September 8, thieves used an electric saw to cut through a fence to enter the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer on the French Riviera, according to investigators.

An alarm sounded and police officers arrived four minutes later, a swift response that “apparently caused the perpetrators to panic,” Bessone said.

The stolen works, “Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well” by impressionist painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, were valued at about 4.2m euros ($4.7m), Bessone said.

The thieves also attempted to steal two other Renoir paintings, “Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading”, which depicts Renoir’s young ‌son ‌Claude. They abandoned them in the museum gardens while fleeing police.

“As they fled, they were unable to take all four paintings and abandoned two of them, which were later found in a protective sleeve,” he said.

The paintings were found hidden behind a false wall in a house on Friday. Both works were damaged and will need ⁠restoration. One of the paintings, “Madame Colonna Romano”, had been torn.

“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”

The recovery came almost exactly one month ⁠after the theft, following an investigation that used ⁠DNA evidence, mobile phone geolocation data and surveillance video.

The two key suspects include a 29-year-old, who was charged after investigators recovered DNA from a bag left behind during the getaway.

They ⁠were charged with organised theft and other offences. A third man, accused of hiding the paintings, was charged with organised handling of stolen goods.

A fourth suspect, who investigators say was approached about buying the artworks, was charged ‌with handling stolen goods and taking part in a criminal conspiracy.

Bessone said the suspects had denied planning a second museum raid, but he added that he did “not believe the principal suspect visited that ‌museum simply out of a love of art”.

articles.title: Season is already over for these four NFL teams after Week 5, you can write them off now
articles.excerpt:
Cole calls on the Jets to fire Aaron Glenn.

Five weeks into the NFL season, we can officially write off four teams. By "write off," we mean teams that are going nowhere. Their fans should be more con...
articles.body_text:
Cole calls on the Jets to fire Aaron Glenn.

Five weeks into the NFL season, we can officially write off four teams. By "write off," we mean teams that are going nowhere. Their fans should be more concerned with draft position than anything their teams might accomplish this season.

We understand how demoralizing it is to concede a season before mid-October. It is, nonetheless, the reality for certain franchises.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

It's not a fun time to be a fan of the Miami Dolphins. (Getty Images)

Let's start with two teams that aren't tanking, per se, but weren't exactly built to contend this season. The Miami Dolphins and Arizona Cardinals are about as bad as expected, despite the latter managing an early-season win.

The positive is that both teams have stockpiled young talent while positioning themselves for a high draft pick. Miami's rookie class is impressive, including Kadyn Proctor, Chris Johnson, Jacob Rodriguez, Caleb Douglas, and Chris Bell. Arizona has the best tight end in football in Trey McBride, while Jeremiah Love, albeit injured, has generational upside.

Unfortunately, the 2027 quarterback class doesn't appear nearly as promising as anticipated. Arch Manning, to this point, hardly resembles the prospect analysts projected him to become.

Elsewhere, the Tennessee Titans might be worse than both the Dolphins and Cardinals. That's particularly concerning because Tennessee spent the offseason actively trying to improve its roster and coaching staff.

Through Week 5, the Titans rank last in the NFL in both scoring and total offense, averaging just 11.6 points and 246.4 yards per game.

The winless Titans shouldn't be expected to win many games this season.

Los Angeles Chargers offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel looks on as quarterback Justin Herbert warms up before a preseason game against the San Francisco 49ers. (Getty Images)

After five weeks, we can also write off the Los Angeles Chargers, who entered the season with nearly the same Super Bowl odds as the Kansas City Chiefs. A team coached by Jim Harbaugh and quarterbacked by Justin Herbert should not be this inept. And yet, they are.

At 0-5, with games remaining against the Rams, Ravens, Chiefs twice, 49ers, and Patriots, it's difficult to find many wins left on the schedule.

A midseason parting with offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel now seems more plausible than a late-season surge toward the playoffs. The Chargers' season, at least in terms of meaningful aspirations, is over.

Based strictly on their play, the New Orleans Saints and Tampa Bay Buccaneers should join this list. Both teams have won just one game and have deficiencies on both sides of the ball. Despite relatively high expectations entering the season, the Saints have a minus-33 point differential.

Neither team figures to be much of a factor in the postseason, if it gets there at all. However, both remain just one game out of first place in the perpetually mediocre NFC South.

Likewise, the 1-3-1 Washington Commanders remain viable playoff threats largely because of the lackluster state of the rest of the NFC East.

Granted, it's hard to take seriously a team that did that in overtime on Sunday

New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson celebrates with teammates Kenyon Sadiq and Isaiah Williams after catching a touchdown pass during the first half of an NFL game against the Cleveland Browns on Sunday, Oct. 11, 2026, in East Rutherford, N.J. (AP Photo/Seth Wenig)

The 2-3 New York Jets are the final team worth discussing. As WWE commentator Michael Cole told OutKick last week, the Jets remain poorly coached and overmatched in the trenches. In all likelihood, they are probably a bottom-10 team in the NFL–again.

But we can't, in good faith, write off a team that sits just one game behind the Patriots and Bills, who play the Rams on Monday night, in the AFC East.

We suspect the Jets will join this list by the end of October. For now, however, they've played well enough — including competitive games against the Lions and Packers — to keep the light on for a few more weeks.

So, through Week 5, the Dolphins, Cardinals, Titans, and Chargers are the only four teams we're officially declaring "season over."

The rest of the fan bases should at least have hope, even for just a short while longer.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russia violated Trump’s ‘energy ceasefire’ – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv power plant among the facilities hit after US president claims ‘energy ceasefire’, while Kremlin yet to confirm any deal

Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war...
articles.body_text:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy says Kyiv power plant among the facilities hit after US president claims ‘energy ceasefire’, while Kremlin yet to confirm any deal

Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

We are restarting our live coverage of the latest developments in Europe after Donald Trump’s announcement of what he called an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Sunday evening that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian energy facilities despite the US president having claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant on Sunday, leading to power outages in the Ukrainian capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, adding: “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day”, referring to a type of Iranian-made drone commonly used in the conflict.

Meanwhile, Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured, Ukrainian officials said. Two children were ‌among the injured, the regional governor said. In western ​Ukraine, ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people, officials ​said.

On Sunday morning Trump had announced that “effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, without further details.

Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me”, while Russia has still not confirmed its agreement. Zelenskyy said on Telegram yesterday that: “Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Nato Supreme Allied Cmdr Europe Alexus Grynkewich is due to deliver a warning to Russia at a security conference in Warsaw over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack from Moscow.

The Lithuanian ⁠foreign minister Kestutis ​Budrys said the EU should designate the Russian ‌intelligence agency GRU ​as ⁠a ​terrorist organisation.

The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Trump’s surprise ceasefire announcement came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel – temporarily lifting US sanactions – prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow.

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times has quoted officials in Europe as saying. They said the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said Russia is trying to tactically use the period of cold weather against Ukraine, targeting the country’s power plants and power grids.

“This winter if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond,” Zelenskyy said, adding that he supports Trump’s energy ceasefire proposal, but vows that if Russia doesn’t agree to it, then Ukraine “will respond”.

“If Russia wants us to stop our long-range strikes against its oil refineries and oil exports, then Russia must stop its strikes against our energy system and critical infrastructure, and stop killing our people. This is only fair,” Zelenskyy said.

“We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree, if they agree. And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burning but at midnight a Russian jet powered Shahed strike against a production facility in Ukraine.”

Addressing the conference virtually, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy commented on Trump’s “sudden but very important” energy ceasefire declaration over the weekend.

He said it is clear that Putin “does not read Truth social”, the site that the US president posted his ceasefire declaration on.

As we have been reporting, Russia’s strikes continued despite the announcement. “Immediately after the post Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system,” Zelenskyy said, noting that Ukraine is facing a wave of escalatory attacks from Russia ahead of the winter.

Speaking at the security conference in Warsaw, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia wants to “dominate” Ukraine and poses a grave threat to Nato.

double quotation markRussia wants to ruin the existing security architecture in Europe to make sure that Russian domination comes back to where it was before 1989. We have no doubt about it.

Tusk says his country, Poland, a Nato and EU member, has heavily invested in defence to be prepared to counter future security challenges.

Tusk said despite the hybrid threats from Russia he is “optimistic” when he thinks of the high level of military readiness for “different scenarios”.

“This is the moment when the entire west, Europe, the United States must show Russia’s Putin that we are ready for a deterrence policy with even harder measures – and I mean mainly sanctions,” he told the conference.

Tusk told parliament last month that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory in the coming months, as part of efforts to prove that “article 5 is more theoretical than practical”.

The EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the EU would welcome a truce on striking energy infrastructure between Ukraine and Russia “when it holds”, after US President Donald Trump announced a ceasefire, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy said was “news to me”.
 Arriving at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday, Kallas said:

double quotation markWe welcome the energy ceasefire when it holds. We haven’t yet seen that also Russia will stick to it.

Kallas said she wanted to see people included in any ceasefire. But an energy truce also had to cover more than just oil refineries in the two countries “where Ukraine has one and Russia has plenty, so it’s definitely in the benefit of the Russians.”

She did not respond directly to a question about Trump’s diesel deal with Vladimir Putin, saying: “That is why we are, of course, continuing our path. We are now adopting 1,600 listings because we only see that pressure on Russia would work.”

The EU will finalise later today sanctions against 1,600 Russian individuals and entities, targeting the military-industrial complex and officials involved in “sham elections” in Ukraine’s occupied territories. 
  Kallas said EU sanctions “would work so much better if our partners from the UK and from the US would be aligned with us”. She went on to say that the UK was aligned, “but if the US would be aligned, if they would enact the Graham bill regarding Russia, we could really put the pressure so that Russia will finish this war”.
  Trump signed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law earlier this month, which is aimed at depleting Russia’s ability to continue funding the war by targeting its natural gas and oil revenues, as well as countries that continue to buy Russian energy.

Donald Tusk, who is one of the staunchest supporters of Kyiv, said for the entire “western world” security is “no longer an academic problem” or a subject of journalistic intrigue, it is a “very concrete result of Russian aggression on Ukraine”.

Tusk said anybody who suggests that Ukraine is responsible for the war “gives a valuable gift to the aggressor”.

The prime minister’s comments come after Donald Trump blamed Volodymyr Zelenskkyy for stalled peace efforts over the weekend, and said he thought it was time for Ukraine to get a new president.

Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, has just begun addressing the security conference in Warsaw. I will bring you any key lines. You can watch it here live.

The biggest prize in economics, the Sveriges Riksbank Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Leading the betting on Polymarket, at 30% this morning, is David Autor, professor of economics at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Autor is a labour economist, who has examined how technology changes the world of work.

Another potential winner is Ariél Pakes, the Thomas Professor of Economics at Harvard University, currently at a 19% chance on Polymarket.

Pakes’s work has focused on developing methods to empirically analyse market responses to environmental and policy changes, such as mergers and deregulation.

Third, at 12%, is Susan Athey, the Economics of Technology Professor at Stanford Graduate School of Business. Athey, the former consulting chief economist for Microsoft, was the first woman to win the John Bates Clark Medal (awarded to the top economist under the age of 40).

There’s also some interest in American macroeconomist and monetary theorist Michael Woodford (currently at 10%) – he’s one of the architects of modern forward guidance, the idea that central banks can control the economy through influencing public expectations about inflation, rather than just through interest rates.

There have been multiple reports of overnight Russian attacks on Ukraine, affecting energy infrastructure and hitting civilian areas.

Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, said this morning that Russia attacked three districts of the region “more than 10 times” with artillery and drones. The strikes caused fires in the Petrykivka and Mykolaiv areas of the Dniprovskyi district, Hanzha added in his Telegram post, which noted there were no injuries from the attacks.

Residents in several streets in Izyum, south-east of Kharkiv in eastern Ukraine, were reportedly left without power after a Russian attack damaged power grids.

Meanwhile, the governor of Ukraine’s Zhytomyr region, Vitaliy Bunechko, said Russian forces have been “repeatedly shelling” the north of the region “since the evening”.

“Railway and energy infrastructure facilities in the Korosten district were under attack,” he added in a Telegram post this morning, noting that the fires were quickly extinguished. Bunechko said there was no information about the victims or their injuries yet.

⁠At ⁠least 12 ​people ⁠were ⁠injured in ​several ‌Russian ‌attacks ‌on Ukraine’s Kharkiv ‌on ​Monday morning, ⁠mayor Ihor ​Terekhov ​said. Here are some of the latest images being sent to us over the newswires from Ukraine’s second largest city:

We are expecting Volodymyr Zelenskyy to speak at the annual security conference in Warsaw alongside Polish prime minister Donald Tusk from 8.30am to 9.30am UK time this morning. Stay with us as we will bring you the key lines from what the two leaders say.

The fast-moving row between Washington and Kyiv began on Friday when Trump announced he was lifting sanctions on Russian diesel exports. He said the move would reduce global and domestic fuel prices before next month’s US midterm elections.

A furious Zelenskyy called the decision “weak” and said it would generate “billions” in extra revenue for Putin, enabling him to wage war “even more intensely”. An equally irate Trump said Zelenskyy should “damn well stop” hitting Russian refineries. Ukraine needed a “new leader”, he said on Saturday.

Responding to Trump, Zelenskyy said it was up to Ukrainians to choose “one or another leader”. He told ABC News he was willing to accept Trump’s demands and to organise elections, but only if Putin agreed to a “total” 60-day ceasefire.

The New York Times has reported that US officials have offered the Kremlin lucrative economic incentives in exchange for a ceasefire. They reportedly include releasing billions in Russian sovereign assets that are frozen. The Trump administration also revisited a plan to sell parts of Russia’s energy company, Lukoil. The multibillion deal would benefit Middle Eastern investors, the paper reported, some with “business ties” to US negotiators. You can read the full story here:

We are restarting our live coverage of the latest developments in Europe after Donald Trump’s announcement of what he called an energy ceasefire in the Russia-Ukraine war.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said on Sunday evening that Russian strikes hit Ukrainian energy facilities despite the US president having claimed both sides had agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy infrastructure.

In a post on X, Zelenskyy said a drone had hit a Kyiv power plant on Sunday, leading to power outages in the Ukrainian capital. Shortly after, he said there had been a strike on a power plant in the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, adding: “Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian ‘shaheds’ all day”, referring to a type of Iranian-made drone commonly used in the conflict.

Meanwhile, Russian ⁠attacks killed six people ⁠in two Ukrainian ⁠cities ​on Sunday, including a strike ⁠on a grocery store in Kharkiv, ​where ‌three people died ‌and 20 were ‌injured, Ukrainian officials said. Two children were ‌among the injured, the regional governor said. In western ​Ukraine, ‌a Russian strike ​killed ​three people, officials ​said.

On Sunday morning Trump had announced that “effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine”. “Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” he wrote on his Truth Social platform, without further details.

Zelenskyy expressed surprise at the announcement, saying the deal was “news to me”, while Russia has still not confirmed its agreement. Zelenskyy said on Telegram yesterday that: “Ukraine is ready to refrain from striking Russian energy infrastructure – and we count on the same readiness from Russia.”

Nato Supreme Allied Cmdr Europe Alexus Grynkewich is due to deliver a warning to Russia at a security conference in Warsaw over the alliance’s ability to counter any attack from Moscow.

The Lithuanian ⁠foreign minister Kestutis ​Budrys said the EU should designate the Russian ‌intelligence agency GRU ​as ⁠a ​terrorist organisation.

The Nobel memorial prize in economics, the final award in this year’s cycle, will be announced at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm from 10.45am UK time.

Trump’s surprise ceasefire announcement came two days after he announced a controversial agreement to buy Russian diesel fuel – temporarily lifting US sanactions – prompting outrage from Ukraine and its European allies, who said it would embolden Moscow.

The Trump administration is threatening to stop the procurement system that provides Ukraine with weapons in order to press Kyiv to halt its deep strikes on Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times has quoted officials in Europe as saying. They said the US was lobbying European capitals and Kyiv in an attempt to end the attacks on Russian oil refineries.

articles.title: UK politics live: Tories accuse Burnham of being ‘dangerous and divisive’ after he confirms Russian interference in Brexit campaign
articles.excerpt:
Shadow minister says referendum was a ‘legitimate vote’ and PM is seeking to ‘reopen debate’ with statement on Russia’s involvement

Burnham to urge MPs to embrace closer ties with EU

Ed Davey, the L...
articles.body_text:
Shadow minister says referendum was a ‘legitimate vote’ and PM is seeking to ‘reopen debate’ with statement on Russia’s involvement

Burnham to urge MPs to embrace closer ties with EU

Ed Davey, the Lib Dem leader, has praised Andy Burnham for confirming that Russia tried to influence the outcome of the 2016 Brexit referendum. (See 9.28am.) In a statement, he said:

double quotation markI’m not going to agree with Andy Burnham on everything, but this statement needed to be said by a prime minister. After the Conservatives suppressed the truth for years, this took courage.

We must do far more to protect our democracy from attack by the Kremlin and other hostile states, before it is too late.

Good morning. The last time Andy Burnham gave a statement to MPs after a recess, it went on for more than three hours. This prompted Kemi Badenoch to make a lewd joke later about the PM’s stamina (which she repeated at a party conference reception with an additional line about how she just had to “sit back and lie there”.) Today we are getting another post-recess, potentially wide-ranging statement from the PM, but the mood might not be so cordial.

Quite a lot has happened since MPs were last in the chamber almost a month ago, and they will want to ask the PM about issues like the cost of living, North Sea oil and gas, the Iran war and Ukraine. We have not been told yet exactly what Burnham’s statement will cover. But, as Aletha Adu reports, Burnham will talk about Brexit, restating what he told Labour’s conference about how he thinks it has done more harm than good and making the case for trying to find a better, closer relationship with the EU.

Burnham has also given an interview to the Rest is Politics podcast and in it he confirmed that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum. This is one of those statements, quite common in politics, which are simultaneously unremarkable and newsworthy. Unremarkable – because it has been obvious to anyone reading the news for the past decade that the Russians were trying to help the leave campaign. And newsworthy – because it is not something that any previous PM has been keen to say.

For some years ministers have been using the line – set out in 2020 in the government’s response to the intelligence and security committee’s report on the threat posed by Russia – that “we have seen no evidence of successful interference in the EU referendum”. That implies there is evidence of unsuccessful interference. But in the past prime ministers have not said that explicity. Post-2016 Tory PMs, whether they voted leave or remain, did not want to cast doubt on the legitimacy of the leave vote, and Keir Starmer was also reluctant to poke his stick into that particular hornets’ nest.

Burnham is taking a different approach. In his interview, Burnham was not asked, and did not say, if he thought that Russian interference had an impact on the result. Stephen Doughty, a Foreign Office minister, has been giving interview this morning and he told Times Radio:

double quotation markThe result is the result, and I think the prime minister has been very clear that he’s talking about attempts to interfere. The security minister has spoken about this before. I’m confident that both the British people and the British state are able to respond to and defend against these types of threats, but we need to be very honest that those threats exist.

(“I think the PM has been very clear” is the sort of thing a minister says when what they mean is “Of course, the PM wasn’t clear at all, but I’m happy to give you the line now.” Doughty later told LBC the Russians “haven’t succeeded in their many, many attempts to undermine our [democratic] processes”.

The Conservatives have criticised Burnham for even raising the topic. Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, told Times Radio this morning:

double quotation markThat Brexit referendum was a legitimate vote. People voted in this country in record numbers to leave the European Union. And I actually think it’s very dangerous and divisive of the prime minister to reopen this debate in such an explosive fashion.

11am: Kanishka Narayan, the AI minister, gives a speech.

11am: Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, and Zia Yusuf, its home affairs spokesperson, hold a press conference.

11.30am: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

2.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Afternoon: MLAs (members of the legislative assembly) will vote on a no confidence motion in Michelle O’Neill, the Sinn Féin first minister, over her support for a protest against the proposed Orange Order march down the Garvachy Road.

After 3.30pm: Andy Burnham makes a statement to MP.

Late afternoon: Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, makes a statement to the Commons on the safety of MPs.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Steve Smith breaks Test fielding record as Australia dominate South Africa
articles.excerpt: Steve Smith has broken the Test record for the most career catches by a fielder as Australia have played themselves into a strong position on the third day of the first Test against hosts South Africa...
articles.body_text:
Steve Smith has broken the Test record for the most career catches by a fielder as Australia have played themselves into a strong position on the third day of the first Test against hosts South Africa.

Smith held four catches on Sunday, taking his total to 223, as South Africa were bowled out for 284 in reply to Australia’s first innings of 390 at Kingsmead Stadium in Durban.

Nic Maddinson (17 not out) and Travis Head (10 not out) added 33 runs off just 5.4 overs to stretch Australia’s overall lead to 139 before bad light ended play for the third day in a row.

Maddinson, who laboured to a 33-ball duck in the first innings, hit two fours off Marco Jansen in the first over of the second innings and added a six off Wiaan Mulder before play was called off.

Australia’s bowlers applied relentless pressure on an easy-paced pitch and a succession of South African batsmen contributed to their own dismissals by playing poor shots.

Six Protea batters reached 30, but David Bedingham’s 49 was the top score.

Australian captain Pat Cummins took three for 54, and Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon claimed two wickets each as Australia’s long-serving bowling quartet combined with customary efficiency.

Smith started the day on 219 catches, one behind Joe Root of England.

He equalled the record when he caught Temba Bavuma. Smith, playing in his 126th Test, broke the record when he lunged to his left from second slip to hold a sharp edge from Bedingham off Cummins.

Smith was in the action again with a spectacular catch to dismiss Verreynne, again anticipating well at slip as the South African wicketkeeper made good contact with a reverse sweep that Smith held in an outstretched right hand.

His fourth catch was from an edge to slip by last man Anrich Nortje off the bowling of Beau Webster.

Smith’s career haul of 223 catches exceeds the total of all but 11 specialist wicketkeepers.

articles.title: India opposition plans New Delhi protest to demand election chief resign
articles.excerpt: Authorities have closed half a dozen Delhi Metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions in New Delhi as opposition parties prepare to march to the Supreme Court to protest against a controversial ...
articles.body_text:
Authorities have closed half a dozen Delhi Metro stations and warned of traffic disruptions in New Delhi as opposition parties prepare to march to the Supreme Court to protest against a controversial revision of voter lists that has led to disruptions in the Indian capital.

Thousands of police officers and security personnel were deployed across central New Delhi on Monday for a third straight day, erecting heavy metal barricades and closing key metro rail stations in advance of a march called by Rahul Gandhi, the leader of the opposition in Lok Sabha, the lower house of Parliament.

Opposition parties and supporters of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) youth movement have taken to the streets almost daily this month to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over revisions to voter lists that critics say benefit Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).

Police detained thousands of protesters over the weekend as supporters of the youth-led movement attempted to hold a protest march but were stopped by security personnel, with thousands of people detained.

The Election Commission of India (ECI), which oversees the voting process in the world’s most populous nation, has denied wrongdoing.

Opposition figures have accused authorities of trying to suppress dissent through mass detentions.

Parliamentarian John Brittas of the Communist Party of India (Marxist) alleged he was “manhandled, dragged, assaulted” by police during the demonstrations on Sunday.

“This is not merely an assault on an MP. It is an assault on democratic freedoms and the rule of law,” he said.

Police did not respond to questions about the detentions or their actions during a news conference on Sunday.

Several journalists covering the protest said they were also detained despite prominently displaying their press cards.

International NGO Reporters Without Borders said at least 16 journalists were “brutally” detained while covering the protests over the weekend.

“Covering events of public interest is not a crime. It is their job. The police’s actions against the press are unacceptable,” it said in a statement.

Gandhi, a Congress party leader, urged supporters to join Monday’s march to the Supreme Court to press for Kumar’s resignation.

“Bring as much police as you want — 10 thousand, 20 thousand, 40 thousand, go ahead. Call as many BJP-RSS goons as you need,” he said in a post on X directed at Home Minister Amit Shah.

“We are not the ones to get scared. We are not the ones to back down. This fight is not going to stop now!”

The leaders of the youth-led CJP movement, which has millions of social media followers, have also pledged to continue their protests until Kumar steps down.

The protests have become one of the most significant political challenges for Modi in his 12 years in power, bringing together opposition parties, student groups and activists angered by the voter roll revisions.

The revisions resulted in more than 133 million names being removed from electoral lists, according to media reports. Critics say minorities, particularly Muslims, were disproportionately affected.

The ECI says the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

articles.title: Alvarez vs M’billi boxing bout to go ahead in Saudi Arabia despite attacks
articles.excerpt: The world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” ‌‌Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month in Saudi Arabia despite attacks on the country’s airports, which have killed at least 14 people i...
articles.body_text:
The world title fight featuring Saul “Canelo” ‌‌Alvarez and Christian M’billi will go ahead this month in Saudi Arabia despite attacks on the country’s airports, which have killed at least 14 people in Riyadh in two days, Saudi sports promoter Turki Al-Sheikh confirms.

Alvarez vs M’billi is scheduled for October 31 in the Saudi capital, which has repeatedly come under attack from Yemen’s Houthis, but Al-Sheikh sought to allay the doubts over the bout on Sunday.

One person was killed and 11 were injured on Sunday when a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, according to Saudi Arabia’s General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA).

A Houthi strike on the same airport on Saturday killed 13 people and injured more than 300, making it the deadliest attack on Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for all four strikes on Saudi airports before Sunday’s attack, which has yet to be claimed by any group.

Alvarez, who has held multiple world titles across several weight classes, will face WBC super-middleweight champion M’billi in a highly anticipated bout.

“Canelo reached out ⁠⁠and told me he’ll still fight in Riyadh this October, no matter what happens,” Al-Sheikh, chairman of Saudi Arabia’s General Entertainment Authority, wrote in a social media post. “He [Alvarez] fears nothing.”

The ‌‌Mexican boxer, a former two-time undisputed super-middleweight champion, has not fought since he was ‌‌beaten ‌‌by American Terence Crawford in September 2025.

articles.title: ABC reporter could face disciplinary action over opinion piece, journalists’ union says
articles.excerpt:
Opinion piece by head of union Michael Slezak sparks disagreement with new ABC director of news, Simon Robinson

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s free weekly media newsletter here

ABC management has ...
articles.body_text:
Opinion piece by head of union Michael Slezak sparks disagreement with new ABC director of news, Simon Robinson

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s free weekly media newsletter here

ABC management has refused to rule out disciplinary action against a journalist and union office-holder for writing an opinion piece for the Australian Financial Review, according to the Media Entertainment and Arts Alliance (MEAA).

The award-winning ABC climate journalist, Michael Slezak, had an article published last week in Nine’s financial newspaper in his capacity as federal president of MEAA.

The AFR described Slezak, who is also head of the ABC house committee, as federal president of media at the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance and an ABC journalist.

The article was about a proposal by the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (Asic) to restrict journalists from accessing information such as the home address and date of birth of company directors, an issue the union is campaigning on.

Last week Slezak was called to a meeting with the new ABC director of news, Simon Robinson, and the head of digital and national news, Lee Glendinning, to discuss his adherence to the ABC’s external work policy.

Robinson was handpicked by the ABC managing director, Hugh Marks, before the incumbent news chief Justin Stevens was asked to resign in May. The former Reuters executive joined the ABC in September.

Sign up to get Guardian Australia’s weekly media diary as a free newsletter

In a letter to ABC union members on Monday, the media union claimed Slezak was being targeted for defending press freedom in his capacity as an elected union office-holder.

“Championing our right to information is something we expect Michael to do and be allowed to do without hindrance,” MEAA said.

A spokesperson for the ABC said the guidelines for external work and public comment were important in protecting the reputation of the ABC.

“The Director of News is meeting with staff to ensure there is a clear and consistent understanding of how the guidelines should be applied and upheld.”

The union’s relationship with Marks has been fraught since more than 2,000 staff walked off the job for a 24-hour strike, forcing ABC services across TV, radio and digital to use BBC content and repeat programming.

Marks was publicly critical of the enterprise bargaining process.

The union claims management refused to rule out disciplinary action including dismissal against Slezak at the meeting.

“Simon and Lee raised the possibility that Michael may have breached the ABC’s external work policy and code of conduct,” the union said. “They refused to rule out disciplinary action, including dismissal.”

The union says Slezak did not need to seek approval for the article because he has an agreement with the ABC which permits him to engage in public comment on behalf of journalists in his MEAA role.

The union has called on Marks and Robinson to confirm Slezak will not face disciplinary action in an open letter signed by 197 ABC union members as of Monday afternoon.

“We see this as an attack on our right to work collectively through our union, a hindrance to our delegates doing the work they are legally entitled to do, and an obstruction to journalists in our industry fulfilling their duty to uphold and champion press freedom,” the letter says.

Union members will meet on Tuesday to discuss a collective response.

articles.title: If Netanyahu goes, does anything really change for Palestinians?
articles.excerpt:
Four rival Israeli political movements have agreed to work together in a bid to unseat Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

The factions – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the...
articles.body_text:
Four rival Israeli political movements have agreed to work together in a bid to unseat Israel’s longest serving prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu.

The factions – the Yashar party, the Democrats, the Yisrael Beytenu party and the Together alliance – span different parts of Israel’s political spectrum but say they are united in their goal to “preserve and strengthen Israel as a Jewish and democratic state”.

The opposition grouping is in a close battle with a pro-Netanyahu coalition heading into the October 27 elections, recent polling indicated, although neither side appeared on track to win a parliamentary majority.

The election comes as Israel faces a series of domestic crises that are tearing at its social fabric, including questions over political accountability for alleged corruption and security failures, disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service and efforts to exclude Arab parties from political life. The country also faces growing backlash abroad, including from allies, over its continuing attacks on Gaza and Lebanon as well as settlements, which are illegal under international law, and settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank.

Analysts said the combination makes the upcoming elections among the most consequential in Israel’s history but even an opposition victory may bring only marginal change for Palestinians suffering record levels of settler violence and mass displacement. While the opposition alliance has taken Netanyahu to task personally, there is little daylight between them when it comes to Israel’s foundational policies in Gaza and the West Bank.

“Palestinians should not expect a fundamental change in Israeli policy if the Netanyahu bloc loses power,” said analyst Samer Jaber, a doctoral researcher specialising in political economy at Royal Holloway, University of London.

“The major political blocs share core positions on the Palestinian question, including support for the existing settlement structure, while the state institutions that formulate and implement policy would remain unchanged,” he added.

The leaders of the four major Jewish-led opposition movements gathered on September 26 and signed a declaration promising not to attack each other in the run-up to the elections and to collaborate in forming a government after the vote.

In addition to Yair Lapid, who leads the official opposition in Israel’s Knesset, the meeting included Gadi Eisenkot, who heads the Yashar party; Naftali Bennett, who leads the Together alliance, cofounded by Lapid; Avigdor Lieberman, who heads Yisrael Beiteinu; and Yair Golan, who leads the Democrats. The declaration does not set out an official leader although Eisenkot is viewed as the opposition’s most likely candidate for prime minister. In a joint statement, the figures said defeating the current government was their “shared highest objective”.

Of the four opposition parties, Yashar is projected to be the strongest. A recent poll by Israel’s Channel 12 suggested Yashar would win 23 seats in parliament, the most of any party and more than the 21 seats projected for Netanyahu’s Likud.

Trailing is the Together alliance, projected to win 13 seats, followed by Yisrael Beiteinu and the Democrats, each projected to win nine.

That would give the opposition a combined 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, seven short of a majority. Netanyahu’s alliance, which includes several ultra-Orthodox and far-right parties, is projected to win 49 seats.

Arab-led parties, representing the Palestinian citizens of Israel, who make up about 20 percent of the population, are projected to win 13 seats, but most leaders of the Jewish-led opposition bloc have ruled out joining forces with them.

Roi Zur, an assistant professor at the University of Essex who leads a research project on Israeli parties’ political ideology and policy, said the anti-Netanyahu coalition has a chance to win if turnout is on its side, noting that several parties that do not “strictly oppose” the prime minister could fall below the 3.25 percent threshold to enter the Knesset, shaking up the balance.

“If these parties waste enough right-wing votes, the opposition might translate their support into power,” Zur told Al Jazeera. “But this might not be enough.”

Even if the opposition alliance manages to find a way to oust Netanyahu, it would likely be weak and incapable – or unwilling – to overhaul Israeli policy in the West Bank and Gaza, analysts said.

“An anti-Netanyahu government will most likely be a very disparate coalition with a very thin majority, if any, in the Knesset. That would make it difficult for such a government to agree on any substantial perceived concessions, such as withdrawing completely from Gaza,” Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israel-Palestine conflict, told Al Jazeera.

“It would also make it difficult for the international community to meaningfully pressure such a government because there will always be a fear that an anti-Netanyahu government could quickly collapse.”

While their positions vary, most leaders of the anti-Netanyahu alliance have taken hardline positions on Gaza and the West Bank that give Palestinians little reason for optimism.

Yashar’s Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief, has called the idea of a Palestinian state “delusional”, and he supports “strengthening” Israeli settlements. However, he opposes full Israeli annexation of the West Bank and has said he would dismantle smaller Israeli outposts not approved by the Israeli government. He also opposes the current government’s E1 settlement plan, which in effect would cut the West Bank in two. On Gaza, Eisenkot supports pursuing a United States-backed peace plan but only from a place of “strength” and only after “Hamas’s total disarmament”.

Israeli attacks across Gaza since the start of a “ceasefire” in October last year have killed nearly 1,500 Palestinians, bringing the overall death toll since the start of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023 to more than 74,000, according to the enclave’s health officials.

Bennett, a former Likud member who served in multiple Netanyahu-led governments, has described himself as “more right-wing” than Netanyahu and advocated exceptionally draconian policies in Gaza, including once calling for a “shoot-to-kill” policy against Palestinians trying to cross into Israel. Bennett staunchly opposes a Palestinian state and supports settlement expansion although he has criticised Israeli settler pogroms against Palestinians. With respect to the future of Gaza, he wants Israeli forces to stay in the enclave until Hamas is disarmed and proposes that Egypt, rather than Turkiye or Qatar, should play a future security role.

Lieberman’s Yisrael Beytenu party also supports settlement expansion, including the E1 plan. He backs annexing all of Area C of the West Bank – which constitutes 60 percent of the territory and is already under full Israeli control – while transferring control of other parts of the territory to Jordan. On Gaza, his party wants Israel to retain “freedom of action”, cut off water and electricity and eventually transfer governance to “an agreed-upon international entity”.

Golan’s Democrats party is the only one to support a form of two-state solution although it frames it as “responsible separation” that includes the “full demilitarisation” of the Palestinian state and complete Israeli security control of the Jordan Valley and other key areas. His party also supports complete demilitarisation for Gaza and a reconstruction process that involves regional states.

Palestinian lawyer and analyst Diana Buttu said each of the opposition leaders “has supported Israel’s genocide in Gaza” while backing settlements or not believing in full “equality for Palestinians”.

This orientation reflects hardening views within Israeli society itself.

According to a September Pew Research Center poll, only 17 percent of Israeli respondents said peaceful coexistence alongside an independent Palestinian state is possible. And according to an August survey by the Jewish People Policy Institute, 38 percent of Jewish Israeli participants favoured annexing the entire West Bank and more than half supported retaining the settlements as part of any future agreement on a Palestinian state.

Nevertheless, some analysts said a new government could roll back or slow down some of the most “controversial and radical steps” of Israel’s current government, which includes far-right settlement proponents Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister of national security, and Bezalel Smotrich, the minister of finance. Smotrich last month said Israel should “go to war” in the West Bank and repeat what it “did in Gaza”.

Changes enacted by a new government would likely include suspending the E1 settlement project and cracking down “on extremist settler violence/terrorism in the West Bank”, said Dov Waxman, a professor of political science at the University of California, Los Angeles, who specialises in Israeli politics and the Israel-Palestine conflict.

A new government would also be expected to “allow more humanitarian aid to enter Gaza in a more predictable, consistent manner and for reconstruction to finally begin there”, he added.

Ehab Jabareen, a Palestinian political analyst and researcher in Israel, told Al Jazeera that a new government led by Netanyahu’s opponents would likely be “more receptive to US and international pressure”, giving more space for potential reconstruction in Gaza.

But overall, Jabareen said, such a government is unlikely to alter Israel’s overarching “paradigm” towards Palestinians. “I would expect the difference to be less about whether Israel maintains control over the Palestinians and more about how the control is exercised, legitimised and managed,” he said.

Amjad Iraqi, senior analyst for Israel and Palestine at the International Crisis Group, said any “shades of difference” would be meaningful for Palestinians who are currently “suffering nearly uninhibited brutality”.

“We’re at a point of mitigation,” Iraqi told Al Jazeera. “It is about trying to lessen the harms. Palestinians are not in a position to expect any kind of radical shift, but every life saved, every piece of land saved matters a lot for people on the ground.”

articles.title: ‘What planet is she on?’: the Seekers take aim at CPAC over use of I am Australian
articles.excerpt:
The carnival is over for use of Australian band’s song they say was played without permission at conservative conference

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

A member of legen...
articles.body_text:
The carnival is over for use of Australian band’s song they say was played without permission at conservative conference

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

A member of legendary Australian band the Seekers has taken aim at a conference featuring Pauline Hanson for using a classic song, confirming no permission had been granted.

Bruce Woodley said the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) featured I Am Australian without approval, while the song’s co-author revealed Hanson had been previously threatened with legal action over its potential use.

I Am Australian was sung as part of CPAC’s opening ceremony in Brisbane on Saturday, after renditions of the national anthem and Waltzing Matilda.

The song – originally co-written by Woodley and the Bushwackers’ Dobe Newton in 1987 – was also advertised as part of the official conference program agenda.

Woodley and Newton lambasted CPAC organisers, saying the song about unity in diversity was at odds with the anti-immigration views expressed at the conference.

Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

“No permission was either sought or given by me for the use of my song,” Woodley said on Monday.

The song’s theme is encapsulated in its line: “We are one, but we are many, and from all the lands of earth we come”.

After the song’s performance, speakers including Hanson and the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, condemned what they called “mass immigration”.

“I would absolutely never endorse the use of the song associated with those purposes,” Newton said.

He said when Hanson tried to use the song in a previous election campaign, he and Woodley threatened her with legal action.

“We said to each other ‘what planet is she on’?” Newton said.

“Bruce and I got a friend of ours to write a furious solicitor’s letter threatening to sue her, and she actually changed her mind.”

He said that during the 2023 voice to parliament referendum, both the yes and no campaigns approached he and Woodley to use the song.

Mark Callaghan, leader of the band Ganggajang and a long-serving board member of copyright management organisations APRA-AMCOS, said CPAC’s unauthorised use of the song was illegal.

“The bottom line is permission must be sought and approved for any public performance, especially in that political context,” he said.

However, he said enforcement was “like playing whack-a-mole”, with his song Sounds of Then (This is Australia) frequently misused for commercial and political purposes without permission.

“We are finding it’s a real problem all over the internet because people put up political posts and then add Sounds of Then, or I Am Australian or (Icehouse’s) Great Southern Land and implying some sort of connection.”

CPAC organisers have been contacted for comment.

The 1997 recording of I Am Australian by late Seekers singer Judith Durham, Air Supply’s Russell Hitchcock and Yothu Yindi leader, the late Dr M Yunupingu, has become an Australian standard, added to the National Film and Sound Archive registry in 2023.

It was used with permission by the Australian Republican Movement in radio and television advertisements during the 1999 referendum.

It is also regularly used in major national and sporting events.

articles.title: Roman fort found in Wales could prove myth of emperor’s camp is real
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality

Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops a...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: Finds suggest account in medieval folklore of a camp near Frenni Fawr hill was rooted in reality

Magnus Maximus, the Roman emperor who ruled Britain in the fourth century, led his troops against the Picts and Scots, but a theory that he also established a military camp near Frenni Fawr hill in Wales has so far been based on folklore.

Now fourth-century coins, among other finds at a newly identified Roman fort in Pembrokeshire, suggest the medieval tale was rooted in reality, to the excitement of archaeologists.

The fort was discovered by Dr Mark Merrony, a leading Roman specialist at the University of Oxford. He heads an excavation that is bringing to life a story about Magnus Maximus, as told in the Mabinogion, a collection of medieval epic tales of myth, magic and miracles.

Merrony expressed excitement that this landscape held the only Roman military site close to where the Mabinogion places the emperor. “If Magnus Maximus was there, there must have been an army there,” he said.

“It’s such a remote area but the tale mentions the easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills, which is where this site is. The presence of a heavily fortified Roman auxiliary fort may help unlock the mystery of a Mabinogion legend that has endured for nearly 1,700 years.”

In The Dream of Macsen Wledig, medieval storytellers used the emperor’s name in Welsh in recounting his rise to power. They described how on his military manoeuvres, he pitched his camp at Frenni Fawr, the 395-metre (1,300ft) easternmost peak of the Preseli Hills.

There had been no archaeological evidence for a Roman marching camp or fort on the summit of the Frenni Fawr or below it until now. Merrony discovered it about 2 miles (3.5km) south-west of the summit in 2024. Satellite imagery had shown a convincing outline in an overgrown field and, shortly after visiting it, his eye was caught by a Roman tile, which turned out to be the first of many.

With financial support from Oxford University and crowdfunding, one of several planned excavations has just finished, confirming his theory of the site and its significance.

Merrony said that before the dig, his brother, Nick, had jokingly asked him to find a couple of coins to prove the Magnus Maximus theory. “He came back and said ‘well, are these any good?’ I said ‘you’ve got to be kidding me’. He’d found two coins dating from the late 4th century.

“It is fascinating to consider that the two coins may be linked to the tale of Macsen Wledig – Magnus Maximus – in the Mabinogion, the Welsh equivalent of the Odyssey.”

Merrony is a leading specialist in the Romano-British period. His previous discoveries include two Roman villas, at Ford in Pembrokeshire and at Cutteslowe in Oxfordshire. He identified a Roman road along the southern shoulder of the Preselis in 2022, challenging assumptions that the Romans did not venture far into Wales.

His research will appear in Antiqvvs, a quarterly magazine dedicated to archaeology, ancient art and history. Magnus Maximus will also feature in Merrony’s forthcoming book, titled Lives of the Roman Emperors: From Augustus to Romulus Augustulus.

Measuring 180 by 150 metres, the fort is on a slope with a commanding view of the surrounding landscape. It is likely to have held about 500 troops, and its discovery overturns assumptions that the area’s Indigenous Celtic tribe was on peaceful terms with the Roman invaders.

It has “a characteristic playing-card form, with rounded corners” and a perpendicular road, Merrony said.

Finds at the site so far include an unusual iron stylus, many pottery shards, large quantities of Roman tiles and extensive compacted clay floors, a common feature on Roman military sites. Even rut marks left by wagons have been preserved.

The geophysical survey confirmed the presence of a rectangular building in the middle of the enclosure and a larger rectangular building immediately to the south.

“This arrangement is consistent with the placement of a headquarters building orientated east and thereby ‘facing the enemy’, and a commander’s house,” Merrony said.

articles.title: The blue wave looks real until you look a little closer
articles.excerpt: Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright and principal at Cornerstone Government Affairs Cassie Smedile discuss midterm strategies as President Donald Trump swings through red states on his campaign ki...
articles.body_text:
Democratic strategist Antjuan Seawright and principal at Cornerstone Government Affairs Cassie Smedile discuss midterm strategies as President Donald Trump swings through red states on his campaign kick.

It’s like watching some sci-fi game with players competing on 470 different fields. Which is your basic definition of crazytown. No human being, without mainlining AI into his or her arm, could possibly track so many contests, so we bounce from one race to the next, with buzzers and bells, like a pinball machine.

Look! Charlie Cook is moving 18 House races in the Democrats’ favor! This is o-vah! The blue wave is getting stronger. Put a cork in this one, it’s done!

But wait a minute. The Republicans have a huge cash advantage. Big-time Democratic donors, for whatever reason, are sitting on their checkbooks. Don’t they realize the stakes? Are they all blinded by the sun on their private islands?

There seems to be a consensus, even privately among Republicans, that the Dems will take the House. The only question is the margin.

President Donald Trump watches a video during a campaign rally at Freeman Coliseum in San Antonio on Oct. 7, 2026. Trump visited Texas to campaign for Republican candidates ahead of the midterm elections. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

So we all wind-surf across the Senate race, even if we know little more than what we read that morning in Politico, or the New York Times or Wall Street Journal.

The GOP just sent another $30 million to Ken Paxton, the Texas Republican who has more baggage than a 747. (Being impeached by your own party doesn’t help.) He was caught on audio saying "everybody’s numbers dropped" after President Trump’s midterm convention. Even Trump calls him "a pain in the *ss sometimes." And this is the guy they want to win?

DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT

His Democratic opponent, James Talarico, went into hiding–what’s up with that? Turns out he had a nasty case of the flu. Still, it’s Texas, the Lone Star State, where Democratic dreams go to die.

Okay, we’re starting to get vertigo. In Maine, is this the year Susan Collins gets knocked off? One poll has her trailing by four points against Democrat Troy Jackson, who replaced weirdo candidate and Nazi tattoo-wearing Graham Platner, who quit after a sexual assault allegation. What a lovely business.

Republicans have a president who’s polling in the low 30s, which perhaps explains why he was campaigning the other day in Syracuse, when New York is among the bluest of blue states.

State Rep. James Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton are in a tight race for the Senate. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images; Ron Jenkins/Getty Images)

The Democrats need a net gain of four seats to control the Senate, and while some are prematurely sipping Champagne, nobody really knows if they can draw that kind of inside straight. If they tell you they do, they’re lying.

MICHIGAN SENATE DEBATE ERUPTS INTO PERSONAL ATTACKS AS ROGERS, EL-SAYED CLASH OVER ISRAEL, IRAN AND MORE

There’s a harsh spotlight on the Michigan Senate race, featuring Democratic socialist Abdul el-Sayed vs. former congressman Mike Rogers. I eagerly watched their high-decibel debate the other night–okay, I was assigned to it--and here’s my takeaway.

El-Sayed won on points–he’s just a smoother and more aggressive debater than Rogers, who looks like a classic pol–and every third sentence was an attack on Trump or the war. This put Rogers at a disadvantage, because he supported the Iran war but now says it should end.

And El-Sayed kept whacking Rogers for owning two yachts, which is sort of irrelevant.

Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers is making a direct pitch to Michigan Democrats following Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images ; JEFF KOWALSKY / AFP via Getty Images))

Rogers called his opponent a "con man" and kept trying to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood. This was a weakness for el-Sayed, who was asked whether he’d send aid if Israel was attacked, and insisted that he’d rather spend the money here at home.

El-Sayed also did a lousy job of defending Medicare for All and why it wouldn’t bring the end of private insurance. Since Michigan is near the border, both men came out against Canadian tariffs–a flip for Rogers–in a noisy segment that was utterly indecipherable to mere mortals.

The whole thing turned into an interrup-ta-thon, with the moderator constantly scolding the contenders.

Aren’t you glad you missed it? Now, thanks to yours truly, you can pretend you saw the debate.

But enough about the midterms. Time to join the punditocracy and speculate about 2028.

Kamala Harris is leading the ridiculously early polls, with a quarter of the Democratic vote.

There’s just one problem. Her husband, the Wall Street Journal reports, has privately told people he doesn’t want her to run. How’s that for a vote of confidence?

So bite your nails, everyone. The fate of the free world, both sides are warning, hangs in the balance.

Howard Kurtz is a media and political analyst and the former host of FOX News Channel's MediaBuzz. Based in Washington, D.C., he joined the network in 2013 and regularly appears on Special Report with Bret Baier and The Story with Martha MacCallum among other programs.

articles.title: Teens at Sydney private religious school made to share beds with teachers, inquiry hears
articles.excerpt:
Former student says nothing untoward happened to her during stays but tells NSW parliamentary inquiry culture of Redeemer Baptist School left much to ‘untangle’ as an adult

Get our breaking news emai...
articles.body_text:
Former student says nothing untoward happened to her during stays but tells NSW parliamentary inquiry culture of Redeemer Baptist School left much to ‘untangle’ as an adult

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Teens at a private religious school were made to share beds with teachers, while its principal once wandered through a common area naked, former students claim.

A NSW parliamentary inquiry on Monday was told of the disturbing allegations from two former students of western Sydney’s Redeemer Baptist School.

Edward Garth, 23, said he was shunned after “escaping” the broader Redeemer community in November.

He told the committee about a study-stay during school holidays when he slept in the same building as principal and church elder Jonathon Cannon.

“I remember one night before dinner, I was in the kitchen getting a drink,” Garth said.

“As I walked into the living room, which was my bedroom at the time, I saw [Cannon], my principal, walk out of the bathroom into the living room naked before heading to his room.

“He was startled, and when they saw me, he ran to his room. I don’t know why he didn’t cover himself with a towel.”

Garth said he reported the incident, but it got back to Cannon, the principal’s brother Noel and the then-pupil’s own parents, who scolded him.

Former student Emma Hughes told the inquiry the culture inside the school left much for students to “untangle” as adults.

School camps, away from parents, were especially anxiety-inducing.

On occasion, a student would have to share a bed with teachers in a caravan park or school-owned cabins to save space, she said.

Her submission stated nothing untoward happened to her during the stays.

“Usually, the student would be a community member, which in itself says they knew maybe they shouldn’t be doing it,” she said.

“But I recall when I was in year 6, I would share a bed with [a] teacher, and in an effort to be fair, she made it so we would rotate every night … so that we all didn’t have to.”

Staff, often known by kinship titles like “uncle”, regularly crossed conversational boundaries, Hughes said.

“Often, personal things were discussed in very public matters,” she said.

“The nature of boundaries is really something which is not particularly, I believe, understood by staff at Redeemer in the way we understand it in most school contexts.”

The school also had an emphasis on surveillance and “dobbing”, public humiliations and punishment, she said.

A boy and girl were made to stand on chairs in front of a year 7 class after teachers intercepted a love note, Hughes said of her time at the school.

Noel Cannon read the note to a collection of students before they were “dressed-down in front of four year groups and many teachers”, she said.

The parliamentary committee is investigating the management of the Parramatta-based school and oversight from government bodies.

The Communities and Justice Department received 15 risks of significant harm notifications since 2004 but they had not triggered a field assessment, an earlier response to questions on notice revealed.

Cannon and other school representatives were invited to appear at the inquiry and state the school’s case.

Committee chair Abigail Boyd said she was disappointed an attempted summons to appear went begging.

AAP has contacted the school for comment on the students’ allegations.
