articles.title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022

Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and y...
articles.body_text:
Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022

Serhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.

Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.

But German police were already closing in on him.

After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.

Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".

Both he and his country have denied any involvement.

Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.

Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor

It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.

There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.

Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.

They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.

Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.

As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.

Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.

But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.

They went on following the forensic crumbs.

The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.

In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.

That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.

He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.

But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.

Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.

By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.

Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.

None of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.

But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them.

"Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."

Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.

That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.

Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution.

"Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.

The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.

Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence.

"At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.

Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".

Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia

Germany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.

Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.

He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.

Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.

Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.

He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.

Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.

In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".

As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."

The implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.

After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.

It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.

It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.

When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".

This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further.

"I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.

He argued that the Nord Stream pipelines had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed that to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe.

"Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."

Serhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.

Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.

Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.

He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.

His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.

And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.

His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.

I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

Sabotage behind Nord Stream gas leaks, says EU

A journey to the site of the Nord Stream explosions

articles.title: Flydubai attacker began a 'drift towards extremism and terrorism' in Australia, UAE says
articles.excerpt:
The Flydubai flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back the aircraft's controls

The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift t...
articles.body_text:
The Flydubai flight was diverted to Saudi Arabia after passengers managed to take back the aircraft's controls

The Omani co-pilot who allegedly attempted to hijack a Flydubai plane started a "drift towards extremism and terrorism" while studying in Australia, United Arab Emirates officials say.

UAE Attorney-General Hamad Saif al-Shamsi also alleged the pilot - widely named as Hamam al-Hammami - was last week trying to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's airport in a "suicide attack".

He wounded the captain in the cockpit with the emergency crash axe before being overpowered by passengers. Another crew on the Dubai-Tel Aviv flight was able to land the aircraft in Saudi Arabia.

Melbourne university RMIT earlier confirmed the pilot had studied there but left before completing his engineering qualification.

What began as a routine flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv turned into a fight for survival when one pilot allegedly stabs another inside the cockpit.

According to Shamsi, interrogations of the 29-year-old pilot revealed he had been inspired by al-Qaeda's 11 September attacks in the US in 2001.

"The findings indicated that signs of his drift towards extremism and terrorism first emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia," the attorney-general was quoted as saying by the UAE's state news agency Wam on Friday.

"During that period, he was influenced by takfiri [radical] ideology through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks."

The Wam report also said the pilot had told investigators "he had prepared himself both psychologically and physically to carry out the plot by intensifying his exposure to material promoting terrorism and training in boxing under a private coach".

"He admitted that he had acted alone, without the involvement of others, although investigations are continuing to verify this claim," Wam said.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation has reported the man was issued an Australian student visa in 2014 and studied in the country in 2015-17, before leaving.

This week, the Sydney Morning Herald unearthed tweets from al-Mammami's now-deleted X account in which he referred to his five years spent studying abroad in Australia, Britain, and New Zealand, as "the golden years of my religious commitment".

More than 170 passengers and crew were on board flight FZ1073 on 30 September.

In the days after the incident, Australian authorities confirmed they were looking into the man's links to Australia.

The Victorian Joint Counter Terrorism Team - made up of the Australian Federal Police (AFP), Victoria Police and the country's security agency ASIO - said it was "investigating the man's links to Australia".

Watch: Tearful pilot recounts moment of Flydubai attack

Indian co-pilot Capt Smit Machchhar has been hailed a hero after managing to unlock the cockpit door while being violently attacked with an axe, allowing passengers to get in and take control of the aircraft.

Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by Flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.

Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.

He was later hired by UAE-based Flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.

Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.

Flydubai co-pilot planned to crash plane into Tel Aviv airport or building, reports say

'I was not going to let others die' - pilot of Flydubai flight describes cockpit attack by co-pilot

articles.title: Intercommunal clashes kill 71 people in South Sudan
articles.excerpt:
Intercommunal clashes have killed 71 people in South Sudan’s town of Rumbek, in Lakes State, the caretaker government said in a statement.

“According to initial security reports, approximately 71 peo...
articles.body_text:
Intercommunal clashes have killed 71 people in South Sudan’s town of Rumbek, in Lakes State, the caretaker government said in a statement.

“According to initial security reports, approximately 71 people were reportedly killed,” including four soldiers, the South Sudanese interim Ministry of Information said in a statement on Friday. The exact number of fatalities has yet to be verified.

According to AFP, witnesses said a group of people from outside Rumbek tried to take control of the town and briefly succeeded. The attackers withdrew when police and military reinforcements arrived. Two witnesses said the fighting moved outside the city limits.

The government statement said, “Rumbek town is currently under the control of Government security forces, and efforts are ongoing to restore normalcy”.

The caretaker government strongly condemned the violence and urged all communities to “exercise maximum restraint and refrain from acts of retaliation that could further escalate tensions”.

On September 22, South Sudan’s President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional government, three months before the country’s first election since its independence in 2011. Kiir appointed a caretaker administration as the country prepares for its first-ever national elections.

His decree ended a power-sharing arrangement set up under a 2018 peace deal that halted a five-year civil war in which about 400,000 people were killed.

Intercommunal conflict has continued across South Sudan, resulting in multiple deadly clashes.

On September 17, 26 people were killed, and 82 were injured during days of fighting in a disputed region on the border between South Sudan and Sudan.

In early March, intercommunal violence left at least 169 people dead after dozens of armed men attacked a town.

articles.title: Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
articles.excerpt:
Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi

A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries ...
articles.body_text:
Nearly 70 potential contacts have been placed under quarantine in Nairobi

A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.

The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.

That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.

More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.

Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.

The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.

The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.

Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).

The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.

The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.

His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.

Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.

Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.

Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.

On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.

We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

Why Uganda is winning the battle against Ebola as virus spreads in DR Congo

However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.

Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.

But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.

Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.

The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.

But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.

It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.

The man's funeral was held under strict safety protocols

Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.

Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.

Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.

Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.

By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.

Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.

He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.

The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.

The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.

Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.

Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.

Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.

"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.

The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.

The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.

articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel
articles.excerpt:
President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volod...
articles.body_text:
President says deal essential to lower US fuel prices but move set to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies

Donald Trump was on a fresh collision course with the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies on Friday after a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, upending years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine.

Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with President Vladimir Putin of Russia, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

In a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.

“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have rocketed due to Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of the global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – with a gallon of fuel now averaging $4.20 – it is the soaring price of diesel, which last month rose to a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm approach.

Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

The agreement was criticized by Democrats, who said it undercut a law Trump signed last month allowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.

“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”

Some Republicans were also critical of the agreement.

“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”

Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.

“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

Trump announced the oil deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met with Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.

“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.

Trump has recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that would stop Moscow attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”

But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.

articles.title: Hollywood feeling more hopeful amid a push for film tax credits and Paramount staying put, filmmaker says
articles.excerpt: As top Democrats throw support behind President Donald Trump's push for a federal film incentive, Stagerunner founder and CEO Jason Fisher told Fox News Digital how the proposal could 'turn on the lig...
articles.body_text:
As top Democrats throw support behind President Donald Trump's push for a federal film incentive, Stagerunner founder and CEO Jason Fisher told Fox News Digital how the proposal could 'turn on the lights' for America's struggling industry.

Now that Paramount is staying put in Los Angeles and state and federal lawmakers are pushing for expanded film tax credits, Hollywood insiders are seeing a glimmer of hope.

On Wednesday, California Gov. Gavin Newsom highlighted the state’s latest efforts to bolster its entertainment industry, including a new post-production tax credit, an expanded film and television tax credit, and new protections for performers against the use of AI-generated content.

"California is the home of entertainment, full stop," Newsom said in a statement. "We’re not just protecting that legacy; we’re investing in its future by expanding our film and television tax credit, launching a new post-production credit and standing up for performers in the age of AI."

"We’re making sure independent filmmakers and the next generation of storytellers and creators have a real shot to build, hire and produce right here in California," he said. "More productions, more good jobs, more California stories told by California workers."

CALIFORNIA LAW PUTS DIGITAL FINGERPRINTS ON AI FAKES

California Governor Gavin Newsom speaks to the media after a press conference in Burbank on Wednesday, July 2, 2025. (Hans Gutknecht/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images)

Meanwhile, at the federal level, a bipartisan coalition of lawmakers is working on a tax credit for film and television productions. The bill is expected to be introduced in Congress in early November, with its backers aiming to secure passage by Dec. 11, before the current Congress concludes its work. If passed, the credit would take effect in 2027 and could be used alongside state production incentives.

Championed by President Donald Trump, the legislation has also received support from one of his most formidable political opponents, Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif. Schiff led the first impeachment effort against Trump and has remained a vocal critic of his leadership.

"I am in strong agreement with the President," Schiff said on X. "Congress should immediately take up and pass a federal film tax incentive to bring back these good-paying jobs that we've lost to other countries."

NETFLIX CHIEF ADMITS TRUMP IS HELPING SHOWBIZ INDUSTRY AS FEDERAL TAX CREDIT BILL AIMS TO FUEL HOLLYWOOD JOBS

President Donald Trump has found an unlikely ally in his push for incentives to bring back the film industry to Hollywood: Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif. (Fox News)

Filmmaker Paul Kampf, a 30-year veteran of the entertainment industry, described California’s incentives as "a really good start."

"No matter where you make your film, whether it's Georgia, Delaware, Puerto Rico, or Europe, if you can do your post-production in California, you're keeping jobs here, especially in independent films," Kampf told Fox News Digital. "We should be incentivizing filmmakers in America to stay in America. And we should also incentivize filmmakers who are outside of America to do their post here."

Kampf, who has produced four feature films and a documentary in Serbia, before embarking on his sixth project there, titled "Harvest," has also found himself embroiled in a situation where a company owned by the Serbian government released the film in Eastern Europe without his permission.

"This film is an example of what happens if we don't protect Americans and entice Americans to film here," Kampf said.

In California, 35 films, including 28 independent projects, have received production incentives for filming in the state. The sequel to Lionsgate’s blockbuster 2026 hit "Michael" is among the projects, along with a new Pixar film.

FILM PRODUCER SAYS 'MADE IN AMERICA' MOVIES CAN HELP REVIVE HOLLYWOOD'S STRUGGLING INDUSTRY

The Hollywood Sign in the Hollywood Hills on Sept. 30, 2025, in Los Angeles. (Photothek via Getty Images)

All told, the projects are expected to generate more than $1 billion in direct production spending, according to the California Film Commission.

"Through our tax credit program, we’re helping bring these stories to the screen while keeping the jobs, investment, and production that bring them to life right here in California," Colleen Bell, director of the California Film Commission, said Wednesday in a statement.

Kampf, who has made films in several countries, told Fox News Digital that California had long been arrogant about its position in the industry, assuming it held a monopoly on filmmaking.

"I've made movies all over the world. I don't make movies in LA, I live here, I lived the taxes of LA and California and I live the sort of challenges of lifestyle here," he said. "I think Hollywood needs a facelift, and it's no pun intended. It needs to be seen as a place that is invigorating and investing in filmmaking again."

"Realistically, what I can say is the tax incentives in America are really maybe the best bipartisan entertainment bill that I've seen in the last 10 years," he added.

articles.title: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nation
articles.excerpt:
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month

As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager ex...
articles.body_text:
Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last month

As dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets.

"There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school.

"We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."

He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.

Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down.

"They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."

The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.

Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in Lille

The protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.

Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.

The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.

Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protesting

The problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.

On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.

But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.

Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.

It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.

When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils).

"It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.

Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for change

On Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.

But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country.

"It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest.

"It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."

Police have been accused of heavy-handed tactics

The unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.

So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.

More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.

But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.

A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.

Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.

A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth.

"For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."

Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.

Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protests

But Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests.

"These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."

Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.

Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring.

"Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."

Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schools

The protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.

More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.

But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.

The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.

Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.

Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.

Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.

Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.

Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrations

Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.

Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.

He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.

Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration.

"I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.

Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.

She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.

The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.

The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social history

The problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.

This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.

Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.

And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.

What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.

The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.

Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.

She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.

For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.

Many students have said they will not back down from protesting

But many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition.

"In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris.

"That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."

As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.

A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street.

The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.

Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

France's school protests: What lies behind the anger

France promises 3,000 extra teachers in first step to calm student protests

articles.title: Texas legend has sky-high hopes for Longhorns ahead of Red River Rivalry game vs Oklahoma
articles.excerpt:
"I really like their coach, Venables. You know, I coached against him. I think he's one of the finest defensive coaches I ever gone against."

The Red River Rivalry makes its return on Saturday, and s...
articles.body_text:
"I really like their coach, Venables. You know, I coached against him. I think he's one of the finest defensive coaches I ever gone against."

The Red River Rivalry makes its return on Saturday, and someone all too familiar with the big game was back in Dallas on Friday gearing up for his former Texas Longhorns to continue their national title hopes.

Colt McCoy never quite reached the promised land in Austin, but he did have the upper hand in the matchup, going 3-1 in his four years, including the 45-35 victory when his Texas squad was fifth in the country, and the Oklahoma Sooners were ranked No. 1.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Texas has won three of the last four matchups after losing 10 of the previous 13, including the 2018 Big 12 Championship Game.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Colt McCoy of the Texas Longhorns passes during Texas' 13-12 win over Nebraska in the Big 12 Conference championship game at Cowboys Stadium in Arlington, Texas, on Dec. 6, 2009. (Corbis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

"Just the history of this game, right in the middle between both schools, played in Dallas, played in the Cotton Bowl, that place, I mean, you just feel the sanctity of that place when you walk down the tunnel, the shared tunnel. The fans are split down the middle, it's always played in October, it's kind of the kickoff into your conference," McCoy said to Fox News Digital in an interview Friday. "It's just a really, really special game, at least the ones that I was a part of.

"And the beauty of rivalries is that you may be the best team in the country, but if you don't strap it up and play that day or if you're off that day, like you got problems. So, I love it. Just being back here is pretty surreal. It's a really, really fun weekend."

McCoy was hanging out with some fans on behalf of Fanatics, which offers official Red River Rivalry merchandise.

"I had a great time, man. Texas fans are the best, dude. They show up everywhere. It's a whole lot of fun to engage with them. And then especially this weekend, this was the one game on your calendar every year that you circled, and you thought about, and you got nervous about all the things. This is a fun one," McCoy said.

"Fanatics is great. Listen, it's a wonderful brand. The gear is incredible. The fans showed out. There was like a million fans in the Texas line and nobody on the Oklahoma side. So, this is exactly what I wanted."

Colt McCoy runs during Texas' 16-13 win over Oklahoma in the Red River Rivalry at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas, Texas, on Oct. 17, 2009. (Corbis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

McCoy admitted that it was tough to stay focused on the game before the Red River Rivalry knowing what was soon on the table.

"Generally, we didn't play great if I can remember right," McCoy said (he went 3-1 in games preceding the rivalry, the loss being a 41-21 upset by unranked Kansas State when they were No. 7). "But then the moment you get back in the locker room after that game, they've got Boomer Sooner playing and they play it all week, and by the time you get to the game, you're just ready to punch somebody in the mouth."

But when McCoy was a third-round pick in the NFL Draft, he had no choice but to throw the rivalry aside.

"I got to admit, I've had some amazing teammates that came out of Oklahoma over the years. Trent Williams for a long time, he is a phenomenal teammate. He may be the greatest left tackle ever. Still playing 17 years at an All-Pro level. It really is unbelievable. A great guy, great friend. Played with Adrian Peterson for a couple years, Tress Way, amazing punter. Kyler Murray is my boy. So, there's unfortunately been some really good dudes come out of Oklahoma."

But now that he's out of the game, it's all Texas and no Oklahoma once again, and he feels like this year's squad has what it takes to bring home its first national title in over two decades.

Colt McCoy of the Texas Longhorns celebrates the win over Oklahoma during the Red River Rivalry at Cotton Bowl Stadium in Dallas, Texas, on Oct. 17, 2009. (Corbis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"Listen, we're 4-0 and number one in the country, and they hadn't really clicked yet, right? The sky's the limit for this team. They're super talented. They're well coached. They kind of have all the makings from both sides of the ball to be really special. And I certainly think that they have a lot of confidence internally, and they just got to go do it. And I really think they will," said McCoy.

"We had a 10-year dry spell that was hard. I think right now what I'll give you is I do think that this is arguably the most talented roster that Texas has had. Just when you look across the board, you look at the coaching staff, you look at the players, you look at just the straight talent, like man-to-man, they're never going to go into a game and be outmatched. And that really got to give everyone on that team a lot of confidence."

articles.title: Thousands of security personnel deployed as Delhi braces for ‘cockroach’ protest
articles.excerpt:
Police have been deployed in big numbers even during demonstrations by opposition parties in the lead up to Saturday's 'cockroach' protest

Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a ...
articles.body_text:
Police have been deployed in big numbers even during demonstrations by opposition parties in the lead up to Saturday's 'cockroach' protest

Parts of the Indian capital, Delhi, have been turned into a fortress, with tens of thousands of security forces deployed, as the influential Gen Z-led "cockroach" movement has called for a major protest on Saturday.

The protesters are seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over allegations of manipulating voters' lists.

The Election Commission has denied this and Kumar is yet to comment on the resignation demand.

Police say they have denied permission for the gathering and all roads leading to Jantar Mantar, the main protest venue, have been closed with huge metal barricades.

Several trains to Delhi have been cancelled and police have ordered dozens of metro stations shut to prevent protesters from gathering.

But Abhijeet Dipke, founder ⁠of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) - the online satirical movement that is spearheading the protests - has said the CJP will march to Jantar Mantar on Saturday morning "come what may".

"If you want to jail us or even shoot us we are prepared," he added, addressing ​Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a post on X.

The CJP held a rally in Bengaluru city on Thursday against CEC Kumar

The CJP's weeks-long protest in the summer seeking education reforms was its first major challenge to Modi's government. The CJP scored a major victory when it forced education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign in July.

The CJP protesters returned to streets last week with a rally in Mumbai city to press for CEC Kumar's resignation. On Thursday, they held a huge rally in the southern city of Bengaluru (formerly Bangalore).

Student groups and opposition parties have also protested in the capital over the past few days.

Saturday's protests are being billed as the biggest in recent times as they are also being supported by several opposition parties, farmer organisations and student groups.

CJP leaders allege the authorities have been preventing many of their supporters from reaching Delhi.

In the capital, more than 30,000 police and paramilitary personnel have been deployed and authorities have appealed to citizens to stay away from protests.

Police official Nupur Prasad told a press conference, external that one of the reasons for denying permission to protest at Jantar Mantar was the "short notice" given by the CJP.

"Under current guidelines, an application to organise an event at Jantar Mantar must be submitted at least 10 days prior to the scheduled date," she said.

Also, she added that in the past, the CJP had not followed "lawful directions" given to them.

"In light of the non-compliance with prescribed procedures, the failure to adhere to past legal directions, and the current state of public safety, law and order, and traffic regulation, permission for the proposed protest at Jantar Mantar is hereby denied."

The CJP have questioned police denying them permission for the protest - they say that legally they only have to inform the police and do not need their approval to gather.

Gyanesh Kumar is at the centre of the voter-roll revision controversy

At the centre of the row is a controversial revision of the country's electoral rolls known as the Special Intensive Revision, or SIR, which began last year.

The Election Commission says it is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries - and so far, 130 million names have been struck off the voters' list.

But opposition parties and activists have alleged that many of those are eligible voters and that the process is being manipulated by CEC Kumar to favour Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) during elections. Both the BJP and the Election Commission have rejected the accusations.

The past few days have also seen a major escalation in the opposition's standoff with the Election Commission.

For three days in a row starting Tuesday, Delhi witnessed dramatic scenes with police breaking up protests by opposition leader Rahul Gandhi and other MPs over the issue.

Videos showing police forcing Gandhi on to a bus and preventing him from climbing out of the bus window subsequently went viral on social media.

articles.title: Headteachers threaten strike ballots after losing confidence in Ofsted
articles.excerpt:
Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action

Tensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing i...
articles.body_text:
Unions tell government to fix ‘overbearing mess’ of inspection regime and its impact on staff wellbeing – or risk industrial action

Tensions between England’s headteachers and Ofsted are developing into a crisis after school leadership unions said they had no confidence in the watchdog and would hold strike ballots unless “significant wellbeing issues” caused by Ofsted’s inspections regime were fixed.

The Association of School and College Leaders​ (ASCL), which includes senior leaders in many secondary schools, described Ofsted’s inspection system as “an overbearing mess” and urged the government to pause inspections to stop teachers leaving the profession.

A spokesperson for ASCL said that “if change is not forthcoming” the union would seek to hold an indicative ballot on industrial action.

The National Association of Head Teachers (NAHT) said it would also consider steps including strike action at a meeting of its leadership next week.

The combative moves come after a survey published by Ofsted showed 88% of schools reported that recent inspections had negatively affected staff wellbeing.

The Guardian reported last week that Lucy Powell, the education secretary, wants Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” and overhaul the framework introduced last year. The new framework was intended to lower the strain and workload caused by inspections, but many heads say the opposite has happened.

In response to ASCL’s announcement, a spokesperson for the Department for Education said: “Inspection and accountability are vital, but they must reflect the reality of what is happening in schools, recognise the context they are working in, and support improvement rather than add to the pressures they already face.

“That’s why we are working with Ofsted and school leaders to ensure accountability is fair, proportionate and focused on helping every school get better, so every child gets the education they deserve.”

An Ofsted spokesperson said: “We have worked hard to reduce the pressure of inspection in recent years, but we know workload and wellbeing remain a challenge.

“We are working with the Department for Education on this and we will keep listening to feedback from professionals as we continue to improve what we do.”

​Hostility ​towards Ofsted has been heightened since the death of Ruth Perry, a popular headteacher in Reading. In 2023 a coroner found that an Ofsted inspection contributed to Perry’s mental health deterioration and her death. Labour pledged to reform school inspections in its 2024 election manifesto.

But ASCL said it had “seen no meaningful progress on the part of Ofsted to address significant wellbeing issues caused by inspections, and that it is increasingly concerned about the welfare and morale of members”.

The motion of no confidence in Ofsted passed by ASCL’s executive stated: “We fear that the disproportionate stress and anxiety exerted by the inspection system will lead to school leaders deciding to leave their posts with a consequent impact on schools, children and young people.”

Pepe Di’​Iasio, ​ASCL’s general ​secretary, said: “​Our repeated attempts to resolve our concerns through discussion and negotiation have hit a brick wall … The current system is not fit for purpose. It is an overbearing mess and urgently needs to be reviewed.”

Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the NAHT, said: “Our deep concerns about this Ofsted framework and the impact it is having on professionals are longstanding. Our executive committee will be meeting at the end of next week and debating the next steps NAHT will take. We fully expect that debate to include the option of pursuing industrial action.”

articles.title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates say
articles.excerpt:
With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Women living with a ...
articles.body_text:
With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.

The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.

Formerly known as polycystic ovarian syndrome, PMOS affects one in eight women. Symptoms can include irregular periods, excess hair growth on the body and face, weight gain and hair thinning.

The lifelong condition, for which there is no cure, can lead to an increased risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease and endometrial cancer.

While GLP-1s are not specifically approved by the Therapeutic Goods Administration to treat PMOS, patients are being prescribed the medications off-label.

Half a million Australians are estimated to be using weight-loss medications regularly, a University of New South Wales study found in July.

Lorna Berry, a spokesperson for the POSAA who was diagnosed with the condition at 32, said she would welcome GLP-1s being subsidised for patients diagnosed with PMOS, in addition to funding for evidence-based research.

“It’s important for people to have access to medications, irrespective of where they live or where they were born … it’s really important that there’s equitable access,” she told the Guardian.

Berry said some women living with the condition were already missing out on being able to access the medications due to their high cost, which can set patients back several hundred dollars each month.

Associate professor Magdalena Simonis, the women’s health spokesperson for the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, said the college did not currently have a position on whether GLP-1s were appropriate for the management of PMOS.

“They’re not necessarily the only tool we have available to us, and that is important because long-term use is expensive, and it doesn’t look like these are going to be on the PBS anytime soon, and maybe not ever for conditions such as PMOS,” she said.

“Because traditionally women’s conditions are not included in these changes.”

Simonis, a GP with an expert interest in PMOS, said should research find the weight-loss medications more effective than existing treatments, a broader discussion about health equity would be needed.

“That is a conversation that we’re having about obesity as a national issue,” she said.

GLP-1 drugs – glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists – mimic a naturally occurring hormone which helps manage blood sugar levels and reduces hunger.

Ozempic is listed by the PBS, but only for the treatment of diabetes.

The Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee last November recommended Wegovy be subsidised for those with a body mass index above 35.

The committee will meet next month when it will consider Novo Nordisk’s revised proposal to list Wegovy for obesity following protracted negotiations.

The Danish pharmaceutical company produces both Ozempic and Wegovy.

They contain the same active ingredient – semaglutide – but Wegovy has a higher dose.

“Novo Nordisk is continuing to work constructively with the Department of Health to try to negotiate a solution for the PBS listing of Wegovy,” a company spokesperson said.

“We remain committed to improving access for eligible Australians living with obesity.”

QENDO, an organisation advocating for people affected by PMOS and other women’s health conditions, said it recognised “growing interest in GLP-1 medications for managing PMOS, particularly for people experiencing metabolic complications and challenges with weight management”.

“While emerging evidence suggests potential benefits for some patients, further research is needed to establish their long-term effectiveness and safety specifically for PMOS,” QENDO’s acting chief executive, Kate Fisher, said.

articles.excerpt:
A quarter of the way into the NFL season, the New York Giants, Carolina Panthers, and Cleveland Browns sit atop their divisions, but Craig Carton isn't buying the hype for a single second.

The New Yo...
articles.body_text:
A quarter of the way into the NFL season, the New York Giants, Carolina Panthers, and Cleveland Browns sit atop their divisions, but Craig Carton isn't buying the hype for a single second.

The New York Giants are one of the NFL's biggest surprises this season, sitting atop the NFC East. But that doesn't mean they're not banged up.

But, in true run-straight-ahead Skattebo style, he seems like he's less worried about it than just about anyone else.

GIANTS' CAM SKATTEBO VOWS TO MAINTAIN VIOLENT PLAYING STYLE AFTER GRUESOME ANKLE INJURY

Cam Skattebo put Giants fans at ease on Friday making it clear that he's not concerned about an injury that limited his practice time this week. (Photo by Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images)

DEONTE BANKS' GAME-SEALING PICK-SIX PROPELS GIANTS INTO PLACE THEY HAVEN'T BEEN SINCE 2015

articles.title: Analysis: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
articles.excerpt:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions an...
articles.body_text:
Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.

Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.

The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.

As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.

The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.

It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.

Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky criticises 'gift to Putin'

For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.

He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.

He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.

His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.

Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear.

It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy".

"Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.

It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.

The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.

Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.

The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.

Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.

With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked.

"Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.

But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.

Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

Trump wants to reduce the cost of fuel as the midterms loom - will it work?

articles.title: Daniel Lurie argues progressivism led San Francisco astray on public safety, drug crisis
articles.excerpt:

San Francisco ...
articles.body_text:
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said during an interview on Thursday that the city had lost its way on progressive politics, arguing it was "entrapped" and lost sight of major issues.

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie said Thursday that the city had lost its way and was focused on the wrong things, arguing that the California city was "entrapped in our progressive values."

"We lost our way as a city," he told CNN's Dana Bash in an interview. "We were focused on the wrong things, and today we're focused on common sense. We're focused on good governance. We're focused on delivering results for the people of San Francisco. I said from day one, public safety was going to be my number one priority. The crisis on our streets, the mental health and drug crisis is another top priority of mine. And I want to get the basics of governance right."

Lurie, a moderate Democrat and heir to the Levi Strauss fortune, was elected in 2024 after defeating incumbent London Breed.

"I mean, we got so entrapped in our progressive values and talking about progressivism, that we weren't taking stock of what was happening on our streets," he told Bash. "We had 810 people die of overdose in San Francisco three years ago. There's nothing progressive about that. There's nothing progressive about 30,000 car break-ins. Everyone had to deal with whether or not their car was going to be broken into," the mayor said, adding that the number of car break-ins had dropped 90%.

SAN FRANCISCO STILL HASN'T RECOVERED SINCE PANDEMIC EXODUS: REPORT

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie speaks during a postgame ceremony honoring broadcaster Mike Krukow at Oracle Park on Sept. 27, 2026, in San Francisco, Calif. (Getty Images)

Bash asked Lurie about progressivism again, specifically how he defined the word. The mayor said he supported progressive values, such as taking care of the city's immigrants, and the LGBTQ+ community.

"But, we got to a point where we said, 'Well, it's that person's right to be on the street using drugs,' or is that person — it's okay for someone to just go in and take what they want from a small business," he said.

"In my mind, that's not progressive," Lurie continued. "There's nothing progressive about small businesses having to shutter up because they're a victim of crime over and over again. There's nothing progressive, as I said before, about 810 people dying of overdose. I'm not going to walk by somebody on the street and not do anything anymore."

NEWSOM BLASTS DEMOCRATS FOR THEIR 'VICTIM MINDSET' THAT ENABLED HOMELESS CRISIS

San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie speaks at an event. (Christina House/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

President Donald Trump praised Lurie during a cabinet meeting in March for "really trying" to improve San Francisco since taking office.

"I know they have a mayor who’s trying very hard. He’s a Democrat, but he’s trying very hard," Trump said at the time.

Socialism has been on the rise in the U.S., as several states have seen socialist candidates win their primary elections. In some places, progressive candidates were rejected for more moderate voices as well.

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff told Fox News Digital that even more liberal voices were calling out progressivism.

"Lurie is right, and it’s not just more moderate voices like his calling this stuff out — we’ve seen AOC try to distance herself from ‘Woke 1’ as well," he said. "Some on the left have absolutely allowed themselves to get bullied into silence and, as funny and extreme a case as it was — that is how you get stories like that Massachusetts lesbian bar with the masking debacle."

"Progressive policies are increasingly popular across the country, particularly on economic issues in these hard economic times," Shroff continued. "But there is also a sense that the DSA left can’t get out of its own way and can never be satisfied."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Homes in San Francisco, California, on Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026.  (Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"It’s not popular to say, but there is a real contingent on the left that uses these movements to center themselves and try to control others — beyond actual progressive aims," he added. "That is what Lurie is hitting on here and that is in some sense what happened in SF before his tenure. Yes, we want policies that are pro-family, pro-worker, pro-immigrant — that doesn’t mean letting the loudest voices dictate everything at the cost of a functioning city."

Hanna Panreck is an associate editor at Fox News.
