articles.title: Search warrants used in Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor raids were unlawful, court rules
articles.excerpt:
Judge makes ruling after former prince brought judicial review of operation linked to Jeffrey Epstein investigation

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police...
articles.body_text:
Judge makes ruling after former prince brought judicial review of operation linked to Jeffrey Epstein investigation

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has won his legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants that led to his arrest.

The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.

On Thursday, Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.

The episode is embarrassing for TVP but police believe it will not affect the success of the investigation.

The warrants were issued by an Old Bailey judge on 18 February and Mountbatten-Windsor was subsequently arrested the following day, on his 66th birthday, on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

The arrest followed information that emerged from the Jeffrey Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein, a convicted child sex offender.

Police began searching the former Duke of York’s residence on the Sandringham estate and his former Windsor home, Royal Lodge, on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.

Hilliard said the search warrants were quashed but police had made an application, which would be heard next year, to retain the seized property on the basis that it would have been lawful to take it under a different statutory provision. Mountbatten-Windsor opposes that application.

The judge said: “The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful.”

A senior police source said: “It’s not going to bring the investigation to a halt or affect the chances of success.”

They added: “The news media might say the police messed up. But it was the judicial decision [to grant the warrant] that was incorrect.”

TVP have been in discussions with lawyers from the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) about the strength of their case and what evidence they would need for a prosecution.

A TVP spokesperson said: “The agreement that led to the quashing of the warrants relates specifically to a decision made by the court regarding the legal basis for these and is not a judgment on our ongoing investigation.

“We ensured the court was presented with all the necessary information and paperwork to inform their decision, following the correct legal processes throughout.

“We accept the position that the initial court’s decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect and therefore these must be legally quashed.”

Hilliard told the court that the grant of a search warrant under section eight of the Police and Criminal Evidence Act (Pace) 1984 was conditional on the issuing judge being satisfied there were reasonable grounds to suspect that the material sought did not include items subject to legal privilege or special procedure material.

Special procedure material includes documents in possession of a person who acquired them in the course of any trade, business, profession or other occupation – for the purpose of any paid or unpaid office – who holds it subject to an express or implied undertaking to hold it in confidence.

The judge said the presence of legally privileged material was expressly envisaged in the application for the search warrants and that material was likely to be in the possession of Mountbatten-Windsor “who had acquired or created it in circumstances which would make it special procedure material”. He concluded that a lawful warrant could only have been issued under section nine of Pace.

Nick Vamos, the former head of special crime at the CPS, said: “Given the technical nature of the errors revealed today, I expect the crown court to rule in due course that the police can keep the material, or at least as much of it as they would have been entitled to seize in the first place, so they may not ultimately pay much of a price beyond today’s red faces.”

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.

articles.title: South Korea recalls Ukraine envoy over prisoner-of-war row
articles.excerpt:
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.

It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ann...
articles.body_text:
South Korea has said it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, the latest escalation in a diplomatic spat between both countries.

It started last month when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that his government had transferred two captured North Korean soldiers to Seoul.

Seoul says Ukraine broke an agreement to keep the transfer a secret but Zelensky's office maintains that there was no non-disclosure agreement in place.

The two North Korean soldiers, who were among thousands from the country supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.

South Korean Vice Foreign Minister Park Yoon-joo had in September lodged a formal complaint with his Ukrainian counterpart Andrii Vieshkin over the matter.

And earlier this week, Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said he received an apology from his Ukrainian counterpart, but added that it fell short of Seoul's expectations, according to local reports.

Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said in a statement on Thursday that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions".

"Despite Seoul's decision to recall its ambassador, Ukraine remains open to restoring a constructive dialogue - even if it takes time," he said.

Earlier on Thursday, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said in a statement it would "continue consultations with the Ukrainian side", adding that it expected that "various outstanding issues...[would] be resolved smoothly".

Ukraine says it captured two injured North Korean soldiers in Russia

Thousands of North Koreans fought for Russia. A memorial hints at the death toll

Zelensky had revealed the transfer at a speech at the UN General Assembly in September, adding that the two North Koreans had not been "easy to capture alive".

It prompted a swift condemnation from South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who called it "greatly disappointing" and said the transfer was a "highly sensitive issue" impacting national security.

President Lee also faced heavy criticism at home in light of the revelation, with local opposition accusing him of wanting to cover up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

But his office said that it had been kept confidential partly to protect the North Koreans' families and added that Kyiv also wanted the transfer kept secret to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.

Lee's office explained Ukraine had indicated the soldiers would be mentioned in Zelensky's address, but not the fact of their transfer.

The spat escalated when Zelensky's office responded claiming that the two countries did not have a non-disclosure agreement.

Seoul later demanded Ukraine apologise for "announcing a falsehood" and said its actions had seriously damaged trust between the two nations.

Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has refused to break from its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

After North Korean troops were deployed to support Russia in 2024, Kyiv stepped up pressure on South Korea to supply cutting-edge anti-air missiles to help defend Ukraine's energy infrastructure from Russian drone and missile attacks.

This July, Seoul had announced a $100 million assistance package to Ukraine. Lee's office said it would be an expansion of earlier assistance which was comprised of non-lethal items including helmets, personal armour and medical equipment.

Meanwhile Russia's foreign ministry has warned it would have "no choice but to retaliate" if South Korea provided Ukraine with arms, without specifying action it might take.

South Korea has long pursued cordial ties with its neighbours who may be at odds with its ally, the US.

Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, it has worked to deepen trade and diplomatic relations with Russia, which borders North Korea, and views both Moscow and Beijing as key partners in efforts to influence Pyongyang.

Teddy Young, 24, from Bedfordshire, charged under National Security Act after arrest by counter-terror police

A serving member of the Royal Navy has been charged with spying, police have said.

Teddy...
articles.body_text:
Teddy Young, 24, from Bedfordshire, charged under National Security Act after arrest by counter-terror police

A serving member of the Royal Navy has been charged with spying, police have said.

Teddy Young, 24, will appear today at Westminster magistrates’ court after he was charged with obtaining protected information that could benefit a unnamed foreign power.

He was arrested at his home in Bedfordshire on 6 October after an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London (CTPL). He had now been charged with a number of offences under the National Security Act, the Metropolitan police said on Thursday.

Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of CTPL, said: “These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces. We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter.”

The Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) authorised the charges on Wednesday. They allege that, between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025, Young engaged in conduct in preparation for committing an offence of disclosing protected information.

It was also alleged that in the same time period, he obtained, copied, recorded or retained protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.

The arrest and charges are not connected to the recent investigation into the incident at RAF Fairford.

A Royal Navy spokesperson said: “A member of the Royal Navy has been charged with National Security Act offences following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing London. As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage.”

articles.title: British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed Miliband
articles.excerpt:
UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced

Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, wi...
articles.body_text:
UK and Israel back away from full diplomatic confrontation, though British presence in Palestine will be much reduced

Israel and the UK have backed away from a full-scale diplomatic confrontation, with Britain announcing it is rebranding its consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​as a UK mission, a move that will result in UK diplomats leaving Israel, with only seven to remain in the building.

The move was forced on the UK by the Israeli government as punishment for the decision by the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, last month to ban trade with illegal settlements and introduce a tougher sanctions regime against those that aided the building of settlements. The UK is seeking to protect the two state solution as the best means of ending the Israeli-Palestine conflict.

Miliband has also backed away from a threat to expel a parallel number of Israeli diplomats from London, as was once planned, arguing it would be unwise to do so during the Israeli election campaign.

There has been a dispute within the UK government over whether taking tough measures against Israel at such a sensitive political moment could help the re-election chances of the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, before polls on 27 October if they would appear to boost his standing as a leader prepared to confront the nation’s critics.

Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to shut on Thursday, and the foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said that it had acted on its threat, describing the consulate as closed.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians. Miliband said in a statement: “The UK government reiterates its longstanding view that East Jerusalem is occupied territory.”

Sa’ar listed four actions to curtail UK activity in Israel, including the removal of the British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat and entry bans to Israel for 12 named individuals, including the former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn . “We established a clear principle: It is not possible to act against Israel without Israel taking appropriate measures in response,” he said. “We did not want to reach this point, but the actions of the UK Labour government brought us here.”

He also accused the UK government of “hostile rhetoric, including false accusations against Israel, such as accusations of ‘ethnic cleansing’”.

Miliband, who is currently visiting Kyiv, said in a statement that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks partly for security reasons, it would be possible to work to build up the presence at the mission in future months.

He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks.

UK sources said Sa’ar had threatened to close the whole consulate, and it was better for Britain to retain its reduced presence in the hope it could be restored and rebuilt regardless of the imminent election outcome.

The sources stressed that the right to take reciprocal action remained, and the UK did not accept that Israel had the legal right to close the consulate, which has stood for 200 years and is placed in East Jerusalem on territory that Britain and international courts recognise as occupied territory.

Miliband said the UK mission would be independent, operational and still able to deliver vital services to the Palestinian people. The value of that assertion will be tested by the small number of diplomats remaining and their reduced diplomatic status. The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Israel last week to negotiate a version of the deal.

Vincent Fean, the UK consul general to Palestine between 2010 and 2014, said: “The term mission is a generic diplomatic term and does not of itself have any meaning … In terms of numbers, losing 20 staff is a big drop but it’s a better outcome than nothing. It leaves a space, a place and team to build up whatever the outcome of the Israeli election.”

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The ‌incident has highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement last month to the UK parliament, Miliband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s government, were committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank. Israel disputes this.

The UK Foreign Office was advised informally by the former attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel would be acting unlawfully if it closed the consulate on the basis it was sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.

Israel has also said it will revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. France and Canada, which joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza, prompted by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis, as Britain became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the deaths of thousands of Palestinians in an effort to render Hamas inoperative, a task successive Westminster governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds he believes this is a matter for international courts to determine.

articles.title: French high school protests continue despite PM’s promise of action – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Demonstrators have rejected a promise by Sébastien Lecornu to present a plan to fix the country’s education system by the end of the month

French education minister Édouard Geffray has invited the th...
articles.body_text:
Demonstrators have rejected a promise by Sébastien Lecornu to present a plan to fix the country’s education system by the end of the month

French education minister Édouard Geffray has invited the three leading high school students associations for further talks at the ministry later this afternoon.

This comes as a recent opinion poll showed that the French public broadly supports the protest – with three-thirds agreeing with the students’ demands, and 55% backing the demonstrations – but is divided on whether they should continue (Europe Live, yesterday).

Back to France, let me bring you more pictures from this morning’s high school protests, which are taking place not just in Paris, but also in other cities, including Nantes and Bordeaux.

We are getting reports of another knife attack at a school in Poland.

The incident took place in Leszczydół-Nowiny, east-central Poland, leaving one person dead and two injured. A 15-year-old boy was apprehended at the scene.

It comes just a day after a 17-year-old boy injured nine people in a separate school stabbing attack (Europe Live, yesterday). An improvised explosive device was discovered in his backpack.

Elsewhere in the country, another 17-year-old has been detained on suspicion of planning a similar knife attack.

In response to the wave of incidents, Polish police said they will step up spot checks near schools to scan for knives and identify suspicious behaviour.

Aisha Down in London, Joseph Gedeon in Washington and Jennifer Rankin in Brussels

In other news, the Trump administration pressured multiple countries to withdraw their sponsorship of a leading European conference on disinformation, with Canada, Lithuania and the EU’s diplomatic service subsequently agreeing to do so, the Guardian understands.

The conference, #Disinfo2026, taking place Wednesday and Thursday, is the annual meetup of Europe’s counter-disinformation community and has drawn hundreds of researchers, journalists, technologists and policymakers to a hotel in Vilnius, Lithuania. It is run by an independent Brussels non-profit, EU Disinfo Lab.

Days before the conference, the logos of its main supporters – the Lithuanian ministry of foreign affairs, the European External Action Service (EEAS) and Global Affairs Canada, the country’s foreign ministry – were wiped off its website.

Photos of the event shared with the Guardian also show white stickers affixed over the logos of these organisations printed on official conference materials, appearing to indicate they were struck from the program in haste.

Three persons familiar with the matter, including European officials, confirmed that the US state department had been in touch with multiple governments over their support for the conference.

Internal state department documents seen by the Guardian also show US officials thanking Lithuania for “taking US concerns seriously”. The document says Washington was “grateful” Lithuania supposedly found a panel framing the US as a foreign information threat “reprehensible and surprising” and welcomed its decision to limit involvement in the conference.

French education minister Édouard Geffray has invited the three leading high school students associations for further talks at the ministry later this afternoon.

This comes as a recent opinion poll showed that the French public broadly supports the protest – with three-thirds agreeing with the students’ demands, and 55% backing the demonstrations – but is divided on whether they should continue (Europe Live, yesterday).

High school protests across France show no sign of slowing down, with nearly 400 educational establishments facing disruptions this morning.

Demonstrators have rejected a promise by prime minister Sébastien Lecornu to present a plan to fix the country’s education system by the end of the month, demanding he fully engages with their demands sooner than that.

In a televised address last night, Lecornu said the country could not be “indifferent” to their concerns, and acknowledged that their anger “does not come from nowhere,” but did not make any immediate headline-grabbing announcements.

“We want real action, and until we get it, we’ll keep mobilising,” a high school student named Marilou in Fontainebleau told AFP.

I will keep an eye on today’s events in France as they unfold.

Over in Spain, I will look at reactions after last night’s death of María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old whose eviction set off a nationwide wave of protests against Spain’s housing crisis.

Elsewhere, Britain’s prime minister Andy Burnham will meet with Germany’s Friedrich Merz in Berlin for political talks. Unusually, however, the pair will not hold a joint press conference.

It’s Thursday, 8 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

Voters choosing replacement for Keir Starmer, who announced he was standing down last month

Polls have opened in Keir Starmer’s old seat in Hol...
articles.body_text:
Voters choosing replacement for Keir Starmer, who announced he was standing down last month

Good morning and welcome to our UK politics live blog.

Polls have opened in Keir Starmer’s old seat in Holborn and St Pancras, where the Green party leader, Zack Polanski, is hoping to break Labour’s longstanding grip in the north London constituency.

He might have his work cut out for him. Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali is projected to retain the seat in today’s byelection, but the party shouldn’t take victory for granted. As the Guardian’s senior political correspondent, Peter Walker, reports, Polanski has mounted an intensive campaign, but the scale of the challenge is clear from the numbers. Starmer won the seat by 11,500 votes in 2024, after Labour majorities of nearly 28,000 in 2019 and more than 30,500 in 2017.

You can read Peter’s report from this morning here:

Andy Burnham is in Berlin today where he will hold meetings with German chancellor Friedrich Merz. On the agenda is a new joint security partnership to counter sabotage, cyber-attacks and other hybrid threats, as well as support for Ukraine, instability in the Middle East, and disruption to global trade routes. We’re expecting to hear from the prime minister this afternoon.

The diplomatic row between Britain and Israel is escalating over the UK’s consular presence in East Jerusalem. Israel said the British consulate has “ceased to function” with 20 diplomats due to leave, but the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the building will remain open and renamed the “UK Mission”.

Here are some of the latest images from the Holborn and St Pancras constituency, which the Guardian’s head office is just on the boundary of:

Labour’s flagship changes to special education in England are at risk of unravelling because parents are rushing to secure support for their children before the system changes, new analysis has found.

The Institute for Government (IfG) thinktank says the government’s plans to largely replace education, health and care plans (EHCPs) in England with more widespread support in mainstream schools may be too optimistic and take longer to complete than its 2030 timeline.

The thinktank’s report calls on the government to review the timetable for the changes. And it suggests that if ministers do not act they “risk basing both their reforms and spending plans on assumptions that the system cannot deliver”.

The news will be seen as a sign that the government’s ambitious plans to overhaul the special education system did not reckon with the scale of worry among parents, many of whom appear to have acted to ensure support and avoid uncertainty in the future.

The Guardian recently reported that councils and schools have reported a surge in applications for EHCPs, with one school describing the level as “unreal” compared with previous years. Several councils are now projecting that at the current rates of increase, nearly one in 10 pupils will have an EHCP by 2029.

Amber Dellar, the author of the IfG report out this week, said the long rollout of the changes created a “moral hazard” that encouraged parents to apply for EHCPs now rather than wait for the new system.

The foreign secretary, ⁠Ed Miliband, has said Britain’s consulate general ⁠building in ⁠East Jerusalem ​will not be closing but will ⁠be known as a UK mission, remaining independent, operational ⁠and serving Palestinian people.

Israel had ​ordered the ‌British consulate ‌in East Jerusalem to close ‌on Thursday over the UK’s plans to impose sanctions on settlements in the West Bank.

Miliband said that having ‌withdrawn a number of staff and families in recent ​weeks, it would now work to build up its presence.

He said Britain would ⁠not take any reciprocal action ​against Israel ​while the ​two sides engaged in ​talks, ‌following speculation it ​could expel some Israeli diplomats from Britain.

Diplomats from other western countries had been worried about any closure setting a precedent, and suggested Britain had to respond strongly to the Israeli move because it had implications beyond the immediate dispute.

The consulate is separate from the UK embassy, based in Tel Aviv, and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza, where it provides consular services to Palestinians.

Israel had threatened to close it in protest at the UK’s decision to ban trade in goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, said Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused the governing Labour party of being hostile towards his country.

The French finance minister, Roland Lescure, said the UK could rejoin the EU “anytime” after Andy Burnham indicated a major review of Britain’s relationship with the bloc.

Lescure said it was up to the British public whether to return to the EU, telling the BBC that “if they’re willing to come back, they will have to decide”.

“But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime,” he added. Ben Quinn has the full report here.

As our political correspondent Aletha Adu reported last week, the prime minister opened the door to the UK rejoining the EU, saying Britain could “go all the way” as he prepares to reconsider Labour’s post-Brexit red lines.
